    The course is assessed (as Lecture 0 describes it) through five programming assignments in Python, graded in a competitive mode on accuracy and run time, and a final project in an implementation track (reproduce a published logistics paper) or a research track. Labs take place every two weeks. Check the current syllabus for exact weights and dates.

    Lecture 0 groups the course into five modules: background (LP, IP, branch and bound), classic logistics problems (TSP, VRP, matching, location, with a short look at computational complexity), TSP and cutting planes, VRP and column generation (branch and price), and a final module on heuristics for TSP and VRP, vehicle and crew scheduling, and collaborative logistics. This site covers the first three modules and the VRP formulations of Lecture 6.

    For $\min\ 5x_1+4x_2$, what is the cost at the LP optimum $x=(4/3,\,8/3)$? Give the value to two decimals if you like.

    Compute $5\cdot\tfrac43+4\cdot\tfrac83$.

    $\tfrac{20}{3}+\tfrac{32}{3}=\tfrac{52}{3}\approx17.33$. This is a lower bound on the integer optimum.

    Is $x=(1,3)$ a feasible plan for the integer program $4x_1+x_2\ge8$, $2x_1+2x_2\ge8$, $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$?

    Check the first inequality; the second holds comfortably.

    $4\cdot1+3=7\lt 8$, so the first inequality fails. Rounding the LP optimum to the nearest point is therefore not safe.

    The LP optimum has $x_2=8/3$. Branching on $x_2$ gives the children $x_2\le 2$ and $x_2\ge ?$. Fill in the missing whole number.

    It is the whole number just above $8/3\approx2.67$.

    $\lceil8/3\rceil=3$. The children are $x_2\le2$ and $x_2\ge3$. Whole-number values of $x_2$ lie in one of these two sets, and the fractional point $8/3$ lies in neither.

    The incumbent plan costs $18$. A sub-problem has a fractional LP optimum with cost $18.5$. In a minimisation, what should branch and bound do with this sub-problem?

    Every plan inside the sub-problem costs at least as much as its LP value.

    Every whole-number plan in the sub-problem costs at least $18.5$, which is more than $18$, so nothing in it can improve the incumbent. We prune it.

    The incumbent costs $18$. A sub-problem has a fractional LP optimum with cost $16.2$. What should happen?

    Is it possible that some whole-number plan inside costs less than $18$?

    The bound $16.2$ is below $18$, so a whole-number plan costing less than $18$ (for example $17$) could still hide inside. We cannot prune; we branch on a fractional variable.

    • Treat the LP relaxation as a bound (a lower bound for a minimisation), not as a plan.
    • Branch on a fractional variable, using $\le\lfloor v\rfloor$ and $\ge\lceil v\rceil$, so no whole-number plan is lost.
    • Rounding an LP answer and calling it optimal.
    • Pruning a sub-problem whose bound is below the incumbent: it may still hide a better plan.
    1. An IP is an LP plus whole-number requirements; dropping them gives the LP relaxation, whose optimal value is a bound (lower for a minimisation).
    2. Branch and bound solves a sequence of LPs, splitting on a fractional variable and pruning sub-problems that are infeasible, whole, or no better than the incumbent.
    3. Tighter relaxations (better formulations and cutting planes) mean fewer branches; this is the thread through Parts 1 to 6.

    Why is the LP relaxation's optimal value never above the IP optimum when minimising?

    Because LPs always have whole-number solutions.
    LP solutions are often fractional, as in the truck example.
    Because the relaxation minimises over a larger set that contains every IP plan.
    A minimum over a bigger set cannot be larger.
    Because the LP uses fewer variables.
    The relaxation keeps the same variables; it only drops the whole-number rule.

    The LP relaxation of a minimisation IP returns a solution with all variables whole. What follows?

    We must still branch on every variable.
    Branching is only needed on fractional variables.
    It is feasible but may not be optimal.
    It is optimal for the relaxation, whose value is a lower bound for the IP.
    It is optimal for the IP as well.
    It is a feasible plan whose cost equals the lower bound, so nothing can beat it.

    A node's LP relaxation turns out to be infeasible. What does branch and bound do?

    Discards the node: it contains no whole-number plans either.
    A plan of the node would be feasible for its relaxation, so an infeasible relaxation means no plans exist.
    Rounds some variables until it becomes feasible.
    Constraints cannot be repaired by rounding.
    Branches anyway on any variable.
    Branching on a problem with no feasible point only creates empty problems.

    Which choice correctly describes the children made from a fractional value $x_j=2.4$?

    $x_j\le 2.4$ and $x_j\ge 2.4$
    The children must exclude the fractional point; these keep it.
    $x_j\le2$ and $x_j\ge3$
    They remove the fractional band $2\lt x_j\lt3$ and keep every whole-number plan.
    $x_j=2$ and $x_j=3$
    That would lose plans with larger or smaller $x_j$, such as $x_j=5$.

    Location; where to put the depot.
    In the TSP the depot is already given.
    Routing; the order in which the customers are visited.
    The unknown is the sequence of the tour.
    Flow; the number of tonnes on each road.

    Only site 2, cost 13.
    Site 2 costs $9+3+1=13$ in total; compare every plan, including the one with the cheaper opening cost.
    Only site 1, cost 10.
    $5+1+4=10$, against $9+3+1=13$ for site 2 alone and $5+9+1+1=16$ for both.

    Which statement about an LP relaxation of a minimisation IP is correct?

    Its optimal value is an upper bound on the IP optimum.
    The relaxation has more choices, so its minimum is not larger.
    Its optimal value is a lower bound on the IP optimum.
    It minimises over a set containing every feasible plan of the IP.
    Its optimum is always the optimum of the IP after rounding.
    Rounding can give an infeasible or poor plan.

    The incumbent cost is 40. A node has LP value 37.5 (fractional). What should branch and bound do?

    Prune the node.
    Pruning needs the LP value to be at least 40.

    A plan costing between 37.5 and 40 may be inside, so the node cannot be discarded.

    It is fractional, so it is not a valid plan.

    Lecture 1 reviews linear programming: how an LP is written, what its feasible region looks like, what a corner point is in matrix language, and how the simplex method walks from corner to corner. Every later lecture (integer programs, branch and bound, even TSP) calls an LP solver as a building block, so this part is the engine room. For the fictional Kaveri Courier of Part 0, an LP is the kind of plan the owner can compute each day, and the running examples below (including the staff canteen) are small stand-ins for it.

    You need: Part −4 (sums, $Ax\ge b$, solving $Bx=b$, rank and independence) and Part −3 (turning a word problem into variables, objective and constraints, and drawing a two-variable LP).

    Writing an LP in canonical and standard form

    A linear programme (LP) minimises or maximises a linear objective subject to linear constraints, and it can always be rewritten in one fixed shape that algorithms like.

    Solvers and the simplex method of this part all expect that fixed shape, so you must convert any problem into it without errors.

    It is like filling in a form: the information is the same, but it only gets processed when it sits in the right boxes.

    A small diet problem

    Kaveri Courier also runs a small canteen for its drivers. The canteen buys two foods. Food 1 costs $3$ per portion and food 2 costs $2$. A portion of food 1 gives $2$ units of protein and $1$ unit of iron; a portion of food 2 gives $1$ unit of protein and $1$ of iron. Each day the meals must contain at least $8$ units of protein and at least $6$ units of iron. How many portions $x_1,x_2$ of each food minimise the cost?

    $$\min\ 3x_1+2x_2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad 2x_1+x_2\ge 8,\quad x_1+x_2\ge 6,\quad x_1,x_2\ge 0.$$

    This is already a linear programme: the objective and every constraint are sums of variables times constants.

    $$\min\ c^\top x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ax\ge b,\ \ x\ge 0.$$ All constraints are "$\ge$" and all variables are non-negative.

    $$\min\ c^\top x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ax=b,\ \ x\ge 0.$$ All constraints are equalities (with $b\ge0$ after multiplying rows by $-1$ if needed) and all variables are non-negative. Linear algebra works with equalities, so simplex needs this form.

    Converting to standard form

    Three rules do all the work.

    • A "$\ge$" constraint becomes an equality by subtracting a surplus variable $s\ge0$ that measures how far above the requirement you are: $2x_1+x_2\ge8$ becomes $2x_1+x_2-s_1=8$.
    • A "$\le$" constraint becomes an equality by adding a slack variable $s\ge0$ that measures unused room: $x_1+2x_2\le10$ becomes $x_1+2x_2+s=10$.
    • A maximisation is turned into a minimisation by flipping the sign of the objective: $\max f$ and $\min(-f)$ have the same optimal point, and the optimal values differ by a sign.

    The diet problem in standard form is $$\min\ 3x_1+2x_2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad 2x_1+x_2-s_1=8,\ \ x_1+x_2-s_2=6,\ \ x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2\ge0.$$ We now have 4 variables and 2 equations. The slack and surplus variables do not cost anything: they appear in the objective with coefficient $0$.

    Careful: surplus and slack have opposite signs: "$\ge$" gets $-s$, "$\le$" gets $+s$. Getting this backwards changes the problem. Check by asking: when the constraint is exactly tight, is $s=0$?
    Try it

    Pick each preset and slide the line value $k$. Find the best point of the running example $\max\,5x_1+3x_2$ ($x_1+x_2\le8$, $x_1+3x_2\le18$, $2x_1+x_2\le12$). Notice where the line last touches the shaded region.

    Solve the diet problem by checking its corner points.

    1. The constraint lines cross the axes and each other. Where $2x_1+x_2=8$ meets $x_1=0$: $(0,8)$. Where $x_1+x_2=6$ meets $x_2=0$: $(6,0)$.

      The feasible region is the area above both lines in the first quadrant: it is unbounded to the upper right, with three corners.

    2. The two lines meet where $2x_1+x_2=8$ and $x_1+x_2=6$: subtracting gives $x_1=2$, so $x_2=4$. Corner $(2,4)$.

      Each corner is where two boundary lines (or a line and an axis) meet.

    3. Costs: $(0,8)\to16$, $(2,4)\to6+8=14$, $(6,0)\to18$.

      A linear objective over a region with corners is best at a corner (Chapter 1.2).

    4. The minimum cost is $14$ at $x=(2,4)$: 2 portions of food 1 and 4 of food 2.

      Both constraints are tight there: $s_1=s_2=0$.

    Go deeper: free variables

    If a variable may be negative (a "free" variable), write it as the difference $x=x^+-x^-$ of two non-negative variables. The lectures later use this when a dual variable is unrestricted in sign.

    The LP $\min 4x_1+x_2$ s.t. $3x_1+x_2\ge9$, $x_1+2x_2\le10$, $x_1-x_2\le2$, $x\ge0$ is converted to standard form. How many variables does the standard form have?

    Each of the three inequalities needs its own slack or surplus variable.

    Two original variables plus one slack or surplus per inequality: $2+3=5$.

    In the LP above, what turns $x_1+2x_2\le10$ into an equality?

    At the tight point the extra variable must be 0, and it must never be negative.

    The left side is below 10 when not tight, so we add the missing amount: $x_1+2x_2+s=10$.

    Write $\max\,3x_1+2x_2$ as a minimisation. What is the coefficient of $x_1$ in the new objective?

    Multiply the whole objective by $-1$.

    $\max(3x_1+2x_2)$ is the same as $\min(-3x_1-2x_2)$, so the coefficient is $-3$.

    What is the minimum cost of the canteen diet problem in this chapter?

    Evaluate $3x_1+2x_2$ at the three corners $(0,8)$, $(2,4)$, $(6,0)$.

    Costs are $16$, $14$ and $18$. The minimum is $14$.

    Is the diet plan $x=(1,5)$ feasible?

    Check the protein constraint $2x_1+x_2\ge8$.

    Protein is $2\cdot1+5=7<8$, so it is infeasible even though iron is $1+5=6\ge6$.

    • Convert one constraint at a time and recheck that a tight constraint gives $s=0$.
    • Keep slack and surplus variables in the objective with coefficient 0.
    • Adding a surplus to a "$\le$" constraint (or a slack to a "$\ge$").
    • Forgetting to flip the sign of the objective when turning max into min.
    1. Any LP can be written as $\min c^\top x$ with $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$ by adding slacks, subtracting surpluses and flipping max to min.
    2. Slack and surplus variables measure unused room and excess; they are zero exactly when a constraint is tight.
    3. For two variables you can solve the LP by looking at corner points: the best value occurs at a corner.

    Which standard-form row comes from $5x_1+2x_2\ge20$?

    $5x_1+2x_2+s=20$
    Adding $s\ge0$ forces the left side to be at most 20, the wrong direction for a "$\ge$" constraint.
    $5x_1+2x_2-s=20$, $s\ge0$
    $s$ is the amount by which the left side exceeds 20.
    $5x_1+2x_2=20$
    That would forbid solutions that exceed the requirement.

    An LP in standard form has 3 equality constraints and 7 variables. How many of the variables does a basic solution set to zero?

    3
    Three variables are basic in the next chapters; count the rest.
    4
    $7-3=4$ non-basic variables are zero.
    7
    That would set every variable to zero.

    If $\max f(x)$ has optimal value $12$, what is the optimal value of the equivalent $\min(-f(x))$?

    12
    The sign of the objective was flipped.
    −12
    The optimal point is the same but the value is negated.
    0
    The values are linked, not cancelled.

    Polyhedra, corners and the four outcomes

    The feasible region of an LP is a polyhedron: the points satisfying a list of linear inequalities. Its corners are called extreme points, and an LP can end in exactly four ways.

    Knowing the shape explains why simplex only needs to look at corners and why a solver can report "infeasible" or "unbounded".

    It is like a cut gemstone: the sparkle (the best value) is always on a corner or a whole flat edge, never in the middle of a face.

    Each linear inequality $a^\top x\le\beta$ cuts space in half: the points on one side of a line (in the plane) or plane (in 3D) are allowed. The set of points obeying all the constraints at once is their overlap.

    A halfspace is a set $\{x: a^\top x\le\beta\}$. A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many halfspaces: $P=\{x: Ax\le b\}$. A bounded polyhedron is a polytope.

    A convex combination of points $x^1,\dots,x^k$ is $\sum_i\lambda_ix^i$ with all $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. The convex hull is the set of all such combinations: the shape you get by stretching a rubber band around the points. A set is convex if it contains the straight segment between any two of its points.

    A point of a convex set is an extreme point (a corner) if it is not a convex combination of two other points of the set, i.e. it does not lie in the interior of any segment inside the set.

    A linear programme either (1) is infeasible (empty region), (2) is unbounded (the objective improves forever), (3) has a unique optimal solution at a corner, or (4) has many optimal solutions, a whole edge of the region (the objective line is parallel to that edge). In (3) and (4) an optimum is always attained at a corner of the region, whenever the region has corners.

    Try it

    Cycle through the four presets. For each one, slide the objective line $k$ and decide: where does the line stop touching the region, and what does that mean? Notice that "Many optima" and "Unique optimum" use the same region but different objective directions.

    Unbounded regions and cones

    A region can run off to infinity. The directions in which it runs are described by a cone: a set closed under adding vectors and scaling by positive numbers. A direction $d\ne0$ is a direction of $P=\{Ax\le b\}$ if starting at any point of $P$ and moving along $d$ forever keeps you inside, which happens exactly when $Ad\le0$. The cone's tip sits at the origin, and its edges are the extreme directions, the directions that cannot be built from others.

    Every polyhedron with at least one corner is the sum of a polytope and a cone: every point is (a convex combination of extreme points) $+$ (a non-negative combination of extreme directions).

    Careful: "extreme point" and "corner point" mean the same thing here, but "extreme direction" is a different object: it describes how the region extends to infinity, not where it ends.

    The region of the running example has corners $(0,0),(6,0),(4,4),(3,5),(0,6)$. Is $(4,2)$ a convex combination of $(6,0)$ and $(0,6)$, and is it inside the region?

    1. Solve $\lambda(6,0)+(1-\lambda)(0,6)=(4,2)$. First coordinate: $6\lambda=4$, so $\lambda=\tfrac23$.

      The first coordinate fixes $\lambda$; the second coordinate must then agree.

    2. Second coordinate: $6(1-\lambda)=6\cdot\tfrac13=2$. It matches, and $0\le\lambda\le1$.

      Both coordinates agree, so $(4,2)$ lies on the segment.

    3. Inside the region: $4+2=6\le8$, $\ 4+6=10\le18$, $\ 8+2=10\le12$, and both coordinates are $\ge0$.

      Membership means every constraint holds.

    Go deeper: why the optimum is at a corner

    If an optimal point were strictly inside a segment of feasible points, then moving along the segment in the improving direction of the linear objective would improve it, a contradiction, unless the objective is flat along the segment. In that flat case the whole segment is optimal, including its endpoints. Repeating this argument moves you to a corner.

    How many corner points does the region $x_1+x_2\le8$, $x_1+3x_2\le18$, $2x_1+x_2\le12$, $x\ge0$ have?

    Walk around the boundary and list each turning point, starting at the origin.

    $(0,0)$, $(6,0)$, $(4,4)$, $(3,5)$ and $(0,6)$: five corners.

    $\max\ x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\le2$, $x_1+x_2\ge2$, $x\ge0$. What happens?

    Can you move to larger $x_1$ and $x_2$ while keeping $x_1-x_2\le2$?

    Take $x_1=x_2=t$: both constraints hold for every $t\ge1$, and the objective $2t$ grows without limit.

    Find $\lambda$ so that $\lambda(6,0)+(1-\lambda)(0,6)=(4,2)$.

    Look at the first coordinate only.

    $6\lambda=4$, so $\lambda=2/3$; check the second coordinate: $6\cdot\tfrac13=2$.

    Is $(3.5,4.5)$ an extreme point of the running region? It is the midpoint of $(4,4)$ and $(3,5)$.

    An extreme point cannot be the midpoint of two other points of the region.

    It is the midpoint of two feasible points, so it is not extreme: it lies in the middle of an edge.

    For the running region, what is the maximum of $2x_1+2x_2$?

    This objective is parallel to the constraint $x_1+x_2\le8$. Evaluate it at $(4,4)$ and $(3,5)$.

    $2(4+4)=16$ and $2(3+5)=16$: the whole edge between them is optimal, with value $16$.

    • Sketch the region and list its corners before running any algorithm.
    • Ask the four-outcome question first: is it empty, unbounded, unique or tied?
    • Assuming the optimum is always unique.
    • Calling a point on an edge a corner.
    1. The feasible region of an LP is a polyhedron, an intersection of halfspaces, and it is convex.
    2. An LP is infeasible, unbounded, uniquely solved at a corner, or solved along a whole edge; the optimum is attained at a corner whenever corners exist.
    3. Extreme points are the corners; extreme directions describe how an unbounded region runs off to infinity.

    The objective line of a maximisation is parallel to one edge of the region, and that edge is the last one touched. What can you conclude?

    The LP is infeasible.
    The line touches the region, so points exist.
    The LP is unbounded.
    The line stops touching the region, so the value is capped.
    Every point of that edge is optimal: there are many optimal solutions.
    The objective has the same value along the edge.

    Which set is NOT convex?

    A triangle with its inside.
    Any segment between two of its points stays inside.
    A halfplane $\{x_1+x_2\le 3\}$.
    A halfplane contains the segment between two of its points.
    The circle line $x_1^2+x_2^2=1$ (only the curve, not the disc).
    The midpoint of two points on the curve is inside it, not on it.

    A region is empty. A solver reports:

    Unbounded
    Unbounded needs feasible points to move along.
    Infeasible
    No point satisfies all constraints.
    Optimal with value 0
    There is no feasible point to attain any value.

    Basic feasible solutions: corners in matrix language

    In standard form $Ax=b$, a corner of the region corresponds to choosing $m$ independent columns of $A$ (a basis), setting every other variable to zero and solving for the rest.

    This turns the geometric idea "go to a corner" into a computation a computer can do: solve a small linear system.

    It is like picking which $m$ of many levers to hold: you set all others to zero and the chosen levers are forced to specific positions.

    Row view and column view

    Take the running example and write it in standard form with slack variables $s_1,s_2,s_3$ for the three constraints: $$x_1+x_2+s_1=8,\qquad x_1+3x_2+s_2=18,\qquad 2x_1+x_2+s_3=12.$$ The matrix has $m=3$ rows and $n=5$ columns, $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1&0&0\\1&3&0&1&0\\2&1&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

    The row view reads each equation as a halfspace boundary in the $(x_1,x_2)$ picture: that is the polygon of the last chapter. The column view reads $Ax=b$ as "mix the five columns of $A$ in amounts $x_j$ to produce the target $b$" (as in Part −4). Simplex works in the column view.

    Pick $m$ linearly independent columns of $A$ and call them the matrix $B$ (the basis); the other columns form $N$. Set all non-basic variables to $0$ and solve $Bx_B=b$, i.e. $x_B=B^{-1}b$. The result is a basic solution. If also $x_B\ge0$ it is a basic feasible solution (BFS).

    A point is a basic feasible solution of $\{x: Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$ if and only if it is an extreme point (corner) of that set.

    So the corners of the polygon are exactly the basic feasible solutions. There are at most $\binom{n}{m}$ bases, here $\binom53=10$. Some bases give negative values: those are points where the constraint lines meet outside the region.

    Try it

    Click through all 10 bases. For each, read the values of $x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2,s_3$ and see where the point lands. Notice which bases give a green dot on a corner and which give a red point outside the region, and which variable is negative there.

    Compute the basic solution for the basis $\{x_1,x_2,s_2\}$, and decide whether it is feasible.

    1. Non-basic variables $s_1=s_3=0$. The equations become $x_1+x_2=8$, $\ x_1+3x_2+s_2=18$, $\ 2x_1+x_2=12$.

      Setting the non-basic variables to zero deletes their columns.

    2. The first and third equations give $x_1=4$ (subtract: $x_1=12-8$), so $x_2=4$.

      Two equations in two unknowns, solved as in Part −4.

    3. The second equation gives $s_2=18-4-12=2$.

      The remaining variable is determined by the remaining equation.

    4. All values $(4,4,0,2,0)$ are $\ge0$: it is a BFS, the corner $(4,4)$.

      Feasible means non-negative; basic means built from a basis.

    Careful: a basic solution need not be feasible. The basis $\{x_1,x_2,s_1\}$ gives $x=(3.6,4.8)$ and $s_1=-0.4$: the lines $x_1+3x_2=18$ and $2x_1+x_2=12$ meet at a point that violates $x_1+x_2\le8$.
    Go deeper: degeneracy

    If a basic feasible solution has a basic variable equal to zero, it is degenerate: more than $n-m$ of the variables are zero, so several different bases describe the same corner. Simplex can then take a step of length zero. Degeneracy does not change the theory but explains why a corner can be "visited" by several bases.

    An LP in standard form has 3 constraints and 5 variables. At most how many bases (choices of 3 columns) are there?

    Count the ways to choose 3 of 5: $\binom53$.

    $\binom53=\frac{5\cdot4}{2}=10$.

    In the running LP, for the basis $\{x_1,x_2,s_2\}$ what is the value of $s_2$?

    First find $x_1,x_2$ from the equations that do not contain $s_2$, then use $x_1+3x_2+s_2=18$.

    $x_1=x_2=4$, so $s_2=18-4-12=2$.

    Is the basic solution for $\{x_1,x_2,s_1\}$ feasible? (It has $x_1=3.6$, $x_2=4.8$.)

    Compute $s_1=8-x_1-x_2$.

    $s_1=8-3.6-4.8=-0.4<0$, so it is not feasible.

    For the basis $\{x_1,s_1,s_2\}$ (so $x_2=s_3=0$), what is $s_2$?

    The equation $2x_1=12$ gives $x_1$. Then use $x_1+3x_2+s_2=18$.

    $x_1=6$, so $s_2=18-6=12$. Also $s_1=8-6=2$: the corner $(6,0)$.

    Of the 10 bases of the running LP, how many are basic feasible solutions (corners)?

    The region has five corners, and each corner comes from at least one basis.

    Five: $(0,0),(6,0),(4,4),(3,5),(0,6)$. The other five bases give points outside the region.

    • Choose the basis, set the rest to zero, solve a square system, then check signs.
    • Link every BFS back to a corner in the picture.
    • Treating a basic solution as automatically feasible.
    • Choosing columns that are linearly dependent (then $B$ has no inverse).
    1. A basis is a set of $m$ independent columns; the basic solution sets the other variables to 0 and solves $Bx_B=b$.
    2. A basic solution that is also non-negative is a BFS, and BFS are exactly the corners of the feasible region.
    3. With $n$ variables and $m$ equations there are at most $\binom nm$ corners, which is why we need a smart way to search them.

    A standard-form LP has $m=4$ constraints and $n=9$ variables. How many variables are zero in a non-degenerate BFS?

    4
    Four variables are basic and may be non-zero.
    5
    $n-m=5$ non-basic variables are zero.
    9
    That would be the zero vector, which is not generally feasible.

    A basic solution has a negative value for one basic variable. What does it represent?

    A corner of the feasible region.
    Corners need all variables $\ge0$.
    The meeting point of boundary lines that lies outside the feasible region.
    It satisfies the equations but breaks a non-negativity requirement.
    An optimal solution.
    Optimal solutions must be feasible.

    Why is it enough to search over basic feasible solutions?

    They are the only feasible points.
    There are infinitely many feasible points.
    If an LP has an optimum, one is attained at a corner, and corners are the BFS.
    That is the "optimum at a corner" fact combined with BFS = extreme point.
    Non-basic variables are always optimal at zero.
    That is not true in general; they are only zero at the current corner.

    The simplex method: walking from corner to corner

    Simplex starts at a corner and repeatedly moves along an edge to a neighbouring corner that improves the objective, stopping when no neighbour is better.

    It avoids checking all $\binom nm$ corners, and it is the algorithm behind every LP solved inside branch and bound in this course.

    It is like climbing a rock face by always stepping to a higher hold along the edge you are on, until every neighbouring hold is lower.

    At a BFS with basis $B$ and non-basic columns $N$, the objective can be written purely in the non-basic variables. Since $x_B=B^{-1}b-B^{-1}Nx_N$, $$z=c_B^\top B^{-1}b+\big(c_N^\top-c_B^\top B^{-1}N\big)x_N.$$ The first term is the current objective value. The bracket is a list of numbers, one per non-basic variable.

    The reduced cost of a non-basic variable $x_j$ is $$\bar c_j=c_j-c_B^\top B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}.$$ It is the change in the objective per unit increase of $x_j$ when the basic variables adjust to keep $Ax=b$.

    If $x$ is a BFS (for a minimisation) and $\bar c_j\ge0$ for every non-basic $j$, then $x$ is optimal: raising any non-basic variable can only increase the objective.

    One simplex step

    If some non-basic $x_j$ has $\bar c_j<0$, raising it lowers the objective. Raise $x_j$ from $0$ to $\eta$ and let the basic variables adapt: the point moves by $\eta d$ with $d_N=e_j$ (a 1 in position $j$, zeros elsewhere) and $d_B=-B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$. The objective changes by $\eta\bar c_j$.

    How far? Keep $x_B+\eta d_B\ge0$. Only entries with $(d_B)_k<0$ shrink, and entry $k$ reaches zero at $\eta=\frac{(x_B)_k}{-(d_B)_k}$. The step length is the smallest of these ratios, the minimum ratio test. The basic variable that hits zero leaves the basis and $x_j$ enters. If no entry of $d_B$ is negative, nothing stops the step: the LP is unbounded.

    1. Start from a basic feasible solution with basis $B$.
    2. Compute the reduced costs $\bar c_N^\top=c_N^\top-c_B^\top B^{-1}N$.
    3. If $\bar c_N\ge0$, stop: $x$ is optimal.
    4. Otherwise pick $j$ with $\bar c_j<0$ and let $d_B=-B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$.
    5. If $d_B\ge0$, stop: the LP is unbounded.
    6. Otherwise $\eta=\min\{(x_B)_k/(-(d_B)_k): (d_B)_k<0\}$; the minimising $k$ leaves the basis.
    7. Replace the leaving column by $A_{\cdot j}$, recompute $x_B=B^{-1}b$ and go to step 2.
    Try it

    Press the "Enter" buttons to run simplex on the running LP. First take $x_1$, then $x_2$. Then Reset and take $x_2$ first. Notice that the two paths differ but end at the same optimal corner, and that every step improves the objective.

    Run simplex on $\min\ -5x_1-3x_2$ with $x_1+x_2+s_1=8$, $\ x_1+3x_2+s_2=18$, $\ 2x_1+x_2+s_3=12$, starting from the basis of slacks $\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}$.

    1. Start: $x=(0,0)$, $s=(8,18,12)$, objective $0$. The basis is slacks, so $c_B=0$ and the reduced costs are the original costs: $\bar c_{x_1}=-5$, $\bar c_{x_2}=-3$.

      With $c_B=0$ the formula gives $\bar c_j=c_j$.

    2. Enter $x_1$ (most negative). Then $d_B=-(1,1,2)$. Ratios: $8/1=8$, $18/1=18$, $12/2=6$. The smallest is $6$, so $s_3$ leaves.

      The third constraint $2x_1\le12$ is the first to become tight.

    3. New corner $(6,0)$: $s=(2,12,0)$, objective $-5\cdot6=-30$. New reduced costs: $\bar c_{x_2}=-\tfrac12$ and $\bar c_{s_3}=\tfrac52$.

      Raising $x_2$ still helps (its reduced cost is negative); raising $s_3$ would hurt.

    4. Enter $x_2$. The basis is $\{s_1,s_2,x_1\}$. The ratios are $s_1$: $4$, $s_2$: $4.8$, $x_1$: $12$. The smallest is $4$, so $s_1$ leaves.

      The constraint $x_1+x_2\le8$ becomes tight first.

    5. New corner $(4,4)$, objective $-32$. Reduced costs: $\bar c_{s_1}=1$, $\bar c_{s_3}=2$, both $\ge0$: optimal. The maximum profit is $32$.

      All reduced costs non-negative means no neighbouring corner is better.

    Careful: simplex moves along edges, so each step lands on a neighbouring corner, never across the interior. The reduced cost tells you the rate of change; the ratio test tells you how far you can go before a constraint blocks you.
    Go deeper: the tableau and what "reduced cost" is made of

    The table the lecture draws (reduced costs on top, then rows $x_B$) is just $c-c_B^\top B^{-1}A$ and $B^{-1}A$ written side by side, so it stores everything one step needs. The numbers $y^\top=c_B^\top B^{-1}$ turn out to be the dual variables. Here (taking the sign flip from max to min into account) $y=(1,0,2)$ and $y^\top b=8+24=32$, matching the optimal profit. That is the story of Lecture 2.

    At the corner $(6,0)$ of the running LP (basis $\{s_1,s_2,x_1\}$), what is the reduced cost of $x_2$?

    Raise $x_2$ by 1. Then $x_1$ must drop by $\tfrac12$ to keep $2x_1+x_2=12$.

    Objective $-5x_1-3x_2$ changes by $-5(-\tfrac12)-3(1)=2.5-3=-0.5$.

    Start at the origin and choose $x_2$ to enter. What is the step length from the ratio test? (Constraints: $x_1+x_2\le8$, $x_1+3x_2\le18$, $2x_1+x_2\le12$.)

    With $x_1=0$ the constraints read $x_2\le8$, $3x_2\le18$, $x_2\le12$.

    The limits are $8$, $6$ and $12$. The smallest is $6$, so $x_2$ rises to $6$ and $s_2$ leaves.

    From the origin, $x_1$ enters with step length $6$ and reduced cost $-5$. By how much does the objective $-5x_1-3x_2$ change?

    Change = step length times reduced cost.

    $6\cdot(-5)=-30$, taking the objective from $0$ to $-30$.

    A variable has a negative reduced cost, and every entry of $d_B=-B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$ is $\ge0$. What does that tell you?

    If no basic variable ever decreases, what stops the step?

    Nothing hits zero, so $x_j$ can grow forever while the objective keeps falling: unbounded.

    Using "most negative reduced cost enters", how many simplex iterations take the running LP from the origin to its optimum?

    Follow the example: origin, then $(6,0)$, then...

    Origin $\to(6,0)\to(4,4)$: two iterations.

    • Check the sign of every reduced cost before stopping.
    • Run the ratio test only over entries where $d_B$ is negative.
    • Stopping when one reduced cost is non-negative but another is negative.
    • Dividing by a positive entry in the ratio test (that entry does not limit the step).
    1. Simplex moves between neighbouring BFS: pick a non-basic variable with negative reduced cost, move until a basic variable hits zero, swap them.
    2. All reduced costs $\ge0$ proves optimality for a minimisation; $d_B\ge0$ with a negative reduced cost proves unboundedness.
    3. Each step changes the objective by (step length) $\times$ (reduced cost), so with non-zero steps the objective strictly improves.

    At a BFS, all reduced costs of the non-basic variables are positive. What do you conclude?

    The LP is unbounded.
    Unboundedness needs a negative reduced cost.
    The BFS is optimal (and uniquely so, if all are strictly positive).
    Every direction away from it increases the objective.
    Simplex must take another step.
    A step is only possible with a negative reduced cost.

    In the ratio test, the basic variable values are $(4,6,3)$ and the direction entries $d_B$ are $(-2,1,-1)$. Which basic variable leaves and what is the step length?

    The second, step 6.
    Its direction entry is positive, so that variable grows and does not limit the step.
    The third, step 3.
    Compute the ratio for the first variable too, and take the smaller one.
    The first, step 2.
    Only the first and third entries are negative. Their ratios are $4/2=2$ and $3/1=3$, and the smaller one, 2, decides.

    At the origin of the running LP, why does $x_1$ entering stop at step length 6 and not 8?

    The objective stops improving at 6.
    The step is limited by feasibility, not by the objective.
    The constraint $2x_1+x_2\le12$ becomes tight at $x_1=6$, before $x_1+x_2\le8$ does at 8.
    The minimum ratio is the first constraint to be hit.
    The reduced cost is $-6$.
    The reduced cost of $x_1$ is $-5$; the 6 comes from the ratio test.

    Converting $2x_1+x_2\ge8$ to standard form gives:

    $2x_1+x_2+s=8$
    That is the form for "at most".
    $2x_1+x_2-s=8$ with $s\ge0$
    $s$ measures the excess over 8.
    $2x_1+x_2=8+s$ with $s\le0$
    Slack and surplus variables are non-negative by convention.

    A region is the overlap of finitely many halfspaces. What is it called?

    A cone
    A cone has its tip at the origin and is closed under positive scaling.
    A polyhedron
    An intersection of finitely many halfspaces.
    A basis
    A basis is a set of columns, not a region.

    $Bx_B=b$ with $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=(4,9)$. What is $x_B$?

    $(3,2)$
    Check the sign of the second entry.
    $(3,-2)$
    $B^{-1}b$: the second entry is negative, so this basic solution would not be feasible.
    $(-3,2)$
    Substitute back into $2x_1+x_2=4$.

    Which statement about simplex is true for a minimisation?

    It stops when any reduced cost is non-negative.
    It must wait for all of them.
    It stops when all non-basic reduced costs are non-negative.
    Then no neighbouring corner improves the objective.
    It picks the variable with the largest positive reduced cost.
    A positive reduced cost makes the objective worse.

    Lecture 2 finishes the LP toolkit. It shows how simplex copes with upper and lower bounds on variables, how every LP has a mirror-image dual LP whose prices certify optimality, how the dual simplex method repairs a solution after the data change, and how to read from the final answer what happens when costs or right-hand sides move. Integer programming (Parts 3 and 4) re-solves LPs thousands of times, and these tools are why that is affordable.

    You need: Part 1 (standard form, basic feasible solutions, reduced costs, the simplex step and ratio test, and the running LP $\max 5x_1+3x_2$ whose optimum is $32$ at $(4,4)$), and Part −4 (solving small linear systems and reading $B^{-1}b$).

    Simplex with upper and lower bounds

    When variables carry bounds $\ell\le x\le u$, simplex keeps every non-basic variable parked at one of its two bounds (not always at zero) and needs only one extra rule in the ratio test: an entering variable may run into its own opposite bound before any basic variable is blocked.

    Bounds appear everywhere in logistics: a van can take at most so many parcels, an arc has a capacity, a binary variable lives in $[0,1]$. Branch and bound (Part 4) tightens bounds all the time, so the LP solver must treat them cheaply.

    It is like a lift with a floor and a ceiling: a passenger can wait at the bottom or the top, and when the lift moves, the trip may simply end at the other end of the shaft instead of at a floor in between.

    A dispatch problem with caps

    A depot sends parcels with two vans. Van 1 earns $3$ units of profit per parcel and can take at most $4$; van 2 earns $2$ per parcel and can take at most $3$. The loading bay can handle $5$ parcels per hour in total. With $x_1,x_2$ the numbers of parcels, $$\max\ 3x_1+2x_2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_1+x_2\le5,\quad 0\le x_1\le4,\quad 0\le x_2\le3.$$ Written as a minimisation with a slack $s\ge0$ for the bay, this is $\min\,-3x_1-2x_2$ with $x_1+x_2+s=5$ and bounds $0\le x_1\le4$, $0\le x_2\le3$, $0\le s$.

    The obvious route is to turn each bound into a row of its own. For $n$ variables with both bounds, that adds $2n$ rows and $2n$ slack variables, so $m+2n$ rows and $3n$ variables. Every simplex step then works with a much bigger basis, for a fact that is nearly free to handle directly.

    The bounded LP is $\min c^\top x$ s.t. $Ax=b$, $\ell\le x\le u$. A basis $B$ is again $m$ independent columns. Every non-basic variable is fixed at a bound: those at their lower bound form $N_\ell$, those at their upper bound form $N_u$. The basic variables follow from the equations: $$x_B=B^{-1}\big(b-N_\ell\,\ell_{N_\ell}-N_u\,u_{N_u}\big).$$ If also $\ell_B\le x_B\le u_B$ the point is a basic feasible solution, and these are exactly the corners of the bounded region.

    When is a corner optimal?

    The reduced cost $\bar c_j=c_j-c_B^\top B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$ keeps its meaning: it is the change in the objective per unit increase of $x_j$ while the basic variables adjust. A variable at its lower bound can only increase; one at its upper bound can only decrease. So:

    A basic feasible solution is optimal if $\bar c_j\ge0$ for every non-basic $x_j$ at its lower bound and $\bar c_j\le0$ for every non-basic $x_j$ at its upper bound.

    Why: raising a variable with $\bar c_j\ge0$ from its lower bound cannot lower the cost, and lowering a variable with $\bar c_j\le0$ from its upper bound cannot lower it either.

    The step, with three possible limits

    Suppose $x_j$ sits at its lower bound with $\bar c_j\lt0$. Raise it by $\eta$; the basic variables move by $\eta d_B$ with $d_B=-B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$ (if $x_j$ is at its upper bound and $\bar c_j\gt0$, lower it and use $d_B=+B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$). The step length $\eta$ is the smallest of three kinds of limit:

    • a basic variable with $(d_B)_k\lt0$ falls to its lower bound: $\eta\le\dfrac{(x_B-\ell_B)_k}{-(d_B)_k}$;
    • a basic variable with $(d_B)_k\gt0$ rises to its upper bound: $\eta\le\dfrac{(u_B-x_B)_k}{(d_B)_k}$;
    • the entering variable reaches its own other bound: $\eta\le u_j-\ell_j$.

    If a basic variable is the winner it leaves the basis, at whichever bound it hit. If the third limit wins, the basis does not change at all: $x_j$ just jumps from one bound to the other, a bound flip. If no limit is finite, the LP is unbounded.

    Try it

    Run the dispatch problem. Raise $x_1$ first and read the step test: is the step stopped by the bay slack $s$ or by $x_1$'s own cap? Then continue until the readout says optimal. Reset and try the other entering order. Notice that one step is a bound flip with no change of basis, and that at the end $x_1$ stays at its upper bound.

    Solve $\min\,-3x_1-2x_2$ with $x_1+x_2+s=5$, $\ 0\le x_1\le4$, $0\le x_2\le3$, $s\ge0$, starting from the basis $\{s\}$ with $x_1,x_2$ at their lower bounds.

    1. Start: $x_1=x_2=0$, so $s=5$ and the objective is $0$. With $c_B=0$ the reduced costs are $\bar c_{x_1}=-3$, $\bar c_{x_2}=-2$. Both variables are at their lower bounds with negative reduced cost, so both can improve.

      At a lower bound, a negative reduced cost means that raising the variable lowers the cost.

    2. Enter $x_1$. Limits: $s=5-\eta\ge0$ gives $\eta\le5$; the cap on $x_1$ gives $\eta\le4-0=4$. The smaller is $4$, and it is the entering variable's own cap.

      The bay still has room when $x_1$ hits its cap, so no basic variable leaves.

    3. Bound flip: $x_1=4$ is now non-basic at its upper bound; $s=1$; objective $-12$. The basis is still $\{s\}$ with $y=c_s/1=0$, so $\bar c_{x_1}=-3\le0$ (fine at an upper bound) and $\bar c_{x_2}=-2\lt0$ at a lower bound: $x_2$ can still improve.

      At an upper bound the sign condition flips: we need $\bar c\le0$, and $-3$ passes.

    4. Enter $x_2$. Limits: $s=1-\eta\ge0$ gives $1$; its own cap gives $3$. The smaller is $1$, so $s$ leaves (at $0$) and $x_2$ enters at value $1$.

      Now the bay constraint is tight: $4+1=5$.

    5. Corner $(x_1,x_2)=(4,1)$, objective $-14$. New basis $\{x_2\}$: $y=c_{x_2}/1=-2$. Then $\bar c_s=0-(-2)(1)=2\ge0$ (at its lower bound, good) and $\bar c_{x_1}=-3-(-2)(1)=-1\le0$ (at its upper bound, good). Optimal: maximum profit $14$.

      Both sign conditions of the optimality theorem hold; a variable can be optimal sitting at either bound.

    Careful: the sign test depends on where the variable sits. A positive reduced cost at an upper bound is a chance to improve (lower the variable), not a sign of optimality. Check each non-basic variable against the condition for its own bound.
    Go deeper: nonzero lower bounds and free variables

    A lower bound $\ell_j\ne0$ is handled by the same formulas; only the starting point moves. A variable with no bounds at all can be left basic permanently once it enters, since it never blocks a step. Solvers such as Gurobi apply exactly this bounded simplex internally, which is why setting lb and ub on variables is better than adding rows.

    In the dispatch problem, $x_1$ sits at its upper bound $4$, $x_2$ at its lower bound $0$, and the slack $s$ is basic in $x_1+x_2+s=5$. What is $s$?

    Substitute the two parked values and solve for $s$.

    $s=5-4-0=1$.

    An LP has $m=4$ equality rows and $n=6$ variables, each with a lower and an upper bound. If every bound were written as an extra row, how many rows ($m+2n$) would the system have?

    Two extra rows per variable.

    $4+2\cdot6=16$ rows. Bounded simplex keeps the basis at size $m=4$.

    In a minimisation, a non-basic variable sits at its upper bound and has $\bar c_j=-1$. Does this variable satisfy the optimality condition (no improvement is available through it)?

    It can only decrease from its upper bound. What does lowering it by one unit do to the cost when $\bar c_j=-1$?

    Lowering by one unit changes the cost by $-\bar c_j=+1$: worse. The condition for a variable at an upper bound is $\bar c_j\le0$, which holds.

    State: $x_1=4$ at its upper bound, $s=1$ basic, $x_2$ at $0$ with cap $3$, row $x_1+x_2+s=5$. $x_2$ enters. What is the step length?

    Compare how far $x_2$ can rise before $s$ reaches $0$ with its own range $u_2-\ell_2$.

    $s$ allows $1$, the cap allows $3$. The step is $\min(1,3)=1$.

    Row $x_1+x_2+x_3=10$ with $x_1$ basic, $x_2$ non-basic at its upper bound $3$, $x_3$ non-basic at its lower bound $1$. Find $x_1$.

    $x_B=B^{-1}(b-\text{contribution of the non-basic columns at their bounds})$.

    $x_1=10-3-1=6$.

    • Record, for each non-basic variable, whether it is at its lower or upper bound before computing $x_B$ and the reduced costs.
    • Include "$u_j-\ell_j$" as a candidate in every ratio test.
    • Assuming non-basic variables are always zero.
    • Declaring optimality because a reduced cost is positive without checking whether the variable is at an upper bound.
    1. With bounds, non-basic variables rest at their lower or upper bound, and $x_B=B^{-1}(b-N_\ell\ell-N_uu)$ gives the basic variables.
    2. Optimality needs $\bar c_j\ge0$ at lower bounds and $\bar c_j\le0$ at upper bounds.
    3. The ratio test has three kinds of limit; when the entering variable's own range wins, it flips bound and the basis stays the same.

    In a minimisation, a non-basic variable at its upper bound has $\bar c_j=+2$. What is true?

    The current point is optimal for this variable.
    That sign is the optimal one for a variable at a lower bound, not an upper bound.
    Lowering it improves the objective, so it is a candidate to move.
    Lowering by one unit changes the cost by $-2$.
    The LP is unbounded.
    Unboundedness needs a direction with no limit; here the variable has a finite range.

    An entering variable has range $u_j-\ell_j=2$, and every basic variable allows a step of at least 3. What happens?

    A basic variable leaves the basis.
    No basic variable is the first to be blocked.
    The LP is unbounded.
    The step is limited by $2$, which is finite.
    The variable flips to its other bound and the basis does not change.
    The smallest limit is the variable's own range.

    Row $x_1+2x_2+x_3=12$, with $x_1$ basic, $x_2$ non-basic at its upper bound $4$ and $x_3$ non-basic at its lower bound $0$. What is $x_1$?

    12
    That ignores the contribution of $x_2$ at its upper bound.
    8
    Remember the coefficient $2$ in front of $x_2$.
    4
    $12-2\cdot4-0=4$.

    Duality: writing the dual and proving it is a bound

    Every LP (the primal) has a partner LP (the dual) built from the same numbers; any feasible solution of one bounds the optimal value of the other, and at the optimum the two values are equal.

    The dual gives a cheap certificate that a solution is optimal, it reveals the prices of resources (Chapter 2.4), and it is the basis of the dual simplex method and of the bounds used in branch and bound.

    It is like a canteen manager and a pill seller: the manager hunts for the cheapest meals that satisfy the nutrition rules, the seller hunts for the highest prices for nutrients that still beat the food, and at the optimum their bills agree to the last unit.

    A canteen and a pill seller

    Recall the canteen of Kaveri Courier from Part 1: portions $x_1,x_2$ of two foods at costs $3$ and $2$, with $$\min\ 3x_1+2x_2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad 2x_1+x_2\ge8\ \ (\text{protein}),\quad x_1+x_2\ge6\ \ (\text{iron}),\quad x\ge0.$$ Its best plan is $x=(2,4)$ at cost $14$.

    A pharmacist offers to sell pure protein units at price $y_1$ and pure iron units at price $y_2$, to replace food altogether. She wants the largest income from the canteen's needs: $8y_1+6y_2$. But the canteen will only buy pills if they are no dearer than the food they replace. A portion of food 1 provides $2$ protein and $1$ iron, so its pill equivalent costs $2y_1+y_2$, and that must not exceed the food's price $3$. Likewise for food 2. So she solves $$\max\ 8y_1+6y_2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad 2y_1+y_2\le3,\quad y_1+y_2\le2,\quad y\ge0.$$ The best prices are $y=(1,1)$: income $8+6=14$, exactly the canteen's best cost.

    $$\text{Primal:}\ \min\ c^\top x\ \ \text{s.t. }Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\qquad\qquad\text{Dual:}\ \max\ b^\top y\ \ \text{s.t. }A^\top y\le c,\ y\ge0$$

    One dual variable $y_i$ per primal constraint; one dual constraint per primal variable (column $A_{\cdot j}$ against cost $c_j$). The dual of the dual is the primal. Dual variables are called shadow prices, or marginal prices: the value one extra unit of the right-hand side is worth.

    Careful: dual row $j$ always uses column $j$ of $A$ against the cost $c_j$ of that variable. For the canteen, row 1 is $2y_1+y_2\le3$: the first column $(2,1)$ against the first price $3$. When a diet has many foods and several nutrients, write each food's column across the dual constraint with its own price on the right, and keep the units of the nutrient table identical to those used in the primal. A slide that copies a different row, or mixes units between two tables of the same diet, gives a dual that is not the dual of that primal.

    Rules for any LP

    Non-canonical LPs follow a table. Read it row by row: the sense of a constraint decides the sign of its dual variable, and the sign of a variable decides the sense of its dual constraint.

    Minimisation problemMaximisation problem
    constraint $\ge$variable $\ge0$
    constraint $\le$variable $\le0$
    constraint $=$variable free
    variable $\ge0$constraint $\le$
    variable $\le0$constraint $\ge$
    variable freeconstraint $=$

    For a maximisation primal, read the table from right to left. For the running LP of Part 1, $\max5x_1+3x_2$ with three "$\le$" constraints and $x\ge0$, the dual is $$\min\ 8y_1+18y_2+12y_3\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_1+y_2+2y_3\ge5,\quad y_1+3y_2+y_3\ge3,\quad y\ge0.$$ A standard-form primal $\min c^\top x$, $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$ has dual $\max b^\top y$, $A^\top y\le c$ with $y$ free.

    Write the dual of $\min\ 2x_1-x_2+3x_3$ s.t. $x_1+x_2+x_3\ge4$, $\ 2x_1-x_3\le5$, $\ x_1+2x_2=3$, with $x_1\ge0$, $x_2\le0$, $x_3$ free.

    1. One dual variable per constraint: $y_1$ for the "$\ge$" row, $y_2$ for the "$\le$" row, $y_3$ for the "$=$" row. Signs from the table (minimisation): $y_1\ge0$, $y_2\le0$, $y_3$ free.

      In a minimisation, a "$\ge$" row gets a non-negative variable, a "$\le$" row a non-positive one, an equality a free one.

    2. Objective: $\max\ 4y_1+5y_2+3y_3$ (right-hand sides times dual variables).

      A minimisation primal gives a maximisation dual with $b$ as the objective.

    3. One dual constraint per primal variable, using its column: $x_1\ge0$ gives $y_1+2y_2+y_3\le2$; $x_2\le0$ gives $y_1+0\cdot y_2+2y_3\ge-1$; $x_3$ free gives $y_1-y_2+0\cdot y_3=3$.

      Variable $\ge0$ gives "$\le$", variable $\le0$ gives "$\ge$", free variable gives "$=$"; the right-hand sides are the costs $2,-1,3$.

    4. Check: the primal optimum is $9$ at $x=(3,0,1)$, and the dual has value $4\cdot0+5\cdot(-3)+3\cdot8=9$ at $y=(0,-3,8)$.

      Equal optimal values are what the strong duality theorem below promises.

    Seeing the dual

    The dual of a two-constraint problem lives in the plane of $(y_1,y_2)$, so you can draw it. Its feasible region is where no food is overpriced, and the objective $b^\top y$ pushes the prices up as far as the region allows.

    Try it

    Drag the price point $y$ around the dual region of each diet. When it is feasible, compare its income to the cost of the best diet (14 or 12). Drag it to the corner that gives the highest income and use "Show optimum". Notice that no feasible price vector ever beats the primal cost, and that the best one exactly equals it.

    Weak duality: every dual value is a lower bound

    This is the first examinable proof of the part; it takes only the two sign facts of the pair.

    If $x$ is feasible for the primal $\min c^\top x$, $Ax\ge b$, $x\ge0$ and $y$ is feasible for the dual $\max b^\top y$, $A^\top y\le c$, $y\ge0$, then $b^\top y\le c^\top x$.

    Prove weak duality.

    1. Since $Ax\ge b$ and $y\ge0$, multiplying each row by a non-negative number keeps "$\ge$": $y^\top Ax\ge y^\top b$.

      Each row $A_{i\cdot}x\ge b_i$ is multiplied by $y_i\ge0$ and the rows are added up.

    2. Since $A^\top y\le c$ and $x\ge0$, each column inequality is multiplied by $x_j\ge0$ and added: $x^\top A^\top y\le x^\top c$, that is $y^\top Ax\le c^\top x$.

      The scalar $x^\top A^\top y$ equals $y^\top Ax$.

    3. Chain the two: $b^\top y\le y^\top Ax\le c^\top x$.

      The middle term $y^\top Ax$ bridges the dual objective and the primal objective.

    Two consequences matter. If $b^\top y=c^\top x$ for a feasible pair, both are optimal (neither can be improved without crossing the other). If the primal is unbounded below, no dual $y$ can exist, because every dual value would have to lie below $-\infty$.

    Strong duality: the bound is tight

    If the primal has an optimal solution $x^*$, then the dual has an optimal solution $y^*$ and $c^\top x^*=b^\top y^*$.

    Sketch of the proof (simplex route): why does an optimal basis hand us an optimal dual?

    1. Write the primal in standard form with surplus variables, and let $B$ be an optimal basis, so $x_B=B^{-1}b$ and all reduced costs $\bar c_j=c_j-c_B^\top B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$ are $\ge0$.

      Simplex terminates at such a basis whenever the LP has an optimal solution (Part 1).

    2. Define $y^\top=c_B^\top B^{-1}$. Then $\bar c_j\ge0$ says $c_j-y^\top A_{\cdot j}\ge0$ for every original column: $A^\top y\le c$. For a surplus column $(-e_i)$ with cost $0$, $\bar c=y_i\ge0$: so $y\ge0$.

      Non-negative reduced costs are exactly dual feasibility.

    3. The dual objective is $y^\top b=c_B^\top B^{-1}b=c_B^\top x_B=c^\top x^*$.

      Equal values for a feasible pair imply optimality by weak duality.

    For the running LP, the optimal basis is $\{x_1,x_2,s_2\}$ and the numbers $y^\top=c_B^\top B^{-1}$ come out as $y=(1,0,2)$ (for the maximisation form, after undoing the sign flip of min versus max): dual feasible ($1+0+4=5\ge5$ and $1+0+2=3\ge3$) with value $8+0+24=32$, the same as the primal optimum.

    Weak and strong duality together restrict the status of a primal-dual pair to the following table.

    Primal \ DualFinite optimumUnboundedInfeasible
    Finite optimumpossibleimpossibleimpossible
    Unboundedimpossibleimpossiblepossible
    Infeasibleimpossiblepossiblepossible

    For the canteen dual $\max8y_1+6y_2$ s.t. $2y_1+y_2\le3$, $y_1+y_2\le2$, $y\ge0$, what is the objective at the feasible prices $y=(1,1)$?

    Check feasibility first: $2+1\le3$ and $1+1\le2$.

    $8\cdot1+6\cdot1=14$, equal to the best diet cost.

    A primal LP has 3 constraints and 5 non-negative variables. How many constraints (apart from sign conditions) does its dual have?

    One dual constraint per primal variable.

    5, one per primal variable. The dual has 3 variables, one per primal constraint.

    For a primal minimisation, $x$ is feasible with cost $20$ and $y$ is dual feasible with dual objective $13$. Between which two numbers must the optimal value lie?

    At least $13$ and at most $20$.

    The dual of the running LP is $\min8y_1+18y_2+12y_3$ s.t. $y_1+y_2+2y_3\ge5$, $y_1+3y_2+y_3\ge3$, $y\ge0$. Evaluate the objective at $y=(1,0,2)$.

    Substitute each value; the middle term vanishes.

    $8\cdot1+18\cdot0+12\cdot2=32$.

    Any dual feasible $y$ would give a finite lower bound.

    A feasible dual point would bound the primal cost from below, which contradicts unboundedness. So the dual is infeasible.

    In a minimisation primal, a constraint is of type "$\le$". What sign condition does its dual variable get?

    Use the table: "$\ge$" gives $y\ge0$, "$=$" gives free.

    A "$\le$" constraint in a minimisation gives a non-positive dual variable.

    • Count first: one dual variable per primal row, one dual row per primal column.
    • Sanity-check a dual by evaluating one feasible primal $x$ and one feasible dual $y$: the primal value must not be below the dual value.
    • Copying the right-hand side $b$ into the dual constraints (it goes in the dual objective; the dual's right-hand sides are the costs $c$).
    • Forgetting that an equality row gives a free dual variable.
    1. The dual of $\min c^\top x$, $Ax\ge b$, $x\ge0$ is $\max b^\top y$, $A^\top y\le c$, $y\ge0$; the sign rules turn any LP into its dual.
    2. Weak duality: every dual feasible value is at most every primal feasible cost, so a dual solution is a certified lower bound.
    3. Strong duality: at an optimal basis, $y^\top=c_B^\top B^{-1}$ is dual optimal and the two optimal values are equal.

    The costs go in the dual constraints, not the dual objective.

    Complementary slackness and the dual simplex method

    At an optimal pair, a constraint with slack carries a zero price and a positive variable has a tight dual row; the dual simplex method exploits the mirror image of the primal simplex, keeping the reduced costs non-negative and chasing feasibility.

    Complementary slackness lets you recover the dual from the primal (or check a candidate answer) without solving anything, and the dual simplex is what a solver runs after you add a constraint or change a right-hand side, which happens at every node of branch and bound.

    It is like a market at equilibrium: a resource nobody uses up is free, and a product that is sold must break even on its ingredient prices.

    Feasible $x$ (primal) and $y$ (dual) are both optimal if and only if $$y_i\,(A_{i\cdot}x-b_i)=0\ \ \forall i\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_j\,(c_j-y^\top A_{\cdot j})=0\ \ \forall j.$$ In words: a constraint with slack has price $0$; a variable that is positive has a tight dual row.

    Prove complementary slackness.

    1. Recall the weak duality chain $b^\top y\le y^\top Ax\le c^\top x$, with $y^\top Ax-b^\top y=\sum_i y_i(A_{i\cdot}x-b_i)$ and $c^\top x-y^\top Ax=\sum_j (c_j-y^\top A_{\cdot j})x_j$.

      Each of the two gaps is a sum written row by row, respectively column by column.

    2. Every term of both sums is $\ge0$: $y_i\ge0$ times $A_{i\cdot}x-b_i\ge0$, and $x_j\ge0$ times $c_j-y^\top A_{\cdot j}\ge0$.

      These are the feasibility conditions of the two problems.

    3. The total gap is $c^\top x-b^\top y=\sum_iy_i(A_{i\cdot}x-b_i)+\sum_j(c_j-y^\top A_{\cdot j})x_j$.

      Adding the two gaps cancels the middle term.

    4. Both are optimal exactly when the gap is $0$ (strong duality), and a sum of non-negative terms is $0$ exactly when every term is $0$. That is the pair of conditions.

      Optimality, zero gap and termwise zero are all equivalent for a feasible pair.

    Using it on the running LP

    For the running LP $\max5x_1+3x_2$ with constraints $c_1,c_2,c_3$, the same statement reads (a "$\le$" constraint now has slack $b_i-A_{i\cdot}x$, and dual rows have excess $A^\top y-c\ge0$): $y_i\cdot\text{slack}_i=0$ and $x_j\cdot\text{excess}_j=0$.

    Try it

    Pick a corner of the running LP and a candidate price vector. The readout lists all five complementary slackness products. Find the one pair that is fully optimal. Then choose $(0,1,2)$ with the corner $(4,4)$: both are feasible and the values differ. Which products are non-zero, and how do they add up to the gap between the values?

    The primal optimum of the running LP is $x^*=(4,4)$. Find the optimal dual $y^*$ using complementary slackness alone.

    1. Slacks at $(4,4)$: $c_1$: $8-8=0$; $c_2$: $18-16=2$; $c_3$: $12-12=0$.

      The second constraint is not tight.

    2. The slack in $c_2$ forces $y_2=0$.

      A constraint with room to spare is worth nothing: $y_2\cdot2=0$.

    3. Both $x_1,x_2$ are positive, so both dual rows must be tight: $y_1+y_2+2y_3=5$ and $y_1+3y_2+y_3=3$. With $y_2=0$: $y_1+2y_3=5$ and $y_1+y_3=3$.

      A positive variable means $x_j\cdot\text{excess}_j=0$ forces the excess to be $0$.

    4. Subtract: $y_3=2$, then $y_1=1$. So $y^*=(1,0,2)$ with value $8+24=32$, which matches $5\cdot4+3\cdot4=32$.

      Equal values for a feasible pair prove optimality of both.

    Careful: complementary slackness does not say that "tight" means "positive price": a tight constraint may still have price $0$ (this happens at degenerate corners). And a pair satisfying all the products but violating dual feasibility proves nothing: try the corner $(6,0)$ with $y=(0,0,2.5)$ in the widget.

    The dual simplex method

    Primal simplex keeps $x$ feasible and works towards non-negative reduced costs (dual feasibility). The dual simplex does the reverse: it keeps all reduced costs $\ge0$ and works towards a non-negative right-hand side (primal feasibility). It is natural whenever the starting point is dual feasible but not primal feasible. Two cases matter:

    • a minimisation with costs $c\ge0$ and constraints $Ax\ge b$: the slack basis has $c_B=0$, so the reduced costs are $c\ge0$, while the basic values $-b$ are negative;
    • a solved LP after a change that damages feasibility but not optimality of the reduced costs: a new constraint, or a changed right-hand side (Chapter 2.4).

    We never write the dual: the tableau is the ordinary primal tableau.

    1. Start from a basis with all reduced costs $\bar c_j\ge0$ (dual feasible).
    2. If every basic value $\bar b_i\ge0$, stop: optimal.
    3. Leaving row: choose a row $r$ with $\bar b_r\lt0$ (usually the most negative).
    4. If no entry of row $r$ is negative, stop: the primal LP is infeasible.
    5. Entering column: among columns with $a_{rj}\lt0$ choose $j$ minimising $\bar c_j/|a_{rj}|$.
    6. Pivot on $(r,j)$ with the usual row operations and go to step 2.

    Why the ratio rule works. After pivoting, a column $k$ has new reduced cost $\bar c_k-\bar c_j\,a_{rk}/a_{rj}$. If $a_{rk}\ge0$ this does not decrease (the pivot $a_{rj}$ is negative). If $a_{rk}\lt0$ it stays $\ge0$ exactly when $\bar c_k/|a_{rk}|\ge\bar c_j/|a_{rj}|$, which is why $j$ must have the smallest ratio. So dual feasibility is never lost. Each pivot raises the objective (for a minimisation) and finally reaches primal feasibility.

    Try it

    Run the three presets. In each tableau, the highlighted row is the leaving row, the "ratio" line shows $\bar c_j/|a_{rj}|$ and the boxed column is the entering one. Press Pivot until the readout reports a result. Notice that the reduced costs (top row) never turn negative, while the right-hand sides turn from negative to non-negative. In the last preset, read why it stops.

    Solve the canteen diet $\min3x_1+2x_2$ s.t. $2x_1+x_2\ge8$, $x_1+x_2\ge6$ with the dual simplex method.

    1. Multiply the rows by $-1$ and add slacks: $-2x_1-x_2+s_1=-8$, $-x_1-x_2+s_2=-6$. With basis $\{s_1,s_2\}$ the reduced costs are $(3,2,0,0)$, all $\ge0$, but the basic values $(-8,-6)$ are negative.

      The slack basis is dual feasible because the costs are non-negative.

    2. Leaving row: $s_1$ (value $-8$, the most negative). Its negative entries are $-2$ in $x_1$ and $-1$ in $x_2$. Ratios: $3/2=1.5$ and $2/1=2$. The smaller is $x_1$, so $x_1$ enters.

      Dividing reduced cost by $|a_{rj}|$ finds the first dual constraint that would become violated.

    3. Pivot on the entry $-2$. New rows: $x_1+\tfrac12x_2-\tfrac12s_1=4$ and $-\tfrac12x_2-\tfrac12s_1+s_2=-2$; reduced costs $(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac32,0)$, objective $12$.

      Still dual feasible; row 2 is the only one still negative.

    4. Leaving row: $s_2$ (value $-2$). Negative entries: $-\tfrac12$ in $x_2$ and $-\tfrac12$ in $s_1$. Ratios: $\tfrac12/\tfrac12=1$ and $\tfrac32/\tfrac12=3$. So $x_2$ enters.

      The smaller ratio keeps all reduced costs non-negative.

    5. Pivot: $x_1=2$, $x_2=4$, reduced costs of $s_1,s_2$ both $1$, objective $14$. All values are $\ge0$: optimal.

      The reduced costs $(1,1)$ of the surplus columns are the dual prices $y=(1,1)$ of the pharmacist, and $8+6=14$ matches the primal cost.

    Go deeper: dual simplex is primal simplex on the dual

    Run primal simplex on the dual LP and translate each basis and pivot back to the primal tableau: you get precisely the rules above (the leaving row corresponds to the entering dual variable, the entering column to the dual ratio test). That is why the objective of a minimisation climbs monotonically during dual simplex: it is the dual objective, which primal simplex on the dual increases.

    $-4/(-2)=2$.
