    In dual simplex, a row has a negative right-hand side and no negative entries in the other columns. What do you conclude?

    The row then reads "non-negative combination of non-negative variables equals a negative number".

    Such a row cannot be satisfied by any $x\ge0$: the primal is infeasible.

    • Check dual feasibility (all reduced costs $\ge0$) before starting dual simplex.
    • Take the ratio only over negative entries of the leaving row.
    • Dividing by positive entries or by zero entries.
    • Taking the minimum ratio over the wrong row: the ratio test of dual simplex runs along the leaving row, not down a column.
    1. Complementary slackness: at an optimal pair, price $\times$ slack $=0$ for each constraint and variable $\times$ dual-row excess $=0$ for each variable; it recovers $y$ from $x$.
    2. Dual simplex keeps reduced costs $\ge0$ and pivots to remove negative right-hand sides; it detects primal infeasibility when a negative row has no negative entry.
    3. Choose the leaving row first (a negative basic value), then the entering column by the smallest $\bar c_j/|a_{rj}|$.

    A constraint has a positive slack at the primal optimum. What does complementary slackness say about its optimal dual price?

    It is positive.
    A positive price on a constraint with unused room would make the products non-zero.
    It is $0$.
    Price times slack must vanish, and the slack is not zero.
    It cannot be determined.
    The condition decides it.

    A variable is positive at the primal optimum. What is true of its dual constraint?

    It has slack.
    That would make $x_j\cdot\text{excess}_j\gt0$.
    It is tight (the excess is $0$).
    Variable times excess must be $0$.
    It is violated.
    The optimal dual is feasible.

    Dual simplex has right-hand sides $(3,-5,-1)$ in the three rows. Which row leaves under the usual rule?

    The first.
    That value is already feasible.
    The second.
    The most negative value, $-5$.
    The third.
    It is negative but not the most negative.

    Why must the entering column minimise $\bar c_j/|a_{rj}|$ over negative entries of row $r$?

    It makes the objective largest.
    The aim is to keep reduced costs from going negative.
    It is the choice that keeps every reduced cost non-negative.
    A larger ratio would make some other reduced cost negative.
    It makes the right-hand side positive immediately.
    It may take several pivots to clear all negative values.

    Sensitivity analysis: reduced costs, shadow prices and ranging

    Once the optimal basis is known, you can read how the answer reacts to small changes in the costs, the right-hand sides, or the model itself without solving the LP again.

    Data are estimates (demand, capacity, costs). A planner wants to know which estimates matter, and branch and bound re-solves slightly changed LPs constantly, starting from the old basis.

    It is like a recipe tested in a kitchen: before changing the oven temperature, you want to know how much it can move before the dish is ruined, and how much each degree is worth.

    Throughout we use the running LP, whose optimal basis is $\{x_1,x_2,s_2\}$, with optimal point $(4,4)$ and slacks $s=(0,2,0)$. Its optimal tableau for $\min-5x_1-3x_2$ (right-hand side of the top row is $-z$) is $$\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}&x_1&x_2&s_1&s_2&s_3&\text{RHS}\\\hline \text{RC}&0&0&1&0&2&32\\x_1&1&0&-1&0&1&4\\x_2&0&1&2&0&-1&4\\s_2&0&0&-5&1&2&2\end{array}$$ so $B^{-1}$ (the three slack columns) has columns $(-1,2,-5)$, $(0,0,1)$, $(1,-1,2)$, and $y=(1,0,2)$.

    What the reduced costs and prices say

    The reduced costs of the non-basic slacks, $1$ and $2$, equal the dual prices $y_1,y_3$: forcing the slack $s_1$ to be one unit (that is, using one fewer unit of the first resource) costs $1$ unit of profit. The slack $s_2$ is basic with value $2$: the second resource is not scarce and its price is $0$. In general, when the optimal basis is non-degenerate, the optimal dual variables are the marginal values of the right-hand sides: $\partial z^*/\partial b_i=y_i$.

    The shadow price of constraint $i$ is the change in the optimal value per unit increase of $b_i$: it equals $y_i^*$. It holds only while the optimal basis stays the same: the range of $b_i$.

    Changing a right-hand side

    Raise $b_i$ by $t$. The reduced costs $c_N^\top-c_B^\top B^{-1}N$ do not involve $b$, so optimality conditions are intact. Only feasibility can fail: $$x_B(t)=B^{-1}b+t\,B^{-1}e_i\ \ge0.$$ The basis stays optimal exactly while this holds, and the optimal value is $z^*+y_i\,t$ in this range. Outside the range, a basic variable would turn negative, the point is dual feasible but primal infeasible, and dual simplex (Chapter 2.3) repairs it.

    Try it

    Choose a constraint and slide its right-hand side. Left: the region and optimal corner; right: the optimal profit as a function of $b_i$. The dashed line is the tangent with slope equal to the shadow price. Find where the slope changes for each constraint, and note that constraint 2 has price $0$ over a long range.

    Find the range of $b_1$ over which the shadow price $y_1=1$ is valid, and the value of the running LP at $b_1=8.2$.

    1. The first column of $B^{-1}$ is $(-1,2,-5)$ and the current basic values are $(x_1,x_2,s_2)=(4,4,2)$. So $x_B(t)=(4-t,\ 4+2t,\ 2-5t)$.

      Increasing $b_1$ by $t$ shifts the basic variables along the column of $B^{-1}$ belonging to constraint 1.

    2. Require all non-negative: $4-t\ge0$ gives $t\le4$; $4+2t\ge0$ gives $t\ge-2$; $2-5t\ge0$ gives $t\le0.4$. So $-2\le t\le0.4$.

      The most restrictive bounds are the lower $-2$ and the upper $0.4$.

    3. The range is $b_1\in[6,8.4]$. Inside it, $z^*=32+1\cdot t$.

      The shadow price $1$ is the slope of the profit curve in this range.

    4. At $b_1=8.2$, $t=0.2$: $z^*=32.2$ at $x=(3.8,4.4)$ (check: $3.8+4.4=8.2$, $5\cdot3.8+3\cdot4.4=32.2$).

      The point is inside the range, so no re-solve is needed.

    The same recipe for the other two constraints: for $b_2$ the column is $(0,0,1)$, so $s_2=2+t\ge0$ gives $b_2\ge16$ with price $0$ (no upper limit); for $b_3$ the column is $(1,-1,2)$, giving $x_B(t)=(4+t,4-t,2+2t)$ and $-1\le t\le4$, so $b_3\in[11,16]$ with price $2$.

    Changing a cost

    A cost change does not move the point $x_B=B^{-1}b$, so feasibility is untouched; only the reduced costs change. For a non-basic variable, only its own reduced cost changes. For a basic variable, $c_B$ changes, so all reduced costs change. The current basis stays optimal while all reduced costs keep their signs.

    Try it

    Slide the profits $c_1,c_2$ of the running LP. The mint line through the optimal corner is the objective line. Find how far $c_1$ can move before the optimal corner changes, and watch for the tie when the objective line lies along an edge.

    Keeping $c_2=3$, find the range of $c_1$ for which $(4,4)$ stays optimal.

    1. With profits $(c_1,3,0)$ on the basis $\{x_1,x_2,s_2\}$, the dual prices are $y^\top=c_B^\top B^{-1}=(c_1,3,0)\,B^{-1}=(6-c_1,\ 0,\ c_1-3)$.

      Multiply $c_B$ by the columns of $B^{-1}$ listed above: $-c_1+6$, $0$, $c_1-3$.

    2. For a maximisation, optimality needs $y\ge0$ (the reduced costs of the slacks, $y_1$ and $y_3$, are non-negative): $6-c_1\ge0$ and $c_1-3\ge0$.

      The basic columns have zero reduced cost by definition; only the non-basic slacks can fail.

    3. So $3\le c_1\le6$. At $c_1=6$ the objective line is parallel to the constraint $2x_1+x_2\le12$ and the edge from $(6,0)$ to $(4,4)$ ties; at $c_1=3$ it is parallel to $x_1+x_2\le8$.

      At the end points the reduced cost of a non-basic variable becomes $0$: there are alternative optima.

    4. Same method with $c_1=5$ fixed: $y=(2c_2-5,\ 0,\ 5-c_2)$, so $2.5\le c_2\le5$.

      The ratio $c_1/c_2$ must stay between the slopes of the two tight constraints: between $1$ and $2$.

    A new variable and a new constraint

    New variable. Add a product $x_6$ with profit $4$ using $(1,1,1)$ units of the three resources. Treat it as non-basic at $0$: the current point is still feasible. Price it out: the resources it uses are worth $y^\top A_{\cdot6}=1\cdot1+0\cdot1+2\cdot1=3$ at the current prices, below its profit $4$. Its reduced cost (in the minimisation) is $-4+3=-1\lt0$, so it enters and simplex continues: the new optimum is $36$ at $x_1=4,x_6=4$. If its profit were $3$ or less, it would stay out.

    New constraint. Add $x_2\le3$. If the current optimum satisfies it, the optimum is unchanged. Here $(4,4)$ violates it, but the old reduced costs remain non-negative once the new slack joins the basis: the new tableau is dual feasible and primal infeasible, the exact situation for dual simplex.

    Re-optimise the running LP after adding $x_2\le3$, starting from the optimal tableau above.

    1. Write the new row with slack $s_4$: $x_2+s_4=3$. Substitute $x_2=4-2s_1+s_3$ from the $x_2$ row of the tableau: $-2s_1+s_3+s_4=-1$.

      The new row must be expressed in terms of the non-basic variables so $s_4$ can be basic.

    2. The basic value $s_4=-1$ is negative: dual simplex. The row has one negative entry, $-2$ in the column $s_1$. Ratio: $\bar c_{s_1}/2=1/2$. So $s_1$ enters and $s_4$ leaves.

      Only $s_1$ has a negative entry, so it is the only candidate.

    3. Pivot. New values: $s_1=\tfrac12$, $x_2=3$, $x_1=4+s_1=4.5$, $s_2=2+5s_1=4.5$; reduced costs of $s_3,s_4$ are $2.5$ and $0.5$.

      All values are non-negative and all reduced costs are positive, so the tableau is optimal.

    4. New optimum: $x=(4.5,3)$ with profit $5\cdot4.5+3\cdot3=31.5$, down from $32$.

      One pivot instead of a restart from the origin.

    Careful: shadow prices are one-at-a-time and local. Changing two right-hand sides together, or one by more than its range, needs a new check of $B^{-1}b\ge0$. And at a degenerate optimum (a basic variable equal to $0$) the left and right slopes of the profit curve can differ, so there is no single price.
    Go deeper: leaving the range

    If $b_2$ drops from $18$ to $15$ (below its range limit $16$), $s_2=2+(15-18)=-1$ becomes negative while the reduced costs are untouched: dual simplex. The row of $s_2$ has the negative entry $-5$ in the column $s_1$, ratio $1/5$, so $s_1$ enters: profit $32-0.2=31.8$ at $(4.2,3.6)$. The new slope of the profit curve below $16$ is therefore $0.2$ per unit, no longer $0$.

    The running LP has $y=(1,0,2)$ and a range $[11,16]$ for $b_3$. How much does the optimal profit rise when $b_3$ goes from $12$ to $13$?

    $13$ is inside the range, so the price applies.

    $y_3\cdot1=2$. Check: at $b_3=13$ the optimum is $(5,3)$ with profit $34$.

    With $x_B(t)=(4-t,\ 4+2t,\ 2-5t)$ for $(x_1,x_2,s_2)$, what is the largest $b_1$ keeping the basis feasible? (Current $b_1=8$.)

    The binding entry is the one that decreases fastest. Solve $2-5t\ge0$.

    $t\le0.4$, so $b_1\le8.4$.

    What is the optimal profit of the running LP when $b_1=8.2$?

    The value is $32+y_1t$ inside the range $[6,8.4]$.

    $32+1\cdot0.2=32.2$.

    With $c_1=5$ fixed, the dual prices on the optimal basis are $y_1=2c_2-5$ and $y_3=5-c_2$. What is the smallest $c_2$ for which $(4,4)$ stays optimal?

    Both prices must be $\ge0$.

    $2c_2-5\ge0$ gives $c_2\ge2.5$ (and $5-c_2\ge0$ gives $c_2\le5$).

    A new product with profit $2.5$ would use $(1,1,1)$ units of the three resources of the running LP. Should the current plan change? (Prices $y=(1,0,2)$.)

    Compare the profit with the worth $y^\top A_{\cdot j}$ of the resources it uses.

    The resources are worth $1+0+2=3\gt2.5$: producing it would lose $0.5$ per unit, so it stays out.

    If $b_2$ falls from $18$ to $15$ in the running LP, what is the new optimal profit? (Hint: $s_2=-1$ after the change; dual simplex pivots in $s_1$ with ratio $1/5$.)

    The objective drops by (ratio) $\times$ (size of the infeasibility), i.e. $\tfrac15\cdot1$.

    $32-0.2=31.8$. Direct check: $x_1+3x_2=15$ and $2x_1+x_2=12$ meet at $(4.2,3.6)$, profit $21+10.8=31.8$.

    • Always report a shadow price together with its range.
    • For a cost change on a basic variable, recompute all reduced costs, not just one.
    • Applying a shadow price beyond its range.
    • Reading "price $0$" as "constraint can be dropped": it only means a small change does not matter.
    1. The optimal dual variables $y_i$ are the shadow prices of the right-hand sides; they hold while $B^{-1}b+t\,B^{-1}e_i\ge0$.
    2. A cost change keeps the basis optimal as long as all reduced costs keep their signs; for the running LP, $3\le c_1\le6$ and $2.5\le c_2\le5$.
    3. New variables are priced out with $y^\top A_{\cdot j}$; a new violated constraint or a right-hand side outside its range is repaired by dual simplex, not by a restart.

    A resource has shadow price $4$ with range $[10,30]$ and its supply is now $20$. Supply rises to $26$. By how much does the optimal value change?

    $0$.
    A positive price means extra supply helps.
    By $4\cdot6=24$.
    $26$ is inside the range, so the price applies to all six units.
    It cannot be said.
    The range tells you the price is valid.

    After a change in $b$, the old basis has all reduced costs $\ge0$ but one basic value is negative. Which method restarts efficiently?

    Primal simplex.
    Primal simplex needs a primal feasible start.
    Dual simplex.
    The basis is dual feasible and primal infeasible.
    Solve the dual from scratch.
    That would discard the basis you already have.

    A new variable has reduced cost $-1$ (minimisation) at the current prices. What happens?

    Nothing; the current solution is still optimal.
    A negative reduced cost is an improving direction.
    It enters the basis and primal simplex continues.
    The current point is still feasible and the new column can improve it.
    The LP becomes infeasible.
    The point is unchanged and still feasible.

    Why is a cost change handled by checking reduced costs, while a right-hand side change is handled by checking $B^{-1}b$?

    Both change the reduced costs.
    A right-hand side change leaves them untouched.
    The costs enter the reduced costs only, and $b$ enters the basic values only.
    Optimality (dual feasibility) depends on $c$, feasibility on $b$.
    The two checks are equivalent.
    They test different things.

    Primal: $\min4x_1+3x_2$ s.t. $x_1+2x_2\ge6$, $3x_1+x_2\ge6$, $x\ge0$. The point $x=(2,2)$ is feasible with cost $14$. The dual is $\max6y_1+6y_2$ s.t. $y_1+3y_2\le4$, $2y_1+y_2\le3$, $y\ge0$, and $y=(1,1)$ is dual feasible. What is guaranteed?

    The optimal cost is exactly $14$.
    $14$ is the cost of one feasible plan, an upper bound only.
    The optimal cost is exactly $12$.
    $12$ is a lower bound from weak duality; equality needs more evidence.
    The optimal cost lies between $12$ and $14$.
    The dual value $6+6=12$ is a lower bound, the primal plan an upper bound.

    At the optimum of an LP, the first constraint has slack $3$ and the first variable is positive. Which statements must hold?

    $y_1=0$ and the first dual row is tight.
    Price times slack is $0$; variable times excess is $0$.
    $y_1\gt0$ and the first dual row has slack.
    Both conclusions are the opposite of what is required.
    $y_1=0$ and the first dual row has slack.
    A positive variable forces its dual row to be tight.

    The running LP has $y_1=1$ for the first constraint and range $b_1\in[6,8.4]$. The planner raises $b_1$ from $8$ to $10$. What is the correct statement?

    Profit rises by exactly $2$.
    $10$ is beyond the range, so the price may no longer apply.
    Profit rises by at most $0.4$ at price $1$ within the range; beyond $8.4$ the basis changes and the price must be recomputed.
    Up to $8.4$ the slope is $1$; after that, the slope drops (to $0$ for this LP).
    Profit is unchanged.
    Up to $8.4$ the price $1$ does apply.

    In a minimisation with bounds, which non-basic variable satisfies the optimality condition?

    At its lower bound with $\bar c=-2$.
    Raising it would improve the cost.
    At its upper bound with $\bar c=-2$.
    It can only decrease, and the cost would rise by $2$ per unit.
    At its upper bound with $\bar c=+2$.
    Lowering it would improve the cost.

    In a primal simplex ratio test the basic values are $(6,4,9)$ and the direction entries are $d_B=(-3,2,-1)$. Which basic variable leaves, and what is the step length?

    The second, step $2$.
    The second entry is positive: that variable grows and never blocks the step.
    The first, step $2$.
    Ratios: $6/3=2$ and $9/1=9$. The smaller one, $2$, belongs to the first variable.
    The third, step $9$.
    The step is the smallest ratio, not the largest.

    The lines $2x_1+x_2=12$ and $x_1+3x_2=18$ meet at which point?

    $(4,4)$
    That is where $x_1+x_2=8$ meets $2x_1+x_2=12$. Check it in $x_1+3x_2=18$: $4+12=16$.
    $(3.6,4.8)$
    From the first, $x_2=12-2x_1$; then $x_1+36-6x_1=18$ gives $x_1=3.6$, $x_2=4.8$.
    $(6,0)$
    At $(6,0)$ the second line gives $6\ne18$.

    Lecture 3 adds one restriction to linear programming, that some variables must be whole numbers, and shows how many routing and logistics decisions (pack this van, open that depot, assign this job) become integer programmes. The second half of the lecture asks which of several correct formulations a solver can actually use: the strong ones. The labs on facility location (Lab 1) and the generalised assignment problem (Lab 2) are the case studies. Throughout Parts 3 to 6 we follow one small, fictional firm, Kaveri Courier in Bengaluru: its owner decides which depot sites to open and how to load parcels onto vans here, then hands those decisions to a solver (Part 4), routes one van (Part 5) and finally the whole fleet (Part 6).

    You need: Part −3 (turning a word problem into variables, objective and constraints), Part −1 (binary logic, forcing constraints, big-M, cover and packing matrices) and Part 1 (polyhedra, convex hulls, corners of an LP).

    Modelling with integer variables: six classical formulations

    An integer programme (IP) is a linear programme in which some or all variables must take whole-number values, most often 0 or 1.

    Choosing which depot to open or which parcel to load is a yes/no or a count, never a fraction, so every plan in this course is an integer programme at heart. The formulations of this chapter are the templates you will recognise again in Parts 4 to 6.

    It is like a seating plan: a guest sits in one chair or another, never in 0.4 of two chairs.

    From LP to IP

    Recall the LP in canonical form, $\min c^\top x$ subject to $Ax\ge b$, $x\ge0$. Add the requirement that the variables are whole numbers and we get the integer programme $$\min\ c^\top x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ax\ge b,\quad x\in\mathbb Z^n_+ .$$ Here $\mathbb Z^n_+$ means vectors of non-negative integers, so the separate constraint $x\ge0$ is no longer needed. If every variable is restricted to $\{0,1\}$ it is a binary programme; if some variables are integer and others continuous it is a mixed integer programme (MIP).

    The picture changes in an important way. The feasible set of an LP is a polyhedron and its best point is at a corner (Part 1). The feasible set of an IP is a cloud of isolated points, and the best of them is generally not a corner of the polyhedron defined by $Ax\ge b$. Chapter 3.2 explores this. For now we learn to write down the models.

    A running story: a courier company has five parcels to load onto a van, several depots from which to dispatch, and a planning horizon of a few days. Every model below answers one question from that story. We write $x$ for quantities or assignments and $y$ for yes/no switches.

    Kaveri Courier

    The owner of Kaveri Courier has a few candidate depot sites around Bengaluru, a handful of vans and parcels for customers across the city. Two questions come up every day: which parcels go on this van, and which depots are worth opening? The first is the knapsack and bin packing formulation below, the second is facility location, and the question of who does which job is the assignment family. Each formulation is one decision the owner really faces.

    A van of capacity $C$ kg may carry parcel $j$ (weight $a_j$, value $c_j$) or not. Let $x_j=1$ if parcel $j$ is loaded. $$\max\ \sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j=1}^n a_jx_j\le C,\quad x_j\in\{0,1\}.$$ One constraint, binary variables, maximise value. It is the simplest IP and the building block of cover inequalities (Chapter 3.3).

    Try it

    Five parcels with weights 9, 8, 5, 4, 3 kg and values 9, 5, 14, 11, 12 must fit a van of capacity 16 kg. Click parcels to load them and try to beat your own score. Then press "LP relaxation" to see what happens when parcels may be loaded in parts. Notice that the fractional plan is worth more than any whole-parcel plan.

    $n$ couriers and $n$ parcels; courier $i$ delivering parcel $j$ costs $c_{ij}$. Let $x_{ij}=1$ if courier $i$ takes parcel $j$. $$\min\ \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j}x_{ij}=1\ \ \forall i,\qquad \sum_{i}x_{ij}=1\ \ \forall j,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.$$ Each courier gets exactly one parcel and each parcel exactly one courier. A remarkable fact, proved in the "go deeper" box of Chapter 3.2, is that the LP relaxation of this model already has integer corners, so a plain LP solver solves it.

    $n$ items of weight $w_j$ are packed into identical bins (vans) of capacity $C$, and we want to use as few bins as possible. Let $y_i=1$ if bin $i$ is used and $x_{ij}=1$ if item $j$ goes into bin $i$. $$\min\ \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j}w_jx_{ij}\le C\,y_i\ \ \forall i,\qquad \sum_{i}x_{ij}=1\ \ \forall j,\qquad x_{ij},y_i\in\{0,1\}.$$ The first row is a forcing constraint (Part −1): an unused bin ($y_i=0$) can hold nothing, a used bin holds at most $C$. We use $n$ bins because $n$ items never need more than $n$ bins.

    Careful: the objective counts bins used and we want fewer of them, so it is a minimisation. The lecture slide writes "max" here; that is a slip, and with "max" a solver would happily open every bin.

    Over periods $t=1,\dots,n$ a depot faces demand $d_t$. Producing in period $t$ costs a fixed set-up $f_t$ plus $p_t$ per unit, and each unit left in stock at the end of period $t$ costs $h_t$. Let $x_t$ be the amount produced, $s_t$ the stock at the end of period $t$ and $y_t=1$ if production happens in period $t$. $$\min\ \sum_{t=1}^n\big(p_tx_t+h_ts_t+f_ty_t\big)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad s_{t-1}+x_t=d_t+s_t,\quad x_t\le M\,y_t,\quad s_0=0,\quad x_t,s_t\ge0,\ y_t\in\{0,1\}.$$ The first row is a stock balance (what we hold plus what we make equals what we ship plus what we keep). The second is the forcing constraint "no production unless the set-up is paid"; $M$ is a big-M that must be at least as large as any possible production quantity. A mixed integer programme: $x,s$ continuous, $y$ binary.

    Careful: this too is a minimisation of cost; the slide's "max" is a slip. Also note that $f_ty_t$ is paid only when $y_t=1$: the forcing row ties $y_t$ to $x_t$.

    $m$ customers can be served from $n$ candidate depots. Opening depot $j$ costs $f_j$; serving customer $i$ from depot $j$ costs $c_{ij}$. Let $y_j=1$ if depot $j$ is open and $x_{ij}=1$ if customer $i$ is served from $j$. $$\min\ \sum_{j}f_jy_j+\sum_{i}\sum_{j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_jx_{ij}=1\ \ \forall i,\qquad x_{ij}\le y_j\ \ \forall i,j,\qquad x_{ij},y_j\in\{0,1\}.$$ "Uncapacitated" means depots can serve any number of customers. The rows $x_{ij}\le y_j$ are forcing constraints again: no service from a closed depot. This is the model of Lab 1.

    $m$ agents (vans, crews) and $n$ jobs. Agent $i$ needs time $t_{ij}$ for job $j$ and has a time budget $s_i$; the assignment costs $c_{ij}$ (or earns profit $p_{ij}$, with "max" instead of "min"). Let $x_{ij}=1$ if agent $i$ does job $j$. $$\min\ \sum_{i}\sum_{j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{i}x_{ij}=1\ \ \forall j,\qquad \sum_{j}t_{ij}x_{ij}\le s_i\ \ \forall i,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.$$ Every job has exactly one agent (a column of the table sums to 1) and no agent exceeds its budget (a row of times is bounded). It generalises the assignment problem: one agent may take several jobs. This is the model of Lab 2.

    ModelVariablesObjectiveConstraint patterns
    Knapsack$x_j$ binarymax valueone capacity row
    Assignment$x_{ij}$ binarymin cost"exactly one" in every row and column
    Bin packing$y_i,x_{ij}$ binarymin binscapacity with forcing $\le Cy_i$; "exactly one" per item
    Lot sizing$x_t,s_t\ge0$, $y_t$ binarymin coststock balance; forcing $x_t\le My_t$
    Facility location$y_j,x_{ij}$ binarymin cost"exactly one" per customer; forcing $x_{ij}\le y_j$
    GAP$x_{ij}$ binarymin cost"exactly one" per job; budget row per agent

    Six items of weights $5,4,3,3,2,2$ are packed into bins of capacity $C=8$. (a) How many variables and constraints does the bin packing model have? (b) What is the fewest bins any plan can use, and is there a plan achieving it?

    1. With $n=6$ items we allow $n=6$ bins. The variables are $x_{ij}$ for 6 bins and 6 items, which is $36$, plus $y_1,\dots,y_6$: in all $36+6=42$ binary variables.

      One $x_{ij}$ for every (bin, item) pair, one $y_i$ for every bin.

    2. Constraints: 6 capacity rows (one per bin) and 6 "exactly one" rows (one per item): $12$ constraints, apart from the binary restrictions.

      Capacity is per bin, assignment is per item.

    3. The total weight is $5+4+3+3+2+2=19$. Two bins hold at most $16\lt19$, so at least $\lceil19/8\rceil=3$ bins are needed.

      A lower bound from adding up weights; no plan can beat it.

    4. Three bins suffice: $\{5,3\}$ weighs $8$, $\{4,2,2\}$ weighs $8$, $\{3\}$ weighs $3$.

      Each bin is within capacity and every item appears once, so the plan is feasible with 3 bins. It meets the lower bound, so it is optimal.

    Lot sizing with demands $d=(20,30,0,40,10)$ in five periods, set-up costs $f=(90,80,70,85,60)$, unit production cost $p_t=2$, holding cost $h_t=1$ per unit per period. Evaluate the plan: produce $50$ in period 1 and $50$ in period 4, nothing else.

    1. Stock balance with $s_0=0$: $s_1=0+50-20=30$, $s_2=30+0-30=0$, $s_3=0+0-0=0$, $s_4=0+50-40=10$, $s_5=10+0-10=0$.

      Apply $s_t=s_{t-1}+x_t-d_t$ period by period; all stocks stay non-negative, so the plan is feasible.

    2. Set-ups: $y_1=y_4=1$, so $90+85=175$.

      Only periods that produce pay their fixed cost.

    3. Production: $2\times(50+50)=200$. Holding: $1\times(30+0+0+10+0)=40$.

      Variable cost is per unit made; holding is per unit left over at the end of each period.

    4. Total cost: $175+200+40=415$.

      This happens to be the optimum (Chapter 3.3 shows that no integer plan is cheaper).

    Go deeper: why $M=\text{total demand}$ is valid but poor

    In lot sizing no period will ever produce more than the demand still to come, $d_t+\dots+d_n$. Any $M$ at least that large is valid, including the total demand over all periods, but the larger $M$ is, the weaker the LP bound (Chapter 3.3). The same remark holds for the bin packing row $\sum_jw_jx_{ij}\le Cy_i$, where $C$ is already the smallest sensible multiplier.

    In the van example (weights 9, 8, 5, 4, 3 kg; values 9, 5, 14, 11, 12; capacity 16 kg) the plan "load parcels 3, 4 and 5" is feasible. What is its total value?

    Add the values of parcels 3, 4 and 5, and check that their weights add up to at most 16.

    Weights $5+4+3=12\le16$; values $14+11+12=37$. (This is the optimum.)

    A bin packing model for $n=5$ items with $n$ bins available uses $x_{ij}$ and $y_i$. How many binary variables does it have?

    Count the (bin, item) pairs, then add one switch per bin.

    $5\times5=25$ variables $x_{ij}$ plus $5$ variables $y_i$: $30$.

    A facility location model has $m=8$ customers and $n=5$ candidate depots. Using the individual forcing rows $x_{ij}\le y_j$, how many constraints are there, not counting the binary restrictions?

    One "exactly one" row per customer, plus one forcing row per (customer, depot) pair.

    $8$ assignment rows plus $8\times5=40$ forcing rows: $48$.

    Same lot sizing data as in the worked example ($d=(20,30,0,40,10)$, $f=(90,80,70,85,60)$, $p_t=2$, $h_t=1$). Evaluate the plan "produce all $100$ units in period 1". What is its total cost?

    Stocks at the ends of periods 1 to 5 are $80,50,50,10,0$.

    Set-up $90$; production $2\times100=200$; holding $80+50+50+10+0=190$. Total $90+200+190=480$, worse than the plan of cost 415.

    In the bin packing model, which is the correct sense of the objective $\sum_iy_i$?

    $y_i=1$ means a bin is used. Do we want more bins or fewer?

    We want as few used bins as possible, so the objective is minimised. Maximising would open all bins.

    • Say in words what each variable means before writing a constraint.
    • Link every yes/no variable to the quantity it controls with a forcing row.
    • Check the objective sense: counts and costs are minimised, values and profits maximised.
    • Writing "max" for bin packing or lot sizing.
    • Forgetting that an unused bin or an idle period must hold or produce exactly zero.
    • Treating the IP as an LP and rounding at the end.
    1. An integer programme is an LP with whole-number requirements; mixed integer programmes keep some continuous variables.
    2. Knapsack, assignment, bin packing, lot sizing, facility location and GAP are built from three patterns: capacity rows, "exactly one" rows and forcing rows.
    3. Bin packing and lot sizing are minimisation problems; always check the sense of the objective.

    Which constraint family makes bin $i$ available for items only if it is used?

    $\sum_iw_jx_{ij}=1$
    That sum mixes bins and has no capacity; look for the row with $y_i$ on the right.
    $\sum_jw_jx_{ij}\le C\,y_i$
    When $y_i=0$ the right side is 0 and no item can be placed; when $y_i=1$ the capacity $C$ applies.
    $\sum_jx_{ij}\ge y_i$
    That forces a used bin to hold something but does not limit its load.

    In lot sizing, period 2 has $s_1=30$, $d_2=30$ and production $x_2=0$. What is $s_2$?

    30
    Apply $s_1+x_2=d_2+s_2$.
    60
    Stock cannot grow without production.
    0
    $30+0=30+s_2$ gives $s_2=0$.

    What does the generalised assignment problem allow that the plain assignment problem does not?

    One agent may take several jobs, as long as its budget allows.
    The "exactly one" row for agents is replaced by a budget row $\sum_jt_{ij}x_{ij}\le s_i$.
    A job may be split between agents.
    The variables are still binary, so each job goes to one agent.
    Agents may refuse all jobs and the problem has no objective.
    The objective is still the total cost or profit of the assignment.

    An integer programme has LP corner points that are not integers. What does this tell you?

    The IP is infeasible.
    Integer points may still exist inside the region.
    The best integer point need not be a corner of the LP region.
    The feasible set is a cloud of integer points, and the LP optimum may be fractional.
    Rounding the LP optimum always gives the optimum.
    Rounding may leave the feasible region or miss better points.

    The LP relaxation: bounds, gaps and the convex hull

    The LP relaxation of an IP drops the integrality requirement; its optimal value is a bound on the IP's optimum, and the closer the relaxed region hugs the integer points, the better the bound.

    Branch and bound (Part 4) is only as fast as these bounds are tight, and two models that look equivalent can differ by orders of magnitude in solving time.

    It is like wrapping a gift: a loose sheet of paper (weak formulation) leaves empty space around the box, a tight one (strong formulation) clings to the corners.

    Relaxing the integrality

    Take an IP $z_{IP}=\min\{c^\top x: Ax\ge b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n_+\}$. Its LP relaxation replaces $x\in\mathbb Z^n_+$ by $x\ge0$ (for binary variables, $0\le x\le1$) and gives $z_{LP}=\min\{c^\top x: Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}$. Every integer feasible point is also feasible for the relaxation, so the relaxation can only do better: $$z_{LP}\le z_{IP}\ \text{ for a minimisation},\qquad z_{LP}\ge z_{IP}\ \text{ for a maximisation}.$$ So the LP value is a bound, and the integrality gap $\dfrac{|z_{IP}-z_{LP}|}{|z_{IP}|}$ measures how far it is from the truth. A zero gap means the LP solves the IP.

    Rounding the LP solution is no cure. In the van example the LP plan loads $4/9$ of parcel 1, and loading the whole parcel would overload the van; in facility location the LP may open every depot a sixth of the way, and rounding up opens them all. Rounding may be infeasible, or feasible but far from optimal.

    Many formulations, one set of integer points

    Let $X$ be the set of feasible integer points. A formulation is any polyhedron $P$ whose integer points are exactly $X$, that is $P\cap\mathbb Z^n=X$. There are infinitely many: we may rescale a constraint, add a redundant one or move a line without passing a new integer point.

    If $P_1$ and $P_2$ are two formulations of the same IP and $P_1\subset P_2$, then $P_1$ is stronger than $P_2$. A stronger formulation never gives a worse bound: minimising over a smaller set can only raise the minimum (and lower the maximum), so $z_{LP}(P_2)\le z_{LP}(P_1)\le z_{IP}$ for a minimisation.

    For $X=\{x^1,\dots,x^k\}$ the convex hull is $\operatorname{Conv}(X)=\big\{\sum_i\lambda_ix^i:\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\ge0\big\}$ (Part 1: the rubber band around the points). It is the smallest convex set containing $X$. When $X$ is finite it is a polytope, so it can be written as $\{x: A^{conv}x\le b^{conv}\}$. It is the strongest possible formulation: it is contained in every convex formulation of $X$.

    Try it

    The dots are the 15 feasible integer points of a small IP (maximise $c_1x_1+c_2x_2$). Switch between three polygons that all have exactly these integer points: "Loose", "As first written" and "Convex hull". Move the objective sliders. For each setting compare the LP optimum (the large dot, red when fractional) with the best integer point (green ring). Notice that on the convex hull the LP optimum is always one of the dots.

    Let $X$ be a finite set of points. Then $\min\{c^\top x:x\in X\}=\min\{c^\top x:x\in\operatorname{Conv}(X)\}$, and the LP over $\operatorname{Conv}(X)$ has an optimal corner that lies in $X$. The same holds for mixed integer programmes (with $X$ the feasible set, then a polyhedron).

    Prove the theorem for the minimisation of $c^\top x$ over a finite $X=\{x^1,\dots,x^k\}$.

    1. Because $X\subseteq\operatorname{Conv}(X)$ (take one $\lambda_i=1$), $\min_{\operatorname{Conv}(X)}c^\top x\le\min_Xc^\top x$.

      The left side minimises over a bigger set.

    2. Let $v=\min_ic^\top x^i$ be the best value over $X$. Take any $x=\sum_i\lambda_ix^i\in\operatorname{Conv}(X)$.

      Every point of the hull has this form by definition.

    3. Then $c^\top x=\sum_i\lambda_i\,c^\top x^i\ge\sum_i\lambda_i\,v=v$, using $\lambda_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$.

      A weighted average of numbers each at least $v$ is at least $v$.

    4. Hence $\min_{\operatorname{Conv}(X)}c^\top x\ge v$, so the two minima are equal. A corner (extreme point) of $\operatorname{Conv}(X)$ cannot be a mix of two other points of the hull, so each corner is one of the $x^i$.

      Part 1: an LP over a polytope is optimal at a corner; here every corner is in $X$.

    Careful: the theorem says the convex hull is ideal, but finding its inequalities is usually as hard as the IP itself. In practice we look for formulations close to the hull and add valid inequalities (Chapter 3.3).

    The van knapsack: weights $(9,8,5,4,3)$, values $(9,5,14,11,12)$, capacity $16$. Compute the LP bound and the integrality gap.

    1. Value per kg: $12/3=4$ (parcel 5), $14/5=2.8$ (parcel 3), $11/4=2.75$ (parcel 4), $9/9=1$ (parcel 1), $5/8=0.625$ (parcel 2).

      In the LP relaxation of a knapsack the best use of capacity is by value per kg: fill with the best ratio first.

    2. Load parcels 5, 3, 4 whole: weight $3+5+4=12$, value $12+14+11=37$. Four kg remain.

      Whole items while they fit.

    3. Fill the remaining 4 kg with parcel 1: fraction $4/9$ of it, value $\tfrac49\cdot9=4$. LP bound: $37+4=41$ at $x=(4/9,0,1,1,1)$.

      The LP may split a parcel; the IP may not.

    4. The best whole plan has value $37$ (parcels 3, 4, 5; adding any other parcel breaks the 16 kg limit), so the gap is $(41-37)/37\approx10.8\%$.

      Since this is a maximisation, the LP bound lies above the optimum.

    Go deeper: why the assignment problem needs no integrality

    In the assignment model every variable appears in exactly two equality rows, one for its courier and one for its parcel, with coefficient 1. Such a constraint matrix is totally unimodular (every square submatrix has determinant $0$, $1$ or $-1$). Then every corner solves $Bx_B=b$ with $\det B=\pm1$, and by Cramer's rule $x_B=B^{-1}b$ is integral when $b$ is. So the LP relaxation is the convex hull and a plain LP solver returns an integer optimum. Shortest-path and transportation models have the same property; GAP and bin packing do not, because of their capacity rows.

    Take the same five parcels (weights 9, 8, 5, 4, 3; values 9, 5, 14, 11, 12) but a van of capacity $11$ kg. What is the LP relaxation bound (fractional loading allowed)?

    Fill by value per kg: parcel 5 (3 kg), parcel 3 (5 kg), then parcel 4 (4 kg) but only what fits.

    Parcels 5 and 3 weigh 8 kg and are worth $26$. Three kg remain, so load $3/4$ of parcel 4 (value $8.25$). Bound $=34.25$. The best whole plan is parcels 3 and 5, value $26$.

    The relaxation is allowed more points than the IP.

    More feasible points can only lower the minimum, so the LP value is a lower bound on the IP optimum.

    • Compare formulations by inclusion: the smaller polyhedron with the same integer points is stronger.
    • Report the gap as a percentage of the integer optimum.
    • Remember the sign: minimisation bounds from below, maximisation from above.
    • Assuming a fractional LP value is "close enough" to round.
    • Believing that adding constraints always shrinks the integer set; valid ones keep every integer point.
    • Thinking the convex hull can always be written down easily.
    1. The LP relaxation gives a bound on the IP; the gap measures its quality.
    2. A formulation $P_1\subset P_2$ with the same integer points is stronger and never gives a worse bound.
    3. Over the convex hull of the integer points the LP and the IP have the same optimum, but the hull is hard to describe.

    For a maximisation IP, the LP relaxation value is 41 and the best integer solution found has value 37. What can you say?

    The optimum lies between 41 and 45.
    The LP is a bound in a definite direction for a maximisation.
    The optimum lies between 37 and 41.
    37 is achievable and 41 is an upper bound.
    The optimum is 41.
    An LP optimum is only attained if it is integer.

    Two formulations $P_1\subset P_2$ describe the same integer points of a minimisation. Which is true?

    $z_{LP}(P_1)\le z_{LP}(P_2)$.
    A smaller region cannot give a smaller minimum.
    $z_{LP}(P_1)\ge z_{LP}(P_2)$.
    Minimising over a smaller set can only raise the minimum, closer to the IP value.
    They always give the same bound.
    Then no formulation would be better than another.

    Why is every corner of $\operatorname{Conv}(X)$ a point of $X$?

    A point of the hull that is not in $X$ is a mix of points of $X$, so it is not extreme.
    Extreme points cannot be convex combinations of other points of the set.
    Because the hull is defined by integer coefficients.
    Integer coefficients are not the reason.
    Because $X$ has more than two points.
    The count of points does not matter.

    An LP relaxation returns an integer optimal solution. For the IP this means:

    It is a feasible integer point and its value equals the LP bound, so it is optimal.
    Any integer solution is feasible for the relaxation; reaching the bound means nothing better exists.
    Nothing; the IP must be solved separately.
    No further search is needed.
    The problem has several optima.
    That does not follow from an integer LP solution.

    Strong formulations: facility location, tight $M$ and cover inequalities

    Two ways of writing the same forcing constraint can give very different LP bounds, and a handful of extra valid inequalities can close most of a gap.

    This is the difference between a solver finishing in seconds and one that runs overnight, and you can control it when you write the model.

    It is like two tax forms asking for the same information: one tells you exactly where each number goes, the other lets you spread it across the page and still get past the clerk.

    Kaveri Courier

    The owner is now choosing which depot sites to open. Writing the model so that the LP relaxation hugs the integer plans decides whether the solver confirms the choice in seconds or searches for hours. The same advice covers the van loads: a tight forcing constraint or a cover inequality is what keeps the loading decision of Chapter 3.1 cheap to solve.

    Facility location: individual versus aggregated forcing

    Part −1 introduced the forcing constraint and the rule "choose the tightest $M$". Lecture 3 applies it to facility location. Call $P_1$ the formulation with a forcing row for every pair, $x_{ij}\le y_j$, and $P_2$ the one with one aggregated row per depot, $$\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}\le m\,y_j\qquad\forall j .$$ Both enforce "no service from a closed depot" for 0/1 variables. But $P_2$ has fewer rows ($n$ instead of $mn$), so which is better?

    $P_1\subseteq P_2$, and the inclusion is strict in general; for example when $n\ge2$ and $m=kn$ with $k\ge2$. Hence the LP bound of $P_1$ is at least the LP bound of $P_2$ for a minimisation.

    Show that every point of $P_1$ lies in $P_2$ but not the other way round (take $m=kn$ with $k\ge2$).

    1. Sum the $m$ rows $x_{ij}\le y_j$ over $i$: $\sum_ix_{ij}\le m\,y_j$. So any point satisfying all individual rows satisfies the aggregated row: $P_1\subseteq P_2$.

      The aggregated row is a sum of the individual ones, so it is implied.

    2. Assign customers to depots in $n$ groups of $k$ customers: $x_{ij}=1$ if customer $i$ is in group $j$, else $0$. Take $y_j=k/m=1/n$ for every depot.

      Each customer is served in full (assignment rows hold) but each depot is only "$1/n$ open".

    3. Aggregated row: $\sum_ix_{ij}=k\le m\cdot(k/m)=k$. It holds with equality: the point is in $P_2$.

      The load $k$ is exactly what $m\,y_j$ allows.

    4. Individual row: for a customer in group $j$ we need $1=x_{ij}\le y_j=1/n$, which is false when $n\ge2$. So the point is not in $P_1$ and $P_1\subsetneq P_2$.

      Fractional openings are allowed by $P_2$ but each customer's own row says "depot must be fully open".

    Try it

    Three depots with fixed costs $30,40,40$ and six customers. Switch between the weak (aggregated) and the strong (individual) formulation and read the LP bound and the opening values $y$. Then slide the fixed-cost scale. Notice how many depots the weak LP opens and how little it pays for them.

    There is even a closed form for the weak bound. In the aggregated model, given the assignments $x$, the cheapest openings are $y_j=\tfrac1m\sum_ix_{ij}$ (the smallest value the row allows). Each customer then pays a $1/m$ share of the fixed cost of every depot it uses, and the LP just lets each customer pick the cheapest depot: $$z_{LP}^{weak}=\sum_{i=1}^m\ \min_j\Big(c_{ij}+\frac{f_j}{m}\Big).$$ The weak bound is typically far below the integer cost, as the next example shows.

    Tight $M$ in lot sizing, and a better formulation

    The same lesson governs lot sizing. The row $x_t\le M\,y_t$ is valid with $M=\sum_kd_k$ (all demand), but period $t$ never needs to produce more than the demand of periods $t,\dots,n$, so $M_t=d_t+d_{t+1}+\dots+d_n$ is valid and smaller, hence stronger.

    A third, still stronger formulation changes the variables. Let $w_{kt}$ be the quantity produced in period $k$ to meet the demand of period $t$ (with $k\le t$). Then $$\sum_{k=1}^tw_{kt}=d_t,\qquad w_{kt}\le d_t\,y_k\ \ (k\le t),\qquad x_k=\sum_{t\ge k}w_{kt}.$$ Each row $w_{kt}\le d_ty_k$ has the tightest possible multiplier: the whole amount $d_t$ that period $t$ needs. Compare the three on the instance of Chapter 3.1.

    The extended formulation reaches the integer optimum here, and this is no accident: for uncapacitated single-item lot sizing, a classical result says its LP relaxation is integral at the corners, so it describes the convex hull in the original variables. To compare formulations in different variable spaces we project out the extra variables: the extended formulation is better if the set $\{(x,y):(x,y,w)\in Q\text{ for some }w\}$ lies inside the original polyhedron. The point $x_t=d_t$, $y_t=d_t/M$ is feasible for the weak formulation but violates $w_{tt}\le d_t\,y_t$ unless $y_t=1$, so it is cut off.

    Valid inequalities and cover cuts

    A second way to strengthen a model is to add inequalities that every integer point already satisfies but some fractional LP points violate.

    An inequality $\pi^\top x\le\pi_0$ is valid for $X$ if every $x\in X$ satisfies it. It is a cut for the LP relaxation if it also excludes the current optimal LP point. Adding valid inequalities keeps all integer points and shrinks the relaxation towards the convex hull.

    For the knapsack row $\sum_ja_jx_j\le C$ (all $a_j\gt0$), a set $S$ of items is a cover if $\sum_{j\in S}a_j\gt C$: it cannot all be loaded together. It is a minimal cover if removing any one item makes it fit.

    If $S$ is a cover then $\displaystyle\sum_{j\in S}x_j\le|S|-1$ is valid for every knapsack solution.

    Prove the cover inequality and apply it to the van: $S=\{1,3,4\}$ (weights $9,5,4$, capacity $16$).

    1. Suppose a feasible binary $x$ had $\sum_{j\in S}x_j=|S|$, so all items of $S$ are loaded.

      Proof by contradiction: the only way to break the inequality is to load every item of $S$.

    2. Then the weight of the load is at least $\sum_{j\in S}a_j\gt C$, because the other loaded items only add weight.

      This is the definition of a cover.

    3. That violates the capacity row, so no feasible $x$ loads all of $S$, and $\sum_{j\in S}x_j\le|S|-1$.

      Integers: a sum of $|S|$ binaries that is not $|S|$ is at most $|S|-1$.

    4. For $S=\{1,3,4\}$: $9+5+4=18\gt16$ and removing item 1, 3 or 4 leaves $9$, $13$ or $14$, all at most $16$, so it is a minimal cover and $x_1+x_3+x_4\le2$ is valid.

      The LP point $(4/9,0,1,1,1)$ has $4/9+1+1=22/9\approx2.44\gt2$, so the cut removes it.

Then press "Add all minimal covers". Notice how the LP bound falls from 41 to the integer optimum. Try also a set that is not a cover: the tool tells you its cut would be invalid.

    Go deeper: lifting and the strength of a cover cut

    A minimal cover inequality is usually not a facet of the knapsack polytope. It can be lifted: items outside the cover that weigh at least as much as the heaviest item inside can be added with coefficient 1, giving an extended cover inequality such as $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4\le2$ for the cover $\{2,3,4\}$ (weights $8,5,4$): item 1 weighs $9\ge8$, and any three of the four items weigh at least $4+5+8=17\gt16$, so at most two can be loaded. Modern MIP solvers separate such cuts automatically at the root node of branch and bound.
