    Which facility location formulation has the stronger LP relaxation, even though it has more constraints?

    The aggregated row is the sum of the individual ones.

    $x_{ij}\le y_j$ for every pair implies the aggregated row but not conversely, so the individual-row formulation is contained in the aggregated one.

    • Prefer many small, tight forcing rows over a few aggregated ones when the LP solves fast enough.
    • Derive $M$ from the data: remaining demand, capacity, or a bound on the variable.
    • Add cover cuts from minimal covers of capacity rows.
    • Using $M=10^6$ "to be safe".
    • Adding a cut that excludes a feasible integer point.
    • Comparing formulations by the number of constraints rather than by their relaxations.
    1. For facility location, individual rows $x_{ij}\le y_j$ give a stronger relaxation than aggregated rows, and the weak bound has a closed form $\sum_i\min_j(c_{ij}+f_j/m)$.
    2. Tight big-M values (such as the demand still to come) and extended formulations tighten fixed-charge models; the extended lot-sizing formulation is exact.
    3. Valid inequalities such as cover cuts shrink the relaxation without removing integer points.

    The weak facility location LP opens a depot $20\%$ and serves $20\%$ of the customers from it, each one completely ($x_{ij}=1$). Which is true?

    It satisfies every individual row $x_{ij}\le y_j$.
    Check one customer: $x_{ij}=1$ against $y_j=0.2$.
    It satisfies the aggregated row but violates individual rows.
    The aggregated row $\sum_ix_{ij}\le m\,y_j$ holds for this point (with equality), while $x_{ij}=1\gt y_j=0.2$ breaks the individual rows.
    It is an integer point.
    A depot open $20\%$ is fractional.

    Why is a cover inequality valid?

    It is the sum of the knapsack row and the bounds.
    The sum would carry the weights $a_j$ and the capacity $C$, not $|S|-1$.
    Loading every item of a cover would break the capacity.
    So at most $|S|-1$ of them can be loaded together.
    Because every cover contains at most one item.
    Covers contain several items.

    Weights $(6,5,4,3)$ and capacity $10$. Which set is a minimal cover?

    $\{1,2,3\}$ with weight 15.
    Is the cover still a cover after removing item 3?
    $\{1,2\}$ with weight 11.
    $11\gt10$, and removing either item leaves 6 or 5.
    $\{3,4\}$ with weight 7.
    7 fits in 10, so it is not a cover.

    An extended formulation with extra variables $w_{kt}$ is declared stronger. What do we compare?

    Its projection onto the original variables, which must lie inside the original relaxation.
    Only then can the two be compared in the same space.
    The number of rows of each model.
    More rows do not mean a tighter relaxation.
    The number of binary variables.
    They can be equal in both.

    Case studies: facility location variants (Lab 1) and the GAP (Lab 2)

    Lab 1 stretches the facility location model to capacities, a fixed number of depots and a worst-case objective; Lab 2 solves the GAP with an LP-based search.

    These are the models you will actually type into Gurobi, and the reading skills from Chapters 3.2 and 3.3 tell you which version to expect to be fast.

    It is like learning four dishes from one base recipe: each variant changes one ingredient and the cooking time changes with it.

    Lab 1 question by question

    Question 1: aggregated rows with the integrality dropped. The lab asks you to run the facility location model with $\sum_ix_{ij}\le m\,y_j$ and $x_{ij}\ge0$ instead of binary variables. Expect from Chapter 3.3 that the optimal $y_j$ are small fractions and that the objective is far below the integer optimum. The point of the experiment is the bound, not the plan. The trade-off to notice: with $m=1000$ customers and $n=100$ candidate depots the aggregated model has $n=100$ forcing rows, while individual rows would need $mn=100{,}000$. The tighter model is larger.

    Question 2: the capacitated version (CFLP). Customer $i$ has demand $d_i$ and depot $j$ handles at most $q_j$ units. A natural model, if each customer is served by exactly one depot, is $$\min\ \sum_jf_jy_j+\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ \sum_jx_{ij}=1,\quad \sum_id_ix_{ij}\le q_j\,y_j,\quad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\},\ y_j\in\{0,1\}.$$ The capacity row doubles as the forcing row: a closed depot has capacity $0$. Two versions follow the lab's wording. The aggregated version uses just this row. The disaggregated version adds $x_{ij}\le y_j$ for every pair; they are redundant for integer $y$ but tighten the LP. If demand may be split, let $x_{ij}\in[0,1]$ be the share of customer $i$'s demand served from $j$: the same rows apply and the model becomes a mixed integer programme with only the $y_j$ integer.

    Question 3: the $p$-median problem. No fixed costs, but exactly $p$ depots must open: $$\min\ \sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ \sum_jx_{ij}=1,\quad x_{ij}\le y_j,\quad \sum_jy_j=p,\quad x_{ij},y_j\in\{0,1\}.$$ Question 4: the $p$-center problem. Instead of the total distance we minimise the largest distance between a customer and its depot. Introduce a variable $z$ for that largest distance: $$\min\ z\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ z\ge\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}\ \ \forall i,\quad \sum_jx_{ij}=1,\quad x_{ij}\le y_j,\quad \sum_jy_j=p,\quad x_{ij},y_j\in\{0,1\}.$$ Because exactly one $x_{ij}$ equals 1 in each customer's row, $\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}$ is customer $i$'s distance, and minimising $z$ pushes it down onto the largest of them (the min-max trick). The lab runs the two $p$-problems with $p$ equal to $10\%$ and $20\%$ of the potential facilities, rounded to a whole number.

    Six sites on a highway lie at kilometre marks $2,7,10,11,12,18$; every site is both a customer and a candidate depot, $c_{ij}=|{\rm km}_i-{\rm km}_j|$, and $p=2$. Compare the $p$-median and $p$-center solutions.

    1. There are $\binom62=15$ choices of two depots; for each, each customer goes to the closer one.

      Given the open depots, the best assignment is nearest-open-depot, so we only enumerate the open sets.

    2. Open the sites at km $2$ and $11$: distances $0,4,1,0,1,7$. Total $13$, maximum $7$.

      The site at 7 is nearer to 11 (4 km) than to 2 (5 km); the site at 18 is 7 km from 11.

    3. Open km $7$ and $18$: distances $5,0,3,4,5,0$. Total $17$, maximum $5$.

      The far site at 18 now has its own depot, so the worst case drops.

    4. Checking all 15 pairs, $\{2,11\}$ is the unique minimiser of the total ($13$) and $\{7,18\}$ the unique minimiser of the maximum ($5$).

      Different objectives, different depots: the $p$-median serves the cluster of sites near 10 to 12 well; the $p$-center protects the worst-off site.

    CFLP check. Customers have demands $d=(4,6,5)$; two depots have capacities $q=(10,9)$ and fixed costs $f=(20,15)$. Is the plan "depot 1 open serving customers 1 and 2, depot 2 open serving customer 3" feasible, and what do the capacity rows say?

    1. Depot 1 load: $d_1x_{11}+d_2x_{21}+d_3x_{31}=4+6+0=10\le q_1y_1=10\cdot1$. Depot 2 load: $5\le9\cdot1$.

      Each capacity row compares the load with $q_jy_j$.

    2. Every customer appears in exactly one depot, so the assignment rows hold.

      Each row $\sum_jx_{ij}=1$ is satisfied.

    3. Fixed cost $20+15=35$. Total demand is $15$ and total open capacity is $19\ge15$, which is necessary.

      If you closed depot 1, open capacity $9\lt15$ would make the model infeasible.

    Lab 2: the generalised assignment problem

    Lab 2 reads GAP instances from files whose first line gives the number of agents and jobs, followed by the cost matrix, the resource (time) matrix and the capacity of each agent, then solves the instances two ways: a hand-written branch and bound that calls an LP solver for the relaxation, and Gurobi with presolve and cuts switched off (both are compared in Part 4). The lecture states GAP as a profit maximisation; the Gurobi script of the lab minimises cost, and the two are equivalent since $\max\sum p_{ij}x_{ij}$ is $-\min\sum(-p_{ij})x_{ij}$.

    Why does the lab need a search at all? Because the capacity rows make the LP relaxation fractional. Below is a small instance of the same model.

    Try it

    Three agents and six jobs; each button shows cost / time. Agents have time budgets 12, 12 and 10. Assign each job to one agent, watch the bars of time used, and try to beat the cost shown for the "Best assignment". Then press "Show LP relaxation": notice which job the LP splits between agents and how much cheaper the LP plan is.

    In a basic (corner) solution of the GAP relaxation, at most $m$ jobs are split between agents, where $m$ is the number of agents.

    Prove the fact above, then check it on the widget's instance, where the LP corner splits one job.

    1. The model has $n$ job rows and $m$ budget rows, so $n+m$ constraints besides the bounds. A basic solution has at most $n+m$ non-zero variables $x_{ij}$.

      Part 1: a basis has one column per constraint row, so at most that many variables are non-zero.

    2. Every job has at least one non-zero $x_{ij}$ (its row sums to 1). A job split between agents has at least two.

      One non-zero entry would have to equal 1, so the job is not split.

    3. If $r$ jobs are split, the number of non-zeros is at least $n+r$. So $n+r\le n+m$, giving $r\le m$.

      Each split job contributes at least one extra non-zero beyond its first.

    4. On the widget instance ($m=3$) the LP optimum splits only job 3, half to agent 1 and half to agent 3, with cost $46$ against the integer optimum $53$.

      One split job is within the bound of 3, and the bound explains why a few branching decisions suffice to remove it.

    Go deeper: reading the lab code

    The lab's script builds exactly the model above with addVars for $x_{ij}$, addConstrs for the "exactly one" rows and the budget rows, and the objective with quicksum (see Part −1, Chapter 3 and Practice/L3). The Lab 1 reader keeps only numeric tokens from the instance file, so any text label in a data file silently shifts the position of every later number. Always print the first few parsed values and compare them with the file before trusting a result.

    A GAP instance has $m=5$ agents and $n=100$ jobs. How many binary variables $x_{ij}$ does the model have?

    One variable per (agent, job) pair.

    $5\times100=500$.

    For the same instance, how many constraints are there besides the binary restrictions?

    One "exactly one" row per job and one budget row per agent.

    $100+5=105$.

    In the widget table, agent 2's cost / time pairs for jobs 1 to 6 are $11/3$, $12/7$, $11/3$, $13/6$, $9/3$, $8/7$. Agent 2 is given jobs 1, 3 and 5. What is the total cost of these three jobs?

    Add the cost (first number) of jobs 1, 3 and 5; the time used is $3+3+3$, within the budget of 12.

    Costs $11+11+9=31$, and the time used is $9\le12$, so the plan is within budget.

    In the highway example, depots at km $7$ and $18$ are open. What is the largest distance between a site and its nearest open depot?

    Check sites at km 2, 10, 11, 12.

    Distances from the sites at 2, 7, 10, 11, 12, 18: $5,0,3,4,5,0$. The largest is $5$.

    A GAP relaxation has $m=3$ agents. At most how many jobs can be split in a basic LP solution?

    Use the counting argument: non-zeros $\le n+m$.

    At most $m=3$.

    • Start every variant from the base facility location model and change one thing: capacity, a count of depots or the objective.
    • Use the min-max trick for worst-case objectives.
    • Print and check parsed instance data.
    • Using the aggregated capacity row alone and expecting a tight LP.
    • Letting the objective of $p$-median drive a $p$-center decision.
    • Assuming a GAP solves as an LP.
    1. Capacitated, $p$-median and $p$-center facility location are small changes to the base model: capacity rows $\sum_id_ix_{ij}\le q_jy_j$, a count row $\sum_jy_j=p$, and a min-max variable $z$.
    2. The GAP relaxation is generally fractional, with at most $m$ split jobs in a basic solution, so a solver needs branching or cuts.
    3. The lectures' maximise-profit GAP and the labs' minimise-cost GAP are the same model.

    Which row turns the uncapacitated facility location model into the $p$-median model (besides removing fixed costs)?

    $\sum_ix_{ij}\le p$
    That limits customers per depot, not depots.
    $\sum_jy_j=p$
    Exactly $p$ depots must be open.
    $z\ge x_{ij}$
    That belongs to a min-max objective.

    In the $p$-center model what does $z$ represent at the optimum?

    The largest distance from any customer to its assigned depot.
    The rows $z\ge\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}$ bound every customer's distance.
    The sum of all distances.
    That would be the $p$-median objective.
    The number of open depots.
    That is fixed to $p$.

    Splittable demand in the CFLP changes the model how?

    The variables $y_j$ become continuous.
    Opening is still a yes/no decision.
    The $x_{ij}$ become continuous shares in $[0,1]$.
    Only the $y_j$ stay binary, giving a MIP.
    The capacity rows are dropped.
    Depots still have limited capacity.

    A GAP relaxation has 4 agents. A basic LP solution can have at most how many split jobs?

    2
    The bound is the number of agents, not half of it.
    4
    At most $m=4$ jobs are split.
    As many as there are jobs.
    The counting argument caps the splits.
    Where we are in the story

    Part 3 has given Kaveri Courier its models: which depots to open (facility location), how to load a van (knapsack and bin packing) and who does which job (the generalised assignment problem). Two things are still missing, a way to actually find the best integer plan and a way to prove it is best. Part 4 supplies both with branch and bound, starting from a two-van planning model of the same kind as the loading decision of Chapter 3.1, and returns to the GAP in Lab 2.

    A depot model uses $x_t\le M\,y_t$. If the largest possible production is 50, which $M$ gives the strongest valid LP relaxation?

    $M=50$
    The smallest valid $M$ forces $y_t\ge x_t/50$, the least fractional opening.
    $M=500$
    Valid but weaker: $y_t$ may be a tenth of what it should be.
    $M=1$
    That would cut off real production quantities.

    For a minimisation, a stronger formulation $P_1\subset P_2$ of the same IP has LP bound ...

    no larger than that of $P_2$
    Think about minimising over a smaller set.
    at least as large as that of $P_2$, and at most the IP optimum
    The smaller region can only raise the LP minimum, never above the IP minimum.
    always equal to the IP optimum
    Only for the convex hull.

    Weights $(9,8,5,4,3)$, capacity 16. The set $\{2,3,4\}$ has weight 17. The cover inequality is:

    $x_2+x_3+x_4\le3$
    That allows all three, which the capacity forbids.
    $x_2+x_3+x_4\le2$
    At most $|S|-1=2$ of the three can be loaded together.
    $x_2+x_3+x_4\le17$
    The weight total is not the right-hand side.

    Which statement about the GAP relaxation is correct?

    It is always integral because the constraint matrix has "exactly one" rows.
    The budget rows break total unimodularity.
    It can split jobs, with at most $m$ split jobs at a corner.
    Counting non-zeros of a basic solution gives $n+r\le n+m$.
    It is infeasible whenever some agent's budget is small.
    The relaxation can use other agents.

    Which constraint says "depot $j$ may serve customers only if it is open" for one customer $i$?

    $y_j\le x_{ij}$
    That reverses cause and effect: opening would force service.
    $x_{ij}\le y_j$
    If $y_j=0$ then $x_{ij}=0$.
    $x_{ij}+y_j\ge1$
    That says "serve or open", a different rule.

    An LP has an optimal solution at a non-integer corner. The same polyhedron's integer points have best value 12 and the LP optimum is 13.2 (maximise). The gap is about:

    1.2%
    Divide the difference by the integer value 12.
    10%
    $(13.2-12)/12=0.1$.
    13.2%
    That is the LP value, not a ratio.

    Lecture 4 shows how an integer programme is actually solved: bracket the unknown optimum between a plan you can achieve and a bound you can prove, then split the problem into smaller pieces until the two meet. This part covers LP-based bounding, branching and the three ways to prune, node and variable choice, GUB/SOS branching, preprocessing, and finally what Gurobi prints while it does all this (Lab 2).

    You need: Part 1 (LP optimum at a corner), Part 2 (dual prices and the dual simplex method, used lightly), and Part 3 (integer programmes, the LP relaxation and the integrality gap, strong formulations, the GAP model of Lab 2).

    Bounds, relaxations and the optimality gap

    To solve an integer programme you squeeze its unknown optimum between a plan you can actually carry out (an upper bound, for a minimisation) and a number you can prove nobody can beat (a lower bound from a relaxation).

    Every solver log you will read at the end of this part reports exactly these two numbers and the gap between them, and branch and bound is the machine that closes that gap. Part 3 ended with Kaveri Courier's models written down; here the owner hands one of them to a solver. The two-van problem below has the same ingredients as the formulations of Chapter 3.1: whole-number variables, a linear cost and linear requirement rows. Only the numbers are new, and Lab 2 later returns to the assign-jobs-to-agents model of Chapter 3.4.

    It is like estimating a journey time: the fastest conceivable time (straight line at top speed) is a lower bound, a trip you have really driven is an upper bound, and the closer they are, the better you know the answer.

    The two-van problem

    One example runs through the next two chapters. Kaveri Courier serves two routes, A and B, every shift. A shift of a type-1 van costs $4$ (in thousands of rupees) and delivers $6$ crates on route A and $6$ crates on route B. A shift of a type-2 van costs $3$ and delivers $2$ crates on route A and $7$ on route B. Route A must receive at least $43$ crates and route B at least $55$. The firm owns at most $12$ vans of each type. How many van shifts $x_1$ (type 1) and $x_2$ (type 2) minimise the cost?

    $$\min\ 4x_1+3x_2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad 6x_1+2x_2\ge 43,\quad 6x_1+7x_2\ge 55,\quad 0\le x_1,x_2\le 12,\quad x_1,x_2\in\mathbb Z.$$

    Vans come whole, so this is an integer programme (IP). Call its optimal value $z^*$; we do not know it yet.

    Drop the integers: the LP relaxation

    Recall from Part 3 that the LP relaxation keeps every constraint but allows fractional $x$. Its feasible region contains every integer plan, so its optimum $z_{LP}$ can only be as good or better: for a minimisation $z_{LP}\le z^*$.

    For the two-van problem both route rows are tight at the LP optimum. Subtracting them gives $5x_2=12$, so $x_2=2.4$, and then $6x_1=43-4.8$, so $x_1=38.2/6\approx6.367$. The cost is $4\cdot6.367+3\cdot2.4=32.667$ (exactly $98/3$).

    Why can nothing cheaper exist, integer or not? Add the two route rows and divide by $3$: $\tfrac13(6x_1+2x_2)+\tfrac13(6x_1+7x_2)=4x_1+3x_2$. Every feasible plan therefore costs at least $\tfrac13(43+55)=98/3$. That one-line argument is a certificate for the lower bound; the weights $\tfrac13,\tfrac13$ are the dual prices of Part 2.

    The LP plan uses $6.367$ type-1 vans and $2.4$ type-2 vans, which no courier can run. A manager rounds each number to the nearest whole van, giving $(6,2)$. What do you expect?

    It is feasible and optimal.
    Check the crates delivered on route A: $6\cdot6+2\cdot2$.
    It is infeasible: route A falls short.
    $6\cdot6+2\cdot2=40<43$.
    It is feasible but costs more than the true optimum.
    It is not feasible at all, so it cannot be compared.

    Rounding down (or to the nearest) removes crates that the LP needed. Rounding every number up gives $(7,3)$, which is feasible but costs $37$. The true optimum is cheaper than that, and the next panel lets you see all of these points.

    Try it

    Click through the five chips: the LP optimum, three roundings and the true integer optimum. Dots on the grid are whole-number plans (solid dots are feasible). Slide the cost level $k$ and watch which feasible dots lie on or below the dashed cost line. Notice that the cheapest rounding is not the optimum, and that the LP value is below every feasible plan.

    Two kinds of bound

    Rounding fails for the reason you just saw: with $n$ variables there are $2^n$ ways to round each up or down, none of them is guaranteed feasible, and a feasible one can be far from optimal. Instead we use two cheap numbers that sandwich $z^*$.

    For a minimisation:

    • An upper bound $z_{UB}$ (also primal bound) is the cost of any feasible integer plan. The best one found so far is the incumbent.
    • A lower bound $z_{LB}$ (also dual bound) is a number that no feasible plan can beat, typically the value of a relaxation such as the LP relaxation.
    • The optimality gap is $$\text{gap}=\frac{z_{UB}-z_{LB}}{|z_{UB}|}\times100\%.$$ It is the largest possible percentage by which the incumbent can still be improved. Gap $=0$ proves the incumbent optimal.

    For a minimisation, $z_{LB}\le z^*\le z_{UB}$ at every moment of a solve. The lower bound can only rise, the upper bound can only fall, and the search stops when they meet.

    Careful: the gap is measured against the incumbent, not against the unknown optimum, so it is a guarantee, not an estimate. It is also undefined when $z_{UB}=0$. If all costs and variables are whole numbers, every plan has a whole-number cost, so you may round a lower bound up: from $32.667$ to $33$.

    Bracket the optimum of the two-van problem using only the LP and a rounding, then tighten the bracket when someone finds the plan $(7,2)$.

    1. Lower bound: $z_{LP}=98/3\approx32.667$. All data are whole, so $z^*\ge33$.

      The cost of a whole plan is a whole number, and the smallest whole number at least $32.667$ is $33$.

    2. Upper bound: round the LP point up to $(7,3)$. Route A: $42+6=48\ge43$. Route B: $42+21=63\ge55$. Feasible, cost $4\cdot7+3\cdot3=37$.

      A feasible plan is all we need for an upper bound, however clumsy.

    3. So $33\le z^*\le37$. Gap with the raw LP value: $(37-32.667)/37=11.7\%$. With the rounded bound $33$: $(37-33)/37=10.8\%$.

      The gap tells us how much we could still be wasting.

    4. Now take the plan $(7,2)$: route A $42+4=46\ge43$, route B $42+14=56\ge55$, cost $28+6=34$. The bracket shrinks to $33\le z^*\le34$ and the gap to $(34-33)/34=2.9\%$.

      A better plan lowers $z_{UB}$; it does not change the lower bound.

    5. The true optimum is $34$ (the next chapter proves it by branch and bound), so the gap of $2.9\%$ was never a mistake of the plan; it was only the lower bound being too low.

      A gap can stay open because the bound is weak even when the incumbent is already optimal. Closing it requires better bounds, which is what branching provides.

    The strength of a formulation is the strength of its bound

    Part 3 showed that two formulations with the same integer points can have different LP relaxations. If $P_1\subset P_2$, then $P_1$ is the stronger formulation and its LP bound is at least as high (for a minimisation). A weak formulation gives a low $z_{LB}$, a large gap, and a long search later. A formulation whose LP region is the convex hull of the integer points would give $z_{LB}=z^*$ at once.

    Application

    Two jobs, $x_1$ and $x_2$, cannot run in the same shift, and we want to schedule as many as possible: $\max x_1+x_2$ with $x_1,x_2\in\{0,1\}$. Writing the conflict as $2x_1+2x_2\le3$ is correct for integers, but its LP bound is $1.5$. Writing it as $x_1+x_2\le1$ describes the same integer points, and its LP bound is $1$, the true answer. Same problem, same integer points, different bound.

    The toolbox around the bounds

    MethodWhat it doesGives
    LP relaxationdrop integrality and solve an LPlower bound (this part)
    Other relaxationsreplace the objective by an easier lower estimate, or move hard constraints into the objective (Lagrangian relaxation, which Lecture 4 postpones to a later lecture; this site does not cover it)lower bound
    Cutting planesrepeatedly find an inequality that cuts off the LP point but no integer point, and add ittighter lower bound (used again for the TSP, Part 5)
    Branch and boundsplit the feasible set and bound each pieceexact optimum (next chapter)
    Branch and cutbranch and bound with cuts added inside the nodesexact optimum, stronger bounds
    Branch and pricewhen there are huge numbers of variables, add columns only when the dual prices say they can improve the LP (column generation)exact optimum for routing-type models
    Heuristicsgreedy rules, local search, large neighbourhood search, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, tabu searchupper bounds (good plans, no proof)
    Go deeper: why the gap is divided by the incumbent

    Different programs divide by the incumbent, by the bound or by the larger of the two. Gurobi divides the difference by the absolute incumbent value, as above, and stops by default when this falls below $10^{-4}$ ($0.01\%$). The choice matters only when the objective is close to zero, where every definition blows up; in that case solvers also check an absolute gap.

    A minimisation run has an incumbent of $46$ and a best lower bound of $40$. What is the optimality gap in percent?

    Divide the difference by the incumbent, not by the bound.

    $(46-40)/46=0.1304$, so $13.04\%$.

    In the two-van problem the plan $x=(6,4)$ is checked: route A gets $36+8=44$ crates and route B gets $36+28=64$. What does its cost of $36$ tell us?

    Is the plan feasible? What does any feasible plan tell us about the optimum of a minimisation?

    Both routes are served ($44\ge43$, $64\ge55$), so the plan is feasible and the optimum cannot be worse than its cost: an upper bound of $36$.

    All costs and all variables of a minimisation IP are whole numbers, and the LP relaxation has value $18.4$. What is the best lower bound you can state for the IP?

    The IP optimum is a whole number that is at least $18.4$.

    The smallest whole number not below $18.4$ is $19$.

    Two binary variables with $\max x_1+x_2$ and the constraint $2x_1+2x_2\le3$. What is the optimal value of the LP relaxation?

    Take $x_1+x_2$ as large as the constraint allows with $0\le x_i\le1$.

    $x_1+x_2\le1.5$ and $(0.75,0.75)$ reaches it, so the LP value is $1.5$ while the IP value is $1$.

    $P_1\subset P_2$ are two formulations of the same minimisation IP. How does the LP bound over $P_1$ compare with the LP bound over $P_2$?

    Minimising over a smaller set can only give a larger or equal minimum.

    Every point of $P_1$ is in $P_2$, so $P_2$'s minimum is at most $P_1$'s. The stronger formulation has the higher (better) lower bound.

    • State both bounds and the gap whenever you quote a result.
    • Round a lower bound up when all costs and variables are whole numbers.
    • Check that a rounded plan is feasible before calling it an upper bound.
    • Rounding the LP point and calling it the answer.
    • Dividing the gap by the lower bound or by $z^*$ (which you do not know).
    • Thinking a large gap means the incumbent is poor: it may be optimal with a weak bound.
    1. The LP relaxation value is a lower bound (for a minimisation) and any feasible integer plan is an upper bound; the optimum lies between them.
    2. The gap $(z_{UB}-z_{LB})/|z_{UB}|$ is a guarantee of how much the incumbent could still be improved, and it is zero exactly when optimality is proved.
    3. Rounding the LP solution may be infeasible or poor; stronger formulations raise the lower bound, and branch and bound is the systematic way to close what remains.

    For a minimisation IP, which statement is always true?

    The LP relaxation value is an upper bound on the IP optimum.
    The relaxation has more feasible points, so it can only do better (lower).
    The LP relaxation value is at most the IP optimum.
    Every integer plan is also an LP plan, so the LP minimum cannot be larger.
    The LP relaxation value equals the IP optimum after rounding.
    Rounding can break feasibility, so the values can differ.

    Gap $=0$ means:

    The LP relaxation is integral.
    It could be, but the gap compares the incumbent with the best bound, not with the root.
    The solver stopped at its time limit.
    A time limit usually leaves a positive gap.
    The incumbent is proved optimal.
    No plan can beat the lower bound, and the incumbent has that value.

    The gap is $5\%$ and nothing else is known. How much cheaper than the incumbent could the true optimum be?

    At most $5\%$ of the incumbent's cost.
    The gap is defined as the largest possible relative improvement.
    Exactly $5\%$.
    The optimum may well be equal to the incumbent.
    At least $5\%$.
    It is a ceiling on improvement, not a floor.

    Which tool normally produces a good upper bound on a hard IP?

    The LP relaxation.
    That is a lower bound for a minimisation.
    A cutting plane.
    Cuts improve lower bounds.
    A heuristic such as local search.
    A heuristic returns a real feasible plan, hence an upper bound.

    Branch and bound: split, solve, prune

    Branch and bound cuts an integer programme into smaller integer programmes by adding a bound on one variable, solves the LP relaxation of each piece, and throws a piece away as soon as its bound proves it cannot hold a better plan.

    It is the engine inside every IP solver, and the exam asks you to run it by hand: solve node LPs, choose a branch, apply the three pruning rules and read off the optimum.

    It is like searching a huge library for the cheapest book: you do not open every book, you read the sign on each section and skip any section whose cheapest possible book already costs more than the one in your hand.

    Divide and conquer

    Let $X$ be the set of feasible integer plans and $z^*=\min\{c^\top x:x\in X\}$. Suppose we split $X$ into smaller sets $X_1,\dots,X_k$ whose union is $X$. If $z_i$ is the best cost inside $X_i$, then $$z^*=\min_i z_i.$$ So it is enough to solve the pieces, and each piece may again be split. The only open question is how to split.

    The standard answer uses the LP solution. Suppose the relaxation of the current piece returns a value $v$ for an integer variable $x_j$ and $v$ is not a whole number. No integer plan has $x_j$ strictly between $\lfloor v\rfloor$ and $\lceil v\rceil$, so every integer plan lies in one of two pieces: $$x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor\qquad\text{or}\qquad x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil .$$ This is branching. No integer plan is lost, and the fractional LP point is cut off from both pieces, so the next LP must move. For a binary variable the pieces are simply $x_j=0$ and $x_j=1$.

    Each piece is a node of a tree. The root is the original problem, and each node carries its own list of added bounds. Splitting in two is common but not required: for the TSP one can create one child per choice of the first city visited, a multi-way branch.

    For a minimisation, the LP value of a child node is at least the LP value of its parent. The child's feasible region is the parent's with one extra constraint, and minimising over a smaller set cannot give a smaller value. Hence bounds only rise as you descend, and the LP value of a node is a lower bound for every plan in its whole subtree.

    A node whose LP relaxation has been solved is pruned (closed, not split further) if

    1. Infeasibility: its LP has no feasible point. Its plans are a subset of its LP's points, so it has none either.
    2. Bound (incumbent): its LP value is at least $z_{UB}$. Every plan below it costs at least that much, so none improves on the incumbent.
    3. Integrality: its LP solution is already integer. It is then the best plan of the node; if it beats $z_{UB}$ it becomes the new incumbent.

    Otherwise the node is split by branching.

    1. Set $z_{UB}=\infty$. Put the root problem on the list of active nodes.
    2. If the list is empty, stop: the incumbent is optimal (or the problem is infeasible if there is none). Otherwise remove one node, and solve its LP relaxation.
    3. If the LP is infeasible or its value is $\ge z_{UB}$, discard the node and return to step 2.
    4. If the LP solution is integer, set $z_{UB}$ to its value, record the plan, and return to step 2.
    5. Otherwise pick a fractional $x_j$ with LP value $v$, create the children $x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor$ and $x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil$, add both to the list, and return to step 2.

    The bounds while it runs

    At any moment the incumbent gives $z_{UB}$ and the smallest bound among the nodes still waiting gives $z_{LB}$ (a waiting node is labelled with the LP value of its parent). The gap $(z_{UB}-z_{LB})/|z_{UB}|$ of Chapter 4.1 is therefore computed live. When the list empties, $z_{LB}$ jumps up to $z_{UB}$ and the gap is zero.

    Why is the result correct? Every integer plan sits in some leaf region. A region is only discarded when it is empty, when its LP bound is no better than a plan we already hold, or when its best plan has been recorded. So the best plan overall survives.

    When a new incumbent arrives, waiting nodes whose stored parent value is at least the new $z_{UB}$ can be deleted without solving their LPs. That saves a whole LP per node.

    Try it

    Run branch and bound on the two-van problem. First pick "My choice" for both rules: click the root to solve it, then choose which variable to branch on, then click waiting (dashed) nodes to solve them. Read the incumbent, bound and gap after every step. Then press Reset and finish with "Run to the end" under each strategy. Notice that the optimum (value $34$ at $(7,2)$) is always the same, but the number of LPs solved changes.

    Solve $\min 4x_1+3x_2$ s.t. $6x_1+2x_2\ge43$, $6x_1+7x_2\ge55$, $0\le x\le12$, $x$ integer, by branch and bound. Branch on $x_1$ at the root and always solve the waiting node with the smallest parent value.

    1. Node 1 (root). The LP optimum is $(6.367,\,2.4)$ with value $32.667$. Both coordinates are fractional; branch on $x_1$ with $\lfloor6.367\rfloor=6$: node 2 adds $x_1\le6$, node 3 adds $x_1\ge7$.

      $z_{UB}=\infty$, so nothing can be pruned yet. The gap is undefined until a plan is found.

    2. Node 2 ($x_1\le6$). Route A needs $6x_1+2x_2\ge43$. With $x_1$ at most $6$, each unit of $x_1$ we give up costs $4$ less but needs $3$ more units of $x_2$ (cost $9$). So keep $x_1=6$: then $x_2\ge3.5$, and route B holds ($36+24.5=60.5\ge55$). LP: $(6,\,3.5)$, value $34.5$. Fractional: branch on $x_2$ into node 4 ($x_2\le3$) and node 5 ($x_2\ge4$), both labelled with parent value $34.5$.

      Each child's LP value is at least $34.5$ (children are never better).

    3. Node 3 ($x_1\ge7$). Route B is now the binding row: at $x_1=7$ it needs $7x_2\ge13$, so $x_2=13/7\approx1.857$; route A holds ($42+3.71\ge43$). LP: $(7,\,1.857)$, value $28+5.571=33.571$. Branch on $x_2$: node 6 ($x_2\le1$) and node 7 ($x_2\ge2$), parent value $33.571$.

      Raising $x_1$ above $7$ would cost $4$ per unit and save only $6/7$ of an $x_2$ (worth $2.57$), so $x_1=7$ stays.

    4. Choose the next node. Waiting: nodes 4, 5 (parent $34.5$) and nodes 6, 7 (parent $33.571$). Smallest parent value: node 6.

      The most promising region is the one whose bound is lowest.

    5. Node 6 ($x_1\ge7$, $x_2\le1$). With $x_2\le1$ the best choice is $x_2=1$ (each unit of $x_2$ given up forces $7/6$ of an $x_1$, costing $4.67$ against a saving of $3$), and route B then forces $6x_1\ge48$, so $x_1=8$: LP $(8,1)$, value $35$. It is integer: new incumbent $z_{UB}=35$. Nodes 4, 5 have parent value $34.5<35$, so they stay. Lower bound now $\min(34.5,\,33.571)=33.571$, gap $(35-33.571)/35=4.1\%$.

      Integrality pruning: a node whose LP is integer needs no more splitting.

    6. Node 7 ($x_1\ge7$, $x_2\ge2$). At $x_2=2$, route B needs $6x_1\ge41$, but $x_1\ge7$ already, so $x_1=7$: LP $(7,2)$, value $34$. Integer and better than $35$: new incumbent $z_{UB}=34$.

      Route A: $42+4=46\ge43$. Route B: $42+14=56\ge55$. Feasible and integer.

    7. Clean up. Nodes 4 and 5 carry parent value $34.5\ge34$. Delete them without solving. The list is empty, so the plan $(7,2)$ with cost $34$ is optimal. Five LPs were solved (nodes 1, 2, 3, 6, 7).

      Bound pruning without even solving the LP. Had we solved them: node 4 ($x_1\le6$, $x_2\le3$) is infeasible since $6x_1+2x_2\le42<43$, and node 5 has value $35.33\ge34$.

If you had solved node 7 before node 6, the incumbent would have been $34$ at once, and node 6 (value $35$) would have been pruned by bound instead of becoming an incumbent.     Go deeper: pruning with whole-number objectives

    If all costs and variables are whole, every plan below a node has a whole-number cost, so a node with LP value $33.571$ can only contain plans costing at least $34$. Solvers therefore prune when the rounded-up LP value is at least $z_{UB}$. Here node 5 has value $35.33$, rounded up $36$, which is far above $z_{UB}=34$. This is also why Gurobi's best bound at the end of a time-limited run is often a whole number (Chapter 4.4).

    The node with bounds $x_1\le6$ and $x_2\le3$ is reached. What happens when its LP is solved?

    What is the largest value of $6x_1+2x_2$ under these bounds?

    With incumbent $34$, the node $x_1\le6$, $x_2\ge4$ has LP solution $(5.833,\,4)$ with value $35.33$. What happens?

    Compare $35.33$ with $34$.

    Its LP value is at least $z_{UB}=34$, so nothing below it can beat the incumbent. (The point is also fractional, but the bound test comes first.)

    A waiting node has stored parent value $34.5$ and the incumbent is now $34$. Do you need to solve its LP?

    Its LP value is at least the parent's value.

    Children are never better than the parent, so this node's LP value is at least $34.5\ge34$: it would be pruned by bound anyway. Delete it unsolved.

    • Label every child with its parent's LP value, so you can delete it later without solving.
    • Update $z_{LB}$ as the smallest value among waiting nodes and quote the gap.
    • Check that the fractional LP point violates both children.
    • Pruning a node just because its LP solution is fractional.
    • Branching on a variable that is already integer in the LP solution.
    • Forgetting that a tie with the incumbent also prunes the node.
    1. Branching on a fractional variable splits the feasible set into $x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor$ and $x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil$: no integer plan is lost and the fractional LP point is cut away.
    2. A node is pruned when its LP is infeasible, when its LP value is no better than the incumbent, or when its LP solution is integer; child LP values never fall below the parent's.
    3. The search ends when no node is waiting; the incumbent is then optimal, and the gap between the incumbent and the smallest waiting bound shows progress all along.

    Which statement about the bound of a child node is correct for a minimisation?

    It is at most the parent's bound, because more constraints help.
    More constraints shrink the feasible set.
    It is at least the parent's bound.
    Minimising over a smaller set cannot decrease the minimum.
    It can be either, depending on the branching variable.
    The set inclusion argument works for any branch.

    The tree is finished when:

    the first integer solution is found.
    Better plans may be hiding in waiting nodes.
    the LP at the root is integer only.
    That is one special case that ends the search at the root.
    no node is waiting.
    Every region has been solved or pruned, so the incumbent is optimal.

    Choosing the next node, the branching variable and the split

    The algorithm of Chapter 4.2 leaves three free choices: which waiting node to solve next, which fractional variable to branch on, and how to split. None changes the final answer, but each can change the work by orders of magnitude.

    These choices are the settings you will meet in a solver (node selection, variable selection, branching direction), and the exam asks when depth-first beats best-first and why GUB/SOS branching balances the tree.

    It is like exploring a cave system: you can follow one tunnel to the end before trying another, always jump to the tunnel that looks most promising on the map, or pick which fork to take first; all of them find the exit, some much sooner.

    Which waiting node next?

    Three classical rules, all using the list of waiting nodes in Chapter 4.2:

    • Depth-first: treat the list as a stack and always take the newest child. You dive to a leaf, then back up. Memory is tiny (only the current path and its siblings) and you reach an integer plan quickly, but you may dive into a bad region.
    • Best-first: always take the node with the smallest bound (its parent's LP value). For a given branching rule, it never solves a node whose bound is above the optimum, so it solves the fewest nodes once the optimum is known; but it keeps many waiting nodes in memory and can take long to find any plan.
    • Breadth-first: a queue, level by level. It ignores the bounds and needs the most memory, so solvers do not use it.

    The practical answer is a hybrid: until the first incumbent exists there is nothing to prune with, so dive depth-first; afterwards switch to best-first to finish the proof of optimality. That is what the lecture recommends and what commercial solvers broadly do.

    On a covering problem with 16 yes/no trucks, you run branch and bound three ways: depth-first, best-first and the hybrid. Which of depth-first and best-first do you expect to find its first feasible plan sooner?

    Depth-first.
    It drives straight to a leaf, where all variables are fixed.
    Best-first.
    It keeps jumping between shallow nodes with low bounds, which are the ones with the most fractional variables.
    They always tie.
    Their orders differ from the very first branch.

    In the experiment below, depth-first has a plan after its 8th LP and best-first after its 14th. Watch what happens to the lower bound, too.

Pick a node-selection strategy and slide the number of LPs solved. Green is the incumbent (upper bound), orange the best waiting bound. Set the tolerance slider to $1\%$ and note at which LP a solver with that tolerance would stop. Compare depth-first with best-first: which closes the gap sooner, and which one needs many more LPs in total?

    Go deeper: the instance behind the panel

    Truck capacities $a_j=(17,11,4,13,10,16,13,20,12,15,18,13,15,15,11,5)$ and costs $c_j=(27,17,8,14,12,25,17,25,19,21,25,21,20,12,13,8)$; binary $x_j$, minimise $\sum c_jx_j$ subject to $\sum a_jx_j\ge93$. Sorting trucks by cost per tonne and filling up gives the LP optimum: whole trucks while they fit and one fractional truck, which is why each node has exactly one fractional variable and branching is easy to follow.

    Which variable to branch on?

    When several variables are fractional you must choose one. A popular rule is most fractional: pick the variable whose fractional part is closest to one half, since it is the most "undecided". With $f_j=v_j-\lfloor v_j\rfloor$, choose $$j\in\arg\max_{j\ \text{fractional}}\ \min\{f_j,\ 1-f_j\}.$$ At the two-van root, $x_1=6.367$ has score $0.367$ and $x_2=2.4$ has score $0.4$, so the rule picks $x_2$.

    Reproduce the table: choose a node rule and a variable rule, press Reset, then "Run to the end", and read the number of LPs solved. Then open the tree for "Best-first" with "Most fractional" and for "Best-first" with "$x_1$ first", and compare their shapes. Notice that the less fractional variable gave the smaller tree here: most fractional is a good habit, not a law.

    Strong branching: look before you branch

    Instead of guessing, a solver can test the candidates. In strong branching it solves (fully, or for a limited number of iterations) both child LPs of each candidate variable, and branches on the candidate whose children look best. A common score is the improvement of the weaker child: the larger the smaller improvement, the more the bound rises on both sides.

    At the two-van root (LP value $32.667$), compare the candidates $x_1$ and $x_2$ by strong branching, scoring each by the smaller of its two bound improvements.

    1. Candidate $x_1$ (value $6.367$): the child $x_1\le6$ has LP value $34.5$ and the child $x_1\ge7$ has $33.571$. Improvements $34.5-32.667=1.833$ and $33.571-32.667=0.905$. Score $\min=0.905$.

      The child LPs are the same ones Chapter 4.2 solved by hand.

    2. Candidate $x_2$ (value $2.4$): the child $x_2\le2$ has LP value $33.333$ (at $(6.833,2)$) and $x_2\ge3$ has $33.667$ (at $(6.167,3)$). Improvements $0.667$ and $1.0$. Score $\min=0.667$.

      Both children must be solved eventually, so the weaker one limits how much the branch gains.

    3. The larger score belongs to $x_1$, so branch on $x_1$.

      This agrees with the run that needed 5 LPs instead of 9. The four test LPs cost extra effort at the root, but the two for the chosen variable become the children's LPs, so only two are wasted.

    Go deeper: cheaper scores

    Strong branching at every node is expensive. Solvers limit the work (a few simplex iterations per test, a handful of candidates) and remember the improvements seen at earlier branches on each variable, called pseudo-costs, to estimate scores for free. The lecture notes that CPLEX offers strong branching as an option.

    Solving each LP quickly

    Branching adds one bound, such as $x_j\le d$, to an LP that has just been solved to optimality. The old optimal basis still has non-negative reduced costs (it is dual feasible) but the old solution violates the new bound (it is primal infeasible). That is exactly the situation of the dual simplex method of Part 2: starting from the parent's stored basis, it typically needs only a few pivots. Because a bound on a single variable is not a new row, solvers also use simplex with bounds (Chapter 2.1) rather than enlarging the matrix.

    Fewer nodes

    Besides pruning, solvers shrink the tree by deleting waiting nodes as soon as the incumbent improves (compare the stored parent value with the new $z_{UB}$), by strong branching, by adding cuts, by presolve (Chapter 4.4), and by branching rules that keep the tree balanced. The last one is next.

    Exactly-one sets and GUB/SOS branching

    Many models contain a constraint of the form $\sum_{j=1}^kx_j=1$ with binary $x_j$: each job goes to exactly one agent, each customer is served by exactly one depot (Part 3). Call it an exactly-one set (a generalised upper bound, GUB, or special ordered set, SOS, in solver language).

    Branching on one fractional $x_j$ gives an unbalanced tree. The child $x_j=1$ forces every other variable of the set to $0$ and is tiny. The child $x_j=0$ still has $k-1$ undecided variables, almost as large as its parent. In the worst case the tree is $k-1$ levels deep for this set alone.

    GUB/SOS branching splits the set of variables instead. Take the variables in a fixed order, and let $r$ be the first index where the running sum of the LP values reaches $\tfrac12$: $r=\min\{t:\sum_{i\le t}x_i^{LP}\ge\tfrac12\}$, and $Q=\{1,\dots,r\}$. The two children are $$\sum_{j\in Q}x_j=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{j\notin Q}x_j=0 .$$ In the first the variables of $Q$ are fixed to $0$ and the one chosen variable must come from outside $Q$; in the second it must come from $Q$. Each child fixes about half of the LP's weight to zero.

    Careful: both children must cut off the LP point. This needs the weight on each side to be positive, which can fail if the running sum reaches exactly $1$ at $r$ (everything left is $0$). Then take $r-1$ instead. A fractional point always has at least two positive entries, so $r-1\ge1$ and its side has positive weight.
    Try it

    Pick one of the three LP solutions on an exactly-one set of eight variables, then switch between "Single variable" and "GUB / SOS split". In the split view the dashed line marks $Q$; read how many variables stay free in each child. Notice in solution C that one big variable gives $r=1$, and in B that the weight is spread over all eight variables, so $r=5$.

    An exactly-one set has eight variables with LP values $x^{LP}=(0.10,\,0.20,\,0.30,\,0.10,\,0,\,0.15,\,0.10,\,0.05)$. Find the GUB/SOS split and check that it cuts off the LP point.

    1. Running sums: $0.10,\ 0.30,\ 0.60,\dots$ The first sum that reaches $\tfrac12$ is at $t=3$, so $r=3$ and $Q=\{1,2,3\}$.

      The sum $0.60$ is the first at or above $0.5$; the previous sum $0.30$ is below.

    2. Child A: $x_1=x_2=x_3=0$. The LP point has $0.60$ on $Q$, so it violates this child. Five variables remain free ($x_4,\dots,x_8$).

      The exactly-one row then forces the single 1 to be among $x_4,\dots,x_8$.

    3. Child B: $x_4=\dots=x_8=0$. The LP point has $0.40$ on $Q^c$, so it violates this child too. Three variables remain free ($x_1,x_2,x_3$).

      Both children are strictly smaller than the parent, and the LP point is in neither.

    4. Repeating the split, the number of free variables roughly halves each time: about $\lceil\log_2 8\rceil=3$ levels pin down the single variable, instead of up to $7$ with single-variable branching.

      The split balances the LP weight, not necessarily the count of variables, which is why the counts are $5$ and $3$ here rather than $4$ and $4$.

    Application

    In the generalised assignment problem of Lab 2, every job has an exactly-one row over the agents, with $5$, $10$ or $20$ variables. Single-variable branching on a job row with $20$ agents can dive many levels before settling one job; a GUB split settles it in about five. The hand-written branch and bound of the lab branches on single variables, which is one reason it struggles in Chapter 4.4.

    Which node-selection rule needs the least memory, keeping essentially only the current path and its siblings?

    Think of a stack.

    Depth-first holds one path from the root and the siblings left behind. Best-first and breadth-first may hold a large part of a level.

    • Dive depth-first until the first incumbent, then switch to best-first.
    • Use GUB/SOS splitting on exactly-one rows with many variables.
    • Compare tree sizes under different rules before blaming the model.
    • Assuming "most fractional" always wins.
    • Using breadth-first search in a real solver.
    • Splitting an exactly-one set at an index that leaves no LP weight on one side.
    1. The node-selection rule changes the work, not the answer: depth-first finds a plan early and is light on memory, best-first proves optimality with the fewest LPs, and a hybrid dives first and then goes best-first.
    2. Variable selection is a heuristic: most fractional is the default and strong branching tests candidates by solving their child LPs; child LPs after one new bound are cheap thanks to the dual simplex method.
    3. On an exactly-one set, splitting the variable set at the point where the LP weight reaches one half halves the problem in both children and keeps the tree balanced.

    Why do solvers dive depth-first at the start and switch to best-first after the first incumbent?

    Best-first cannot be used with an incumbent.
    It uses the incumbent to prune.
    Without an incumbent there is nothing to prune with, so a quick leaf helps; afterwards best-first needs the fewest LPs to prove optimality.
    Both statements are the two halves of the hybrid strategy.
    Depth-first always finds the optimal plan first.
    It finds some plan quickly, not necessarily the best.

    After adding the bound $x_j\le d$ to an optimal LP basis, the reduced costs are still non-negative but $x_j$ is too large. Which method re-solves fastest?

    Primal simplex from scratch.
    That throws away the parent's work.
    Dual simplex from the parent's basis.
    The basis is dual feasible and primal infeasible, the dual simplex situation.
    Rounding the LP solution.
    That does not solve the LP.

    For an exactly-one set with LP values $(0.6,\,0.4,\,0,\,0)$, which split is valid and cuts off the LP point?

    $r=2$: $x_1+x_2=0$ versus $x_3+x_4=0$
    The second child does not remove the LP point, which has weight $0$ on $x_3,x_4$.
    $r=1$: $x_1=0$ versus $x_2+x_3+x_4=0$
    The LP point has $0.6$ on $x_1$ and $0.4$ on the rest, so both children cut it off.
    Branch on $x_3$.
    It is not fractional.

    The tree for single-variable branching on an exactly-one set of $k$ variables is unbalanced because:

    the $x_j=0$ child is tiny.
    That is the child that is nearly as large as the parent.
    the $x_j=1$ child fixes all other variables while the $x_j=0$ child leaves $k-1$ free.
    One side shrinks to almost nothing, the other hardly shrinks.
    the LP point is not cut off.
    It is cut off from both children; the issue is their sizes.

    Preprocessing, and what a solver prints: Lab 2

    Before the first LP is solved, a solver shrinks the model by tightening variable bounds, deleting rows that can never bind, fixing variables whose best value is obvious, and sharpening big-M coefficients. Lab 2 then runs branch and bound on the generalised assignment problem with these tricks switched off, and you learn to read the log it prints.

    Preprocessing can turn a hopeless model into an easy one, and the log is how you tell whether a run is converging; both are standard exam material, and the log is what you actually see when you use Gurobi.

    It is like tidying the workshop before starting a job: nothing you do changes what the job is, but every later step is faster, and a progress report on the wall tells you when to stop.

    The activity range of a row

    Take a row $\sum_{j}a_jx_j\le b$ with bounds $\ell_j\le x_j\le u_j$ on every variable. Even without knowing the $x_j$ we can say how small and how large the left side can be. The smallest value uses the lower bound where $a_j>0$ and the upper bound where $a_j<0$; the largest does the opposite: $$L=\sum_{a_j>0}a_j\ell_j+\sum_{a_j<0}a_ju_j,\qquad U=\sum_{a_j>0}a_ju_j+\sum_{a_j<0}a_j\ell_j.$$ Everything preprocessing does with a row starts from $L$ and $U$. (A "$\ge$" row is multiplied by $-1$ first.)

    1. Infeasible: if $L>b$, the row can never hold, so the whole problem is infeasible.
    2. Redundant: if $U\le b$, the row holds for every choice of bounds and can be deleted.
    3. Tighten: the other variables contribute at least $L-a_k\ell_k$ (for $a_k>0$), so $a_kx_k\le b-(L-a_k\ell_k)$: $$a_k>0:\ x_k\le\frac{b-(L-a_k\ell_k)}{a_k},\qquad a_k<0:\ x_k\ge\frac{b-(L-a_ku_k)}{a_k}.$$ For an integer variable round the new upper bound down and the new lower bound up. Repeat over all rows until nothing changes.
    Try it

    Choose a row and slide $b$. Read the smallest and largest left side, then the verdict: infeasible, redundant, or able to bite, and the tightened bounds. Switch rounding off to see what integrality adds. In the second row (all variables binary) find a value of $b$ where one variable is forced to $0$, and one where the row disappears.

    Integer variables with $0\le x_1\le5$, $0\le x_2\le4$, $0\le x_3\le3$ and the rows R1: $4x_1+3x_2-2x_3\le9$; R2: $x_1+x_2+x_3\le9$; R3: $2x_2+x_3\ge8$. Preprocess.

    1. R1. $L=0+0-2\cdot3=-6$. For $x_1$: $x_1\le(9-(-6))/4=3.75$, rounded down to $3$. For $x_2$: $x_2\le(9+6)/3=5$, already weaker than $4$. For $x_3$ ($a_3=-2$): $x_3\ge(9-0)/(-2)=-4.5$, nothing new. Now $x_1\le3$.

      The other terms of R1 can be as low as $-6$, so $4x_1$ can be at most $15$.

    2. R3 in $\le$ form is $-2x_2-x_3\le-8$. $L=-2\cdot4-3=-11$. For $x_2$: $x_2\ge(-8-(-11+8))/(-2)=2.5$, rounded up to $3$. For $x_3$: $x_3\ge0$, nothing new. Now $x_2\ge3$.

      Even with $x_3=3$, the term $2x_2$ must supply at least $5$, so $x_2\ge2.5$, hence $3$.

    3. R1 again, now with $\ell_2=3$: $L=0+9-6=3$, and $x_1\le(9-3)/4=1.5$, rounded down to $1$. Now $x_1\le1$.

      The new lower bound on $x_2$ raises $L$ and tightens R1. This is why we repeat until nothing changes.

    4. R2. With the new bounds the largest left side is $1+4+3=8\le9$, so R2 is redundant and is deleted. (With the original bounds it was $5+4+3=12>9$ and could bite.)

      Tightening one row made another redundant.

    5. Result: $x_1\in[0,1]$, $x_2\in[3,4]$, $x_3\in[0,3]$; R1 and R3 remain, R2 is gone. The box shrank from $6\cdot5\cdot4=120$ points to $2\cdot2\cdot4=16$ points.

      No integer solution was lost: each bound change only removed values that violate a row.

    Fixing variables

    Some variables can be set to a bound before any search, either from the signs in the model or from the bounds of the LP.

    For $\min c^\top x$ s.t. $Ax\ge b$, $\ell\le x\le u$: if $a_{ij}\ge0$ in every row $i$ and $c_j<0$, set $x_j=u_j$; if $a_{ij}\le0$ in every row and $c_j>0$, set $x_j=\ell_j$. Raising a variable with non-negative coefficients never harms a "$\ge$" row, and with $c_j<0$ it lowers the cost (the second rule is the mirror image). In dual language, the reduced cost then has the sign that keeps the variable at that bound.

    $\min\,-2x_1+3x_2+x_3$ s.t. $x_1+2x_2\ge3$, $3x_1-x_3\ge-2$, $0\le x_j\le5$. Fix what you can.

    1. $x_1$: cost $-2<0$, coefficients $(1,3)$ both $\ge0$. Fix $x_1=u_1=5$.

      More of $x_1$ helps both rows and lowers the cost.

    2. $x_3$: cost $+1>0$, coefficients $(0,-1)$ both $\le0$. Fix $x_3=\ell_3=0$.

      Less of $x_3$ costs less and only loosens the second row, which has $x_3$ with a negative sign.

    3. The rows become $5+2x_2\ge3$ (always true) and $15\ge-2$ (always true): both redundant. Then $x_2$ has $c=3>0$ and no coefficients left, so $x_2=\ell_2=0$.

      Fixing is repeated after every deletion.

    4. Solution: $x=(5,0,0)$ with value $-10$ found with no search at all.

      Enumerating the 216 integer points confirms it is optimal.

    Fixing with the incumbent: reduced-cost fixing

    Once an incumbent $z_{UB}$ exists, the LP of a node can eliminate values using its reduced costs. Suppose the LP value is $z_{LP}$ and a non-basic variable $x_j$ sits at its lower bound with reduced cost $\bar c_j>0$ (Part 1). Raising $x_j$ by $t$ raises the LP objective by at least $\bar c_jt$. Any plan that can beat the incumbent has LP objective at most $z_{UB}$, so $$x_j\le\ell_j+\frac{z_{UB}-z_{LP}}{\bar c_j}.$$ For a non-basic variable at its upper bound the same argument bounds it from below.

    In the two-van problem the root LP has value $98/3=32.667$. Use reduced-cost fixing with the incumbent $35$ found at node 6 in Chapter 4.2.

    1. Let $s_A=6x_1+2x_2-43\ge0$ and $s_B=6x_1+7x_2-55\ge0$ be the surplus crates on each route. These are the non-basic variables at the root, and each has reduced cost $\tfrac13$ (the dual prices).

      Part 2: the reduced cost of a surplus variable equals the dual price of its row.

    2. The identity behind the bound: $s_A+s_B=12x_1+9x_2-98=3(4x_1+3x_2)-98$, so the cost equals $\tfrac{98+s_A+s_B}{3}$.

      The cost exceeds the LP value by exactly $\tfrac13$ of the total surplus.

    3. A plan costing at most $35$ needs $s_A+s_B\le3\cdot35-98=7$. So each route can be oversupplied by at most $7$ crates: $6x_1+2x_2\le50$ and $6x_1+7x_2\le62$.

      This matches the formula $(z_{UB}-z_{LP})/\bar c_j=(35-32.667)/(1/3)=7$.

    4. With the final incumbent $34$ the limit shrinks to $3\cdot34-98=4$. The optimum $(7,2)$ has surpluses $3$ and $1$, total $4$, so it sits exactly on the limit.

      A tighter incumbent removes more of the region, and the optimum stays.

    Coefficient tightening and big-M

    Logical models use rows such as $x\le My$ (Part 3): if the depot is closed ($y=0$) nothing is shipped, and if it is open the row should do nothing. The constant $M$ only has to be large enough for the second case; anything larger is legal but weakens the LP, because the relaxation lets $y$ be tiny while $x$ is large.

    Try it

    A depot must ship at least the demand of $30$ units, so $x\ge30$, opening costs $60$ and each unit costs $2$: $\min 60y+2x$, $x\le My$, $y\in\{0,1\}$. Move $M$ and watch the LP optimum (red dot) slide along the bottom edge. Then choose "M = 30 (tight)". Notice the root gap, and that the integer answer never changes.

    Here no optimal plan ships more than the demand, so $M=30$ loses nothing; $M=300$ is valid but wasteful. The LP bound is $60\cdot\tfrac{30}{M}+60$: $66$ for $M=300$, $72$ for $150$, $90$ for $60$ and $120$ for $30$, against the true optimum $120$. The root gaps are $45\%$, $40\%$, $25\%$ and $0\%$.

    The same idea works on any row. For $\sum a_jx_j\le b$ with a binary $x_k$, $a_k>0$, and maximum activity $U$: if $U-a_k

    Tighten $8y_1+3y_2+2y_3\le10$ with binary $y$.

    1. Maximum activity $U=8+3+2=13$. For $y_1$ ($a_1=8$): $U-a_1=5<10$, so the test passes.

      With $y_1=0$ the left side is at most $5$, far below $10$.

    2. New coefficient $U-b=13-10=3$ and new right-hand side $U-a_1=5$: the row becomes $3y_1+3y_2+2y_3\le5$.

      With $y_1=1$ the original row reads $3y_2+2y_3\le2$ and the new row reads $3y_2+2y_3\le2$: identical. With $y_1=0$ both allow every $(y_2,y_3)$.

    3. The six feasible binary points are the same in both rows. But the fractional point $(0.5,1,1)$ is feasible for the original row ($4+5=9\le10$) and infeasible for the new one ($1.5+5=6.5>5$).

      If we maximise $y_1+y_2+y_3$, the original LP gives $2.625$ and the tightened LP gives $2$, which equals the integer optimum.

    Probing

    Bound tightening looks at one row at a time. Probing tries a binary variable at one value, propagates the consequences through all rows, and learns from the outcome: if setting $x_k=1$ leads to a contradiction, then $x_k=0$ in every feasible plan, so fix it. If both values of $x_k$ force the same value of another variable, fix that variable. If only one value forces something, remember the implication.

    Binary variables with R1: $6x_1+4x_2+3x_3\le8$, R2: $x_1+x_2+x_3\ge2$, R3: $x_3+x_4\le1$. Looking at each row on its own, can you fix any variable?

    No: every row alone leaves all four variables free.
    R1 alone only says $x_1\le1.33$; R2 alone needs two of three; R3 alone allows both.
    Yes, $x_1=0$ from R1.
    $6x_1\le8$ allows $x_1=1$ when $x_2=x_3=0$ (and then R2 fails, but that needs two rows).
    Yes, $x_4=0$ from R3.
    $x_3+x_4\le1$ allows $x_4=1$ with $x_3=0$.

    Single-row propagation is stuck, and probing breaks the deadlock. Try it in the panel.

    Try it

    Probe $x_1=1$ and read the messages: which variables does it force, and what contradiction follows? Once $x_1$ is fixed, probe $x_3=0$, then continue until every variable is fixed. Press Reset and probe $x_4=1$ first to see a different route to a contradiction.

    Solve the three-row system above by probing.

    1. Probe $x_1=1$. R1 becomes $4x_2+3x_3\le2$, so $x_2=0$ and $x_3=0$. R2 then reads $1+0+0\ge2$, false.

      A contradiction: $x_1=1$ is impossible in any feasible plan, so $x_1=0$.

    2. With $x_1=0$, R2 needs $x_2+x_3\ge2$, forcing $x_2=x_3=1$. Check R1: $4+3=7\le8$. Then R3 gives $x_4\le0$, so $x_4=0$.

      Plain propagation now runs through all rows.

    3. The only feasible plan is $(0,1,1,0)$.

      The model was solved by preprocessing alone, and branch and bound never starts.

    Careful: preprocessing never changes the optimal value of the IP. It may remove tied optimal plans and it only ever tightens the LP relaxation, raising a lower bound. In Lab 2 it is switched off on purpose, so that you see plain branch and bound.

    Case study: Lab 2, the generalised assignment problem

    The GAP of Part 3: $m$ agents, $n$ jobs, $x_{ij}=1$ if agent $i$ does job $j$, cost $c_{ij}$, resource use $r_{ij}$, agent capacity $s_i$: $$\min\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_ix_{ij}=1\ \ \forall j,\qquad\sum_jr_{ij}x_{ij}\le s_i\ \ \forall i,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.$$ The six instances come from Beasley's OR-Library, named by size: b05100 has $5$ agents and $100$ jobs, b10200 has $10$ agents and $200$ jobs, and so on, from $500$ to $4000$ binary variables. Each job row is an exactly-one set.

    The lab has two programs, and the contrast is the lesson.

    • Your own branch and bound (GAP_Exercise.py): Gurobi only solves the LP at each node (dual simplex, presolve off). You code the tree: depth-first until an incumbent exists then best-first by parent bound, most-fractional branching, deleting nodes against the incumbent, a 120 s limit.
    • Gurobi's own MIP engine (GAP_Gurobi.py): the same model, with Presolve = 0 (no preprocessing), Cuts = 0 (no cutting planes), TimeLimit = 120, branching direction left automatic. It is plain branch and bound, but still with Gurobi's heuristics and its fast node processing.

    Gurobi offers a free academic licence for students; Part −1 points to the set-up notes.

    InstanceRoot LPGurobi: best plan (nodes)Own B&B after 120 s: best plan (nodes)
    b051001831.331843 (3,244)2319 (38,359)
    b052003547.413552 (8,971)4056 (32,133)
    b101001400.671407 (751)1739 (48,642)
    b102002815.052827 (1,318,914); bound 2823 at the limit3365 (21,323)
    b201001155.181166 (21,059)no plan found (31,922)
    b202002331.142339 (504,407)no plan found (14,715)
    Try it

    Select an instance and switch between the three bar charts. Compare the root gap with the number of nodes Gurobi needed. Which instance has the smallest root gap, and which needs the most nodes? Then look at the hand-written results: which instances never found a plan?

    Four observations from the data:

    • The LP root bound is already within $0.13\%$ to $0.93\%$ of the optimum, yet hundreds to millions of nodes are needed. The bound is good, but proving that no plan hides in the last fraction is hard.
    • Difficulty follows neither size nor root gap: b10200 ($2000$ binaries, root gap $0.42\%$) is the only instance that hit the time limit, while b20200 ($4000$ binaries) finished in about $72$ s.
    • The hand-written search solves a node with the same LP engine but explores about $60$ times fewer nodes per second on b10200 ($21{,}323$ against $1{,}318{,}914$), has no heuristics, and on the $20$-agent instances its dive never reached an integer leaf.
    • Gurobi's own run closes five of six instances even with presolve and cuts off; with them on, instances like b10200 usually become much easier (that is why solvers enable both by default).

    Reading a MIP log

    Gurobi prints a table while it searches. Here are its columns.

    Columns of the log
    Expl / Unexpl
    nodes explored so far, and nodes created but still waiting
    Obj
    LP value of the node just solved; the words cutoff (pruned by bound) or infeasible (pruned by infeasibility) can appear here
    Depth, IntInf
    depth of that node in the tree, and how many integer variables are fractional in its LP
    Incumbent
    the best plan found: the upper bound $z_{UB}$
    BestBd
    the best lower bound: the smallest bound among waiting nodes
    Gap
    $(\text{Incumbent}-\text{BestBd})/|\text{Incumbent}|$
    It/Node, Time
    average simplex iterations per node, and seconds so far

    In the first column, H marks a plan found by a heuristic and * a plan found because a node's LP happened to be integer. Lines before the table show a heuristic solution found before the root and the root relaxation value. After the table, Gurobi reports why it stopped ("Optimal solution found" or "Time limit reached"), the best objective, the best bound and the final gap.

    Try it

    Answer the questions by clicking the right number in the log. Use the chips to switch between a log that finished (b05100) and one that hit the time limit (b10200). These are real excerpts from running the lab model with presolve and cuts off.

    Read the end of the b10200 log: last row Incumbent $2827$, BestBd $2823.6849$; footer "Time limit reached ... best bound $2.824\times10^3$, gap $0.1061\%$". Explain each number.

    1. The plan has cost $2827$ and nobody found a better one since second $3$ of the run.

      The incumbent column stays at $2827$ for the last $117$ seconds.

    2. The row gap is $(2827-2823.6849)/2827=0.1173\%$, shown as $0.12\%$. The bound has risen from $2815.05$ (the root LP) to $2823.68$.

      All progress after second $3$ was in the bound, not the plan.

    3. The footer bound is $2824$, not $2823.68$: every plan has a whole-number cost, so the bound is rounded up. The gap is $(2827-2824)/2827=0.1061\%$.

      This is the rounding of Chapter 4.1: a lower bound for whole-number costs may be rounded up.

    4. The true optimum is therefore between $2824$ and $2827$. The lab run on the course machine ended with bound $2823$ and gap $0.14\%$; repeated runs differ because the multi-threaded search takes different paths.

      A time-limited run proves a bracket, not an optimum.

    Integer variables $0\le x_1,x_2\le10$ and the row $3x_1+5x_2\le31$. What is the best upper bound on $x_2$ that bound tightening gives?

    The smallest possible value of $3x_1$ is $0$. Then round down.

    $L=0$, so $5x_2\le31$, $x_2\le6.2$, rounded down: $6$.

    The row $2x_1+3x_2\le20$ with $0\le x_1\le4$ and $0\le x_2\le3$ is checked. What is the verdict?

    Compute the largest possible left side $U$ and compare with $20$.

    $U=2\cdot4+3\cdot3=17\le20$, so the row holds for every point of the box and can be deleted.

    At a node the LP value is $100$, a non-basic variable $x_j$ at lower bound $0$ has reduced cost $4$, and the incumbent is $112$ (minimisation). Reduced-cost fixing bounds $x_j$ by what?

    Use $x_j\le\ell_j+(z_{UB}-z_{LP})/\bar c_j$.

    $(112-100)/4=3$, so $x_j\le3$.

    Tighten the coefficient of $y_1$ in $5y_1+4y_2+3y_3\le8$ with binary variables, using $a_k'=U-b$.

    Find the maximum activity $U$ and check that $U-a_1

    $U=12$, $U-5=7<8$. New coefficient $12-8=4$, new right-hand side $12-5=7$: $4y_1+4y_2+3y_3\le7$. It allows the same six binary points.

    A log row shows Incumbent $1849$ and BestBd $1833.18429$. What gap does Gurobi print (in percent)?

    Divide the difference by the incumbent.

    $(1849-1833.18429)/1849=0.00855$, printed as $0.86\%$.

    • Tighten bounds, delete redundant rows and fix variables before blaming the solver.
    • Use the smallest valid big-M; derive it from the bounds of the variables.
    • Read three numbers first in any log: Incumbent, BestBd and Gap.
    • Using $M=10^6$ "to be safe".
    • Expecting a time-limited run to prove optimality.
    • Judging difficulty by instance size alone: b10200 beat b20200.
    1. Preprocessing uses each row's smallest and largest left side to detect infeasible and redundant rows, tighten bounds, fix variables, shrink big-M coefficients and (by probing) learn implications; it never changes the optimum.
    2. With an incumbent, reduced costs let a node fix more variables: a non-basic variable cannot rise by more than $(z_{UB}-z_{LP})/\bar c_j$.
    3. A solver log shows Incumbent (upper bound), BestBd (lower bound) and their gap; H, *, cutoff and infeasible name how plans and prunings arise, and Lab 2 shows the same algorithm taking seconds or hitting the time limit depending on the instance and the engineering around it.

    Setting x_k = 1 in a probe leads to a violated row. What may you conclude?

    $x_k=1$ in every optimal plan.
    The contradiction concerns $x_k=1$, so it is excluded.
    $x_k=0$ in every feasible plan, so $x_k$ can be fixed to $0$.
    The only other value of a binary variable is $0$.
    The model is infeasible.
    Only if $x_k=0$ also fails.

    Two models have the same integer points. One uses $x\le300y$, the other $x\le30y$ where $x\le30$ always. Which gives the higher LP lower bound for a minimisation with a positive fixed cost?

    The one with $300$.
    It allows $y$ to be ten times smaller in the relaxation, hence a lower bound.
    The one with $30$.
    It forces $y\ge x/30$, so the fixed cost is paid more fully in the LP.
    They are equal because the integer points are equal.
    The LP relaxations differ even when the integer points do not.

    The Obj column of a log row says cutoff. The node was:

    infeasible.
    That would be printed as infeasible.
    found to have an integer LP solution.
    That is marked by * in the first column.
    pruned by bound: its LP value was not better than the incumbent.
    The word means the node was cut off by the incumbent.

    Why does Lab 2 set Presolve = 0 and Cuts = 0?

    Gurobi cannot solve the GAP with them.
    It can, and usually faster.
    So that the search is plain branch and bound on the model exactly as written, making node counts and times a measure of the algorithm itself.
    Presolve and cuts would hide most of the tree.
    To make the LP relaxation tighter.
    Switching them off makes bounds weaker, not tighter.
    Where we are in the story

    Kaveri Courier's owner now has a solver that brackets the best plan between an incumbent and a bound, branches on fractional variables and prunes with preprocessing. That covers the choice of depots, loads and assignments. What it does not yet cover is the order in which one van visits its customers. Once the customers on a van are known, that order is a travelling salesman problem, and Part 5 takes it up with the same bounding mindset: an integer programme, an LP relaxation and cuts added where the relaxation misleads.

    A minimisation has root LP value $198$ and the best plan found costs $210$. What does the gap tell you?

    The optimum is exactly $204$.
    The gap gives a range, not a point.
    The incumbent can be improved by at most $(210-198)/210\approx5.7\%$.
    The optimum lies in $[198,210]$.
    The LP is infeasible.
    It has a value, so it is feasible.

    $P_1$ and $P_2$ are two formulations of the same IP with $P_1\subset P_2$. Which statement is true for a minimisation?

    Branch and bound with $P_1$ starts from a lower bound that is at least as high.
    A smaller relaxation region cannot lower the minimum.
    Branch and bound with $P_1$ may find a worse optimum.
    Both formulations have the same integer points and so the same optimum.
    The bounds are always equal.
    That holds only if the extra part of $P_2$ contains no better LP point.

    In the two-van problem the dual prices of both route rows are $\tfrac13$. If route A's requirement rises from $43$ to $44$ crates (the basis staying optimal), the root LP bound moves from $32.667$ to about:

    $32.667$ (no change)
    A tight row with a positive price does change the optimum.
    $33$
    The optimum rises by the dual price $\tfrac13$.
    $33.667$
    That would be a price of $1$.

    After branching on $x_j$, the child LP is solved starting from the parent's final basis by the dual simplex method because:

    the child has more variables.
    The variable set is unchanged; only a bound changed.
    the parent's basis is still dual feasible but the new bound makes it primal infeasible.
    That is exactly the situation the dual simplex method is built for.
    the primal simplex cannot handle bounds.
    It can (Chapter 2.1); the dual is just faster here.

    An LP optimum of an integer programme is $(3.0,\,4.6)$. By Part 1 it is a corner of the LP region. After branching on $x_2$ into $x_2\le4$ and $x_2\ge5$, what happens to this corner?

    It stays a feasible corner of both children.
    $4.6$ violates both $x_2\le4$ and $x_2\ge5$.
    It is cut off from both children, and every whole-number point is kept in exactly one child.
    That is the purpose of the branch.
    It becomes the new incumbent.
    It is not integer, so it cannot be an incumbent.

    An assignment row $\sum_{i=1}^{16}x_{ij}=1$ has LP values $(0.4,\,0.3,\,0.3,\,0,\dots,0)$. Where does a GUB/SOS split put $Q$?

    $Q=\{1\}$, because the largest value is first.
    The running sum $0.4$ is below $\tfrac12$.
    $Q=\{1,2\}$, since $0.4+0.3=0.7\ge\tfrac12$ first at $t=2$.
    The other side has weight $0.3>0$, so both children cut the LP point.
    $Q=\{1,2,3\}$, because the sum must reach $1$.
    The threshold is $\tfrac12$.

    Lecture 5 studies the most famous routing problem: one vehicle, many stops, the cheapest closed route. We write it as an integer programme with exponentially many constraints (the DFJ formulation), learn how a solver adds them only when needed, meet the compact alternatives of Miller–Tucker–Zemlin and of flow models, compare their strength, and finish with the variants of the lecture (time windows, optional customers, road networks, clusters, street-covering routes) and the heuristics that find good tours quickly.

    You need: Part −2 (graphs, the notation $E(S)$ and $\delta(S)$, tours, Euler circuits, spanning trees and matchings; maximum flow and minimum cut are introduced in Ch. −2.2 and used again in Ch. 5.2), Part −1 (forcing constraints and why a small big-$M$ matters), Part 3 (LP relaxation and formulation strength), and Part 1 (what an LP bound means).

    From tours to the DFJ formulation

    The travelling salesman problem asks for the cheapest closed route that visits every city once. Writing it as an integer programme takes one yes/no variable per road, a rule that every city has two chosen roads, and a family of rules that forbids a route from breaking into separate loops.

    In the story of Kaveri Courier, the small Bengaluru courier firm of Part 3, the owner has by now chosen the depot and the loads for the vans (Ch. 3.1 and Ch. 3.4) and has seen how a solver finds such answers (Part 4). After Part 4 the owner knows which customers go on this van; what remains is the order in which it should visit them. Every vehicle routing model in Part 6 contains a TSP inside it, and the "forbid separate loops" idea of this chapter returns in every one of them. The two equivalent forms of that rule, and the proof that they agree, are standard exam material.

    It is like threading one string through all the beads of a necklace: giving every bead two neighbours is not enough, because you might end up with two small necklaces instead of one large one.

    The problem and a six-city example

    Take one van of Kaveri Courier. It starts at the depot that was opened in Part 3 (the choice of Ch. 3.3 and Lab 1 in Ch. 3.4), must call at every customer on its load exactly once, and returns to the depot. Driving between places $u$ and $v$ costs $c_{uv}$, the same in both directions. Call the places cities; there are $n$ of them. Take the complete graph $G=(V,E)$ on the cities (Part −2): every pair of cities is joined by an edge $e=\{u,v\}$ with cost $c_e$. A tour is a cycle through all cities, and the TSP asks for the tour of least total cost.

    Because the first city is only a starting point, there are $(n-1)!/2$ different tours: $60$ for six cities, $181{,}440$ for ten, about $6.1\times10^{16}$ for twenty (Part −2 turned that into years of computing). We cannot list them, so we need a model.

    Our running example has six cities with these costs (an edge not in the table costs $9$). For the story, city $1$ is the depot, cities $2$ and $3$ are the customers in Indiranagar and Domlur, and cities $4$, $5$ and $6$ are the customers in Jayanagar, BTM Layout and Banashankari.
