    LP relaxationbound% of optimum
    Two-index, degrees only83.0884.2
    + fractional capacity cuts $x(\delta(S))\ge 2d(S)/C$86.0887.2
    Load variables (MTZ-type, arcs between customers that do not fit together removed)87.8088.9
    + rounded capacity cuts $x(\delta(S))\ge 2r(S)$96.2097.5
    Set-partitioning LP98.71100

    The lesson matches Part 3. Rounding the vehicle count (from $2.4$ vans to $3$) is what turns a weak model into a strong one, and the MTZ-type compact model is weak because its load variables can be fractional. The set-partitioning LP is at least as strong on this instance (it reaches the integer optimum) and, in the literature on exact CVRP methods, is usually among the strongest, but with exponentially many columns. This is an observation about the example, not a theorem: a set-partitioning LP solution can violate a rounded capacity cut, because a fractional mix of routes can serve a set of customers with fewer than $r(S)$ vans (three customers of demand $4$ with $C=10$, covered by the three two-customer routes at weight $\tfrac12$ each, use $1.5$ vans for a set that needs $r(S)=2$). The two-index model with cuts lies close behind with a trivial number of variables, which is why it is the workhorse of branch and cut.

    The three-index model, with identical vans, adds no strength: averaging the $K$ vans' variables $x^k$ gives a two-index point of the same cost, and conversely a two-index point is split into $K$ equal parts. Its LP bound on the running example is $83.08$, the same as the degree-only two-index bound (it never reaches the $96.20$ of the rounded cuts). It is useful when the vans differ.

    Try it

    Step through the five relaxations and the optimum. Notice that the biggest single jump (steps 3 to 4) comes from rounding the vehicle count in the cuts, not from adding variables, and that the last step needs exponentially many columns.

    A solver reports the LP bound $96.20$ at the root and has found a plan of cost $99.04$. What can you say about the best possible cost, and what is the gap?

    1. The optimum $z^*$ satisfies $96.20\le z^*\le 99.04$.

      The LP gives a lower bound for a minimisation, the feasible plan an upper bound.

    2. The gap, as defined in Part 4, is $(99.04-96.20)/99.04\approx 2.87\%$.

      The gap is measured against the incumbent (the plan in hand); at most $2.87\%$ of its cost can still be saved.

    3. With the degree-only bound $83.08$ the same plan only certifies a gap of $(99.04-83.08)/99.04\approx16.1\%$.

      A weaker bound gives the same plan a worse certificate and leaves more nodes to explore.

    Undirected three-index model, $n=10$ customers, $K=3$ vans, variables $x^k_e$ for all edges of the complete graph on $11$ locations and $y^k_i$ for all $11$ locations. How many variables?

    Edges: $\binom{11}{2}$. Multiply each family by $K$.

    Edges $=55$, so $x$ has $3\cdot55=165$ variables; $y$ has $3\cdot11=33$. Total $198$.

    Four identical vans are all used. How many relabellings of the vans give the same plan (and hence equivalent three-index solutions)?

    Count the orderings of four vans.

    $4!=24$.

    With $n=6$ customers, how many customer subsets of size at most $3$ (candidate columns, assuming all fit in a van) are there?

    Add $\binom61+\binom62+\binom63$.

    $6+15+20=41$.

    In a restricted master, the duals of customers $a$ and $b$ are $\pi_a=18$ and $\pi_b=16$ (there is no route-count row). A candidate route serving exactly $a$ and $b$ costs $30$. What is its reduced cost?

    $\bar c=c_j-\sum_i a_{ij}\pi_i$.

    $30-(18+16)=-4$. Negative, so the column should enter the master.

    A minimisation has an LP bound of $90$ and the optimum is $100$. What is the relative gap $(z^*-\text{bound})/z^*$ in percent?

    Divide the difference by the optimum.

    $(100-90)/100=10\%$.

    • Choose set partitioning when route costs are complicated or when you need a strong bound, and pay with column generation.
    • Choose the three-index model when the vans differ in capacity or cost.
    • Using three-index with identical vans "for strength": it gives none and adds symmetry.
    • Believing a compact load-variable model matches rounded capacity cuts: on the example it reaches 88.9% of the optimum against 97.5%.
    1. The three-index model adds a van index to every variable; it can say who drives what (heterogeneous fleets) but is large and symmetric.
    2. Set partitioning chooses whole routes, keeps rows few and columns exponential, and is solved by column generation: price routes with the duals until none has negative reduced cost.
    3. LP strength differs sharply: on the running example the bounds are 84% (degrees), 89% (load variables), 97.5% (rounded cuts) and 100% (set partitioning) of the optimum; rounding the vehicle count is what makes the difference.

    Which model can price a route that has overtime charges and a different cost for each van type?

    The two-index model, by changing the edge costs.
    It cannot tell which van uses an edge, nor price a whole route in one number.
    None; route costs must be sums of edge costs.
    This is exactly what set partitioning relaxes.
    The set-partitioning model, since each column carries its own cost $c_j$.
    The cost of a route is computed beforehand in any way you like.

    In column generation, a candidate route has $\bar c_j=-3$. What do you do?

    Discard it: only positive reduced costs help a minimisation.
    Recall from Part 2: a negative reduced cost means entering the column lowers the objective.
    Add it to the master and re-solve.
    It improves the restricted LP; new duals then price the remaining routes again.
    Stop: the LP is optimal.
    Optimality needs no column with negative reduced cost.

    Why does rounding $2d(S)/C$ up to $2r(S)$ strengthen the two-index LP?

    It reduces the number of variables.
    The variables are unchanged; only right-hand sides rise.
    It makes the cuts easier to separate.
    Finding violated rounded cuts is not easier.
    It raises right-hand sides, removing fractional points such as the blend that used 2.4 vans' worth of crossing.
    A smaller feasible region can only raise the LP minimum, as Part 3 showed.

    Identical vans, three-index model: what does the extra index mostly buy?

    A stronger LP bound.
    Averaging the vans gives a two-index point of equal cost, so no.
    Nothing useful, apart from symmetry ($K!$ copies of each plan).
    It becomes useful only when vans differ in capacity or cost.
    Fewer constraints.
    It has more variables and constraints.

    Variants: when the real world adds rules

    Real routing problems add rules to the CVRP: customers want delivery within a time window, goods must be picked up before they are dropped off, vans differ, depots must be chosen. Each rule changes a few constraints.

    You will be asked to write or recognise these models, and a project in practice almost never meets the plain CVRP. The skill is to see which part of the base model each rule touches.

    It is like adapting a recipe for allergies: the ingredients list changes in one or two lines, the method stays.

    Time windows (VRPTW)

    Customer $i$ must begin service in a window $[a_i,b_i]$ and service takes $s_i$ time units. A van arriving early waits; arriving after $b_i$ is not allowed. As in Ch. 5.4 (TSP with time windows, where the start time is called $y_i$), a continuous variable $w^k_i$ records the time at which van $k$ starts serving $i$. The lecture adds a copy $n+1$ of the depot as the end of every route with $d_0=s_0=d_{n+1}=s_{n+1}=0$, so every route is a path from $0$ to $n+1$.

    $$w^k_j\ \ge\ w^k_i+s_i+t_{ij}-M_{ij}\,(1-x^k_{ij})\ \ \forall k,\ (i,j)\in A,\qquad a_i\le w^k_i\le b_i,$$

    together with route constraints (each van leaves $0$ once and arrives at $n+1$ once, flow conservation at customers, exactly one van serves each customer) and the load limit $\sum_{i}d_i\,x^k(\delta^+(i))\le C_k$. Here $t_{ij}$ is the travel time. The first constraint says: if van $k$ drives $i\to j$, service at $j$ starts no earlier than service at $i$ ends plus the drive. If $x^k_{ij}=0$ the constraint must be harmless, which is the job of $M_{ij}$. A tight choice is $M_{ij}=b_i+s_i+t_{ij}-a_j$.

    Why that $M_{ij}$ works: with $x^k_{ij}=0$ the constraint reads $w_j\ge w_i+s_i+t_{ij}-M_{ij}$. Its hardest case is the latest start $w_i=b_i$ with the earliest start $w_j=a_j$, and it still holds there exactly when $M_{ij}\ge b_i+s_i+t_{ij}-a_j$. A smaller valid $M$ gives a stronger LP (Part 3: use the smallest valid big-M). In addition, an arc $(i,j)$ can be deleted from the model before solving if $a_i+s_i+t_{ij}>b_j$ (even leaving $i$ at the earliest moment, one arrives at $j$ too late) or if $d_i+d_j>\max_kC_k$.

    Running example for time windows

    A van leaves the depot at time $0$ and must serve four stops. Windows and service times: stop 1 $[8,20]$, 3 min; stop 2 $[15,30]$, 4 min; stop 3 $[5,14]$, 2 min; stop 4 $[34,45]$, 5 min. The depot is open $[0,60]$. Travel times (symmetric): $t_{01}=6$, $t_{02}=9$, $t_{03}=5$, $t_{04}=12$, $t_{12}=7$, $t_{13}=4$, $t_{14}=10$, $t_{23}=8$, $t_{24}=6$, $t_{34}=11$.

    Try it

    Choose the stops one by one. The bars show each window, the green blocks show service, the gold line shows waiting. Find the visiting order that works. Notice that an early arrival is harmless (the van waits) while a late arrival cannot be repaired, so tight windows fix the order.

    Check the order $0\to3\to1\to2\to4\to0$ for the example, and find $M_{31}$ and decide whether the arc $1\to3$ can be deleted.

    1. Stop 3: arrive $0+5=5$, window starts at $5$, so serve $5\text{–}7$.

      Service start is $\max(\text{arrival},a_i)$; it must not exceed $b_i$.

    2. Stop 1: arrive $7+4=11\in[8,20]$, serve $11\text{–}14$. Stop 2: arrive $14+7=21\in[15,30]$, serve $21\text{–}25$.

      Arrival is the end of the previous service plus the drive.

    3. Stop 4: arrive $25+6=31$, wait until $34$, serve $34\text{–}39$. Back at the depot at $39+12=51\le60$. Feasible.

      The van waits $3$ minutes, as the gold line showed.

    4. $M_{31}=b_3+s_3+t_{31}-a_1=14+2+4-8=12$.

      The largest amount by which the constraint might otherwise be violated when arc $3\to1$ is unused.

    5. Arc $1\to3$: $a_1+s_1+t_{13}=8+3+4=15>b_3=14$, so the arc can be deleted.

      Even the earliest possible departure from stop 1 reaches stop 3 after its window closes. Checking all $24$ orders, only $3\text{-}1\text{-}2\text{-}4$ is feasible.

    Pickup and delivery (VRPPDTW, dial-a-ride)

    Now a request is a pair: pick up at node $i$, drop off at node $n+i$. Pickups are $P=\{1,\dots,n\}$, drop-offs $D=\{n+1,\dots,2n\}$, and each van $k$ has its own start $o_k$ and end $e_k$ (it need not return to a common depot). The model, written with the vehicle index, keeps three families of conditions beyond the VRPTW time constraints.

    • Same van, in order. The van that visits $i$ must visit $n+i$ (a pairing constraint on $x^k$), and the pickup comes first: $w^k_i+t_{i,n+i}\le w^k_{n+i}$.
    • Load. The load variable $q^k_i$ after visiting $i$ obeys $q^k_j\ge q^k_i+d_j-O_{ij}(1-x^k_{ij})$ with $d_j>0$ at pickups and negative at drop-offs, and $q^k_i\le C_k$; here $O_{ij}$ is a big-$M$ constant, chosen as small as possible like $M_{ij}$.
    • Time windows as before; for people (dial-a-ride) a maximum ride time is added to stop long detours.

    The point of the example below is that capacity depends on order: the same set of requests can be feasible in one order and not in another.

    Van capacity $6$. Request 1 carries $3$ units, request 2 carries $4$. Compare the visiting orders $P_1,P_2,D_1,D_2$ and $P_1,D_1,P_2,D_2$.

    1. Order $P_1,P_2,D_1,D_2$: loads after each stop are $3,\ 7,\ 4,\ 0$. Maximum $7>6$: infeasible.

      Both parcels are on board at once.

    2. Order $P_1,D_1,P_2,D_2$: loads $3,\,0,\,4,\,0$. Maximum $4\le6$: feasible.

      The first parcel leaves before the second joins; the cost may be higher in distance, but it respects capacity.

    The rest of the family

    VariantWhat changesModel effect
    Backhauls (VRPB)Some customers are delivered to (linehaul $L$), some are collected from (backhaul $B$); all linehaul stops come first on a route.Delete arcs $B\to L$ and depot$\to B$; capacity is checked separately for the delivery load and for the collection load. For a set $S$ that mixes both kinds, the vans needed are the larger of the two bin-packing numbers $r(L\cap S)$ and $r(B\cap S)$.
    Two-echelon (2E-CVRP)Large trucks bring goods from the depot to satellites (small depots); small vans take them on to customers.Two levels of arcs $A_1$ (depot, satellites) and $A_2$ (satellites, customers); variables $x_{ij}$ (first level), $y_{ijs}$ (second level from satellite $s$) and $z_{si}$ (customer $i$ served from satellite $s$); satellite capacities.
    Location routing (LRP)The depots themselves are chosen from candidate sites $D$ with fixed costs $f_i$ and capacities $W_i$.Objective $\sum c\,x+\sum_{i\in D}f_iy_i$; assignment $z_{ij}$ of customer $j$ to depot $i$; capacity $\sum_jd_jz_{ij}\le W_iy_i$; linking constraints forbid a van from depot $i$ serving a customer assigned elsewhere. Facility location of Part 3 and routing together.
    Multi-depot and heterogeneous fleetVans start from different depots, or vans differ in capacity and cost. (Not separate models on the slides; they are what the vehicle index and the depot sets already allow.)Use the three-index form with $C_k$, $c^k_{ij}$ and a start depot $o_k$ per van; the two-index model cannot express it.

    A pattern emerges. Time, order and precedence require time or load variables, so the model becomes a three-index model with big-M constraints (weak LP, as in Part 3), or a set-partitioning model where the route-feasibility test hides the complication. Choosing where to put things (depots, satellites) brings in the binary open/close variables and forcing constraints of facility location.

    Go deeper: why set partitioning absorbs time windows

    In the route-based model the question "is this route feasible?" is answered outside the LP, by a dynamic programme that tracks time and load along the route. Column generation then needs a pricing problem that respects those resources, a shortest path with resource constraints. That is why the strongest exact codes for time-window problems use branch and price (the Baldacci et al. paper in Resources/Exact VRPs treats the CVRP and VRPTW with the same method).

    For arc $(i,j)$: $b_i=20$, $s_i=3$, $t_{ij}=6$, $a_j=8$. Compute the tight $M_{ij}=b_i+s_i+t_{ij}-a_j$.

    Just add and subtract.

    $20+3+6-8=21$.

    $a_i=10$, $s_i=4$, $t_{ij}=7$, $b_j=20$. Can the arc $(i,j)$ be deleted?

    Compare $a_i+s_i+t_{ij}$ with $b_j$.

    $10+4+7=21>20$: even the earliest possible arrival is too late. Delete it.

    A van leaves the depot at time $0$. Stop A has window $[10,20]$, service $3$, depot-to-A time $7$. Stop B has window $[12,30]$, A-to-B time $5$. At what time does service at B start?

    Arrive at A at 7, but A opens at 10: the van waits. Service at A then lasts 3.

    Start at A $=\max(7,10)=10$; finish $13$. Arrive at B $13+5=18\ge12$, so service at B starts at $18$.

    Pickup loads $+3$ at $P_1$ and $+4$ at $P_2$ (drop-offs release the same amounts). In the order $P_1,P_2,D_1,D_2$ what is the maximum load?

    Both parcels are on board after the second pickup.

    $3$, then $3+4=7$, then $4$, then $0$. Maximum $7$.

    Backhaul problem, $C=10$: linehaul demands $(6,6,5)$ and backhaul demands $(4,3)$. What is the smallest number of vans?

    Pack each side separately and take the larger of the two answers: a van delivers first, then collects.

    Linehaul: any two weigh at least $11>10$, so $3$ vans. Backhaul: $4+3=7\le10$, so $1$ van. A van can serve both sides, so $\max(3,1)=3$.

    • Delete impossible arcs before solving: it shrinks the model and strengthens the LP.
    • Use the smallest valid big-M for each arc, not one global constant.
    • Treating a time window as a constraint on arrival: early arrival is allowed, the van waits.
    • Forgetting the precedence "pickup before drop-off" and the same-van requirement.
    1. Time windows add continuous start-time variables with big-M constraints $w_j\ge w_i+s_i+t_{ij}-M_{ij}(1-x_{ij})$; a tight $M_{ij}=b_i+s_i+t_{ij}-a_j$ and arc deletion keep the model small.
    2. Pickup and delivery adds pairing, precedence and a load variable that goes up at pickups and down at drop-offs, so capacity depends on the order of visits.
    3. Backhauls, satellites, depot choice and mixed fleets each edit a few constraints of the base model; set partitioning absorbs complicated route rules into the definition of a feasible route.

    A van reaches stop $j$ before the window opens. What happens in the VRPTW?

    The route is infeasible.
    Only arrival after $b_j$ is a violation.
    It waits until $a_j$ and then serves.
    That is why the time variable is $\max(\text{arrival},a_j)$ and why $a_j\le w_j$.
    It skips the stop and returns later.
    The model requires that every customer be served once.

    Why is $M_{ij}=b_i+s_i+t_{ij}-a_j$ preferred to a huge $M$ such as $10^6$?

    It guarantees an integer solution.
    Integrality does not depend on $M$.
    It is the smallest value that makes the constraint harmless when $x_{ij}=0$, so the LP relaxation is tighter.
    Same lesson as the facility-location forcing constraints in Part 3.
    The solver rejects constants larger than $1000$.
    Solvers accept them, but they cause numerical trouble and weak bounds.

    Which variant makes the model contain depot-opening binaries and customer-to-depot assignment variables?

    Backhauls.
    Backhauls change arcs and capacities, not depots.
    Location routing.
    It combines facility location (Part 3) with routing: $y_i$ open, $z_{ij}$ assignment.
    VRPTW.
    That adds time variables.

    Why can a two-index model not handle a fleet with different capacities?

    It uses too few constraints.
    The issue is information, not the count.
    Different capacities make the problem infeasible.
    Feasible plans exist; the model just cannot express them.
    It never records which van drives which edge.
    Capacity and cost depend on the van, which needs a vehicle index.

    Heuristics, bounds and the CVRP project

    Exact methods prove optimality but slow down as the number of customers grows. Heuristics give a good plan in seconds, with no proof. Together, a heuristic plan (upper bound) and an LP bound (lower bound) pin the optimum between them.

    You will use a heuristic to provide a starting solution, to judge a model's answer, and to check the course project's results. You must also be able to run the savings algorithm by hand.

    It is like a taxi driver's rule of thumb against a route planner with a guarantee: the rule is fast and usually good; the planner proves that nothing better exists.

    Clarke-Wright savings

    Start with the worst plan: each customer on its own out-and-back route. Joining two routes into one saves a trip to and from the depot. Joining customers $i$ and $j$ replaces $c_{0i}+c_{j0}$ (end of one trip, start of the other) with the direct edge $c_{ij}$, so the saving is $$s_{ij}=c_{0i}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}.$$ Large savings come from customers that are far from the depot but close to each other.

    1. Compute $s_{ij}$ for all pairs and sort them in decreasing order. Start with one route per customer.
    2. Take the next pair $(i,j)$. If $i$ and $j$ are the ends of two different routes next to the depot, and the combined load is at most $C$, merge the two routes at those ends.
    3. Otherwise skip the pair. Repeat until the list is exhausted.
    Try it

    Step through the pairs with "Next pair". Watch which merges are rejected (capacity or not route ends). Drag customers to change the savings, and switch $C$ to $14$ and $20$. Notice that with $C=10$ the final plan uses five routes, one more than the minimum, and still lies within a fraction of a percent of the optimum.

    Run the savings algorithm on the running example ($C=10$). The largest savings are $s_{12}=13.42$, $s_{18}=11.16$, $s_{78}=11.03$, $s_{34}=10.50$, $s_{23}=9.08$, $s_{56}=8.49$, $s_{67}=8.43$.

    1. $(1,2)$: loads $6+6=12>10$. Rejected.

      Capacity is the only reason a high saving is skipped here; customers 1 and 2 alone weigh too much.

    2. $(1,8)$: loads $6+3=9\le10$. Merge: route $[1,8]$.

      Both are single-customer routes, so both are ends.

    3. $(7,8)$: customer 8 is in $[1,8]$ with load $9$, customer 7 has load $5$: $14>10$. Rejected.

      Merging routes sums their loads, not only the two customers.

    4. $(3,4)$: $6+3=9$. Merge: $[3,4]$. $(2,3)$: $6+9=15$. Rejected. $(5,6)$: $4+2=6$. Merge: $[5,6]$. $(6,7)$: $6+5=11>10$. Rejected.

      Later pairs with positive savings fail on capacity too.

    5. Final plan: $[1,8],[2],[3,4],[5,6],[7]$, five routes, cost $99.04$. The optimum is $98.71$, so the gap is $0.33\%$.

      The savings plan is also the cheapest possible plan with exactly five routes; it uses one route more than the optimum, which packs the loads more tightly.

    Sweep

    The sweep algorithm (cluster first, route second) works with coordinates. Compute the angle of each customer around the depot, sort by angle, and sweep a ray around the depot, adding customers to the current route until the next one would exceed $C$, then start a new route. Finally, order the customers of each route by solving a small TSP. It is fast and natural for round regions, but it needs plane coordinates and ignores distance from the depot.

    Sweep the running example. Angles around the depot (degrees, anticlockwise from east): customer 4: $15.9$, 3: $54.5$, 2: $110.6$, 1: $135.0$, 8: $172.9$, 7: $209.7$, 6: $261.9$, 5: $315.0$. Start at customer 4.

    1. Customers 4, 3: load $3+6=9$. Adding 2 gives $15>10$: close route $[4,3]$.

      Capacity decides where to cut the sweep.

    2. Customer 2 ($6$): adding 1 gives $12>10$: close $[2]$. Customers 1, 8: $6+3=9$; adding 7 gives $14$: close $[1,8]$.

      The same rule each time.

    3. Customers 7, 6: $5+2=7$; adding 5 gives $11$: close $[7,6]$. Last: $[5]$.

      The ray has come full circle.

    4. Five routes, cost $99.10$ (for the sweep order within each route). Starting from other customers gives costs between $101.8$ and $102.0$, so the starting ray matters.

      A common remedy is to try every starting customer and keep the best.

    Local search

    Take any feasible plan and try small changes that keep feasibility and lower the cost: relocate a customer to another route or position, swap two customers between routes, 2-opt (reverse a stretch inside a route, as in Ch. 5.4). Repeat while some move helps. The plan then is a local optimum: no single move improves it, but a better plan may exist. Metaheuristics (simulated annealing, tabu search, large-neighbourhood search) accept some worsening moves to escape.

    Savings plan $[1,8],[2],[3,4],[5,6],[7]$ costs $99.04$. Is it a local optimum for single relocations? Can two moves reach the optimum?

    1. Test all single relocations that respect capacity. The least costly one (moving 6 into route $[7]$) raises the cost to $99.10$. None improves.

      The plan is a local optimum for this neighbourhood.

    2. Move customer 5 into route $[2]$ (loads $6+4=10$). New routes $[1,8],[2,5],[3,4],[6],[7]$ cost $107.14$, up by $8.10$.

      This single move is bad: customer 5 lies far from customer 2.

    3. Now merge $[6]$ and $[7]$ (loads $2+5=7$). The plan $[1,8],[2,5],[3,4],[6,7]$ costs $98.71$.

      It is the optimal plan. The first move worsens, the second repairs it more than enough: a local search that takes only improving single moves cannot see this, which is why richer neighbourhoods and metaheuristics exist.

    Bounds and the gap

    A heuristic only provides an upper bound. The LP of a formulation gives a lower bound (Chapter 6.2). On the running example the savings plan ($99.04$) and the LP with rounded capacity cuts ($96.20$) already guarantee that no plan is more than $2.87\%$ cheaper than the savings plan (gap $=(99.04-96.20)/99.04$, as in Part 4). Real instances are larger, but the logic is the same.

    Case study: the CVRP project

    Project

    The course project (Exact solution approaches for the CVRP) compares two formulations with Gurobi on benchmark instances, following the pattern of Labs 1 and 2: model, solve, study the LP bound and the solve time.

    Baseline. The two-index model of Chapter 6.1 with rounded capacity cuts, added lazily. The solver starts with only the degree constraints. Whenever it finds an integer solution, a callback looks for a violated cut and, if there is one, adds it and rejects the solution.

    Comparison. A multi-commodity flow (MCF) formulation (the paper by Letchford and Salazar-González, 2015, in Resources/Exact VRPs, whose abstract says its relaxations are stronger than earlier compact flow models). Extra flow variables track load along each route, so the model is a single static integer programme and no cutting is needed. As Chapter 6.2 showed, compact load models can be weak, so how much the MCF models improve on them is exactly what the project tests.

    Data and measures. Augerat A- and B-series instances with 15 to 50 customers (names such as A-n32-k5 usually mean 32 locations including the depot and 5 vehicles). For each instance and model, record the LP bound, branch-and-bound nodes, solve time and optimality gap at a time limit.

    1. Build the degree constraints and set the solver's lazy-constraint parameter (in Gurobi: Model.Params.LazyConstraints = 1).
    2. In the callback, when the solver reports a new integer solution (where == GRB.Callback.MIPSOL), read the values with cbGetSolution.
    3. Separate: build the used-edge graph, remove the depot, and take each connected group $S$ of customers. If $x(\delta(S))<2r(S)$ (use $\lceil d(S)/C\rceil$ if $r(S)$ is too slow), the cut is violated.
    4. Add the violated cut with cbLazy. If no group violates its cut, the solution is a feasible plan; accept it.

    On a fractional point of the LP there may be violated cuts that no connected group reveals; codes then use greedy growth heuristics to find sets $S$, since finding the most violated rounded capacity cut exactly is NP-hard in general (already evaluating $r(S)$ is a bin-packing problem). For integer solutions, components suffice, as the next example shows.

    The solver proposes the plan "loop $1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}1$, and vans $0\text{-}4\text{-}0$, $0\text{-}5\text{-}0$, $0\text{-}6\text{-}7\text{-}0$, $0\text{-}8\text{-}0$". Find the cut to add, and say why a heavy-route plan $0\text{-}1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}0$ with three further vans would also be caught.

    1. Remove the depot. The used edges leave components $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{4\}$, $\{5\}$, $\{6,7\}$, $\{8\}$.

      Each component is a candidate set $S$.

    2. For $S=\{1,2,3\}$: $x(\delta(S))=0$, while $2r(S)=6$ (or $2\lceil18/10\rceil=4$ with the cheap bound). Violated. Add $x(\delta(\{1,2,3\}))\ge6$.

      The next solution must connect these customers to the depot through enough vans.

    3. For the heavy-route plan the component $\{1,2,3\}$ has $x(\delta(S))=2<4\le6$. Violated as well.

      Both defects are caught by the same cut family, as Chapter 6.1 showed.

    Depot costs $c_{0i}=12$, $c_{0j}=15$ and $c_{ij}=9$. Compute the Clarke-Wright saving $s_{ij}$.

    $s_{ij}=c_{0i}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}$.

    $12+15-9=18$.

    Routes $[1,2]$ (load $6$) and $[3,4]$ (load $5$), capacity $10$. The next pair is $(2,3)$ and these are route ends. Is the merge allowed?

    Add the loads of the two routes.

    $6+5=11>10$: the merge would overload the van. Skip.

    Sweep with capacity $C=8$. In angular order the customers $1,2,3,4$ have demands $4,5,3,4$. How many routes does the sweep produce?

    Add customers until the next one does not fit: $4$, then $4+5$?

    Customer $1$ alone ($4+5=9>8$); then customers $2,3$ ($5+3=8$, adding customer $4$ gives $12$); then customer $4$. Three routes.

    Relocate move: customer $i$ lies between $p$ and $q$ with $c_{pi}=5$, $c_{iq}=6$, $c_{pq}=8$. It is inserted between $u$ and $v$ with $c_{ui}=4$, $c_{iv}=7$, $c_{uv}=6$. What is the total change in cost (negative means improvement)?

    Removing saves $c_{pi}+c_{iq}-c_{pq}$; inserting costs $c_{ui}+c_{iv}-c_{uv}$.

    Remove: $-(5+6-8)=-3$. Insert: $4+7-6=+5$. Net $+2$, a worse plan, so reject.

    A heuristic plan costs $99.04$ and an LP lower bound is $96.20$. Give the optimality gap $(\text{UB}-\text{LB})/\text{UB}$ of Part 4 in percent.

    $99.04-96.20=2.84$; divide by the incumbent $99.04$, not by the bound.

    $2.84/99.04\approx0.0287$, i.e. $2.87\%$. (Dividing by the bound $96.20$ would give $2.95\%$, which is not the gap a solver prints.)

    • Report a heuristic result together with a lower bound or the exact optimum when you have one.
    • Run a heuristic from several starting points or with several rules and keep the best.
    • Reading a local optimum as a global one.
    • Merging routes at customers that are not ends of their routes.
    Where we are in the story

    Kaveri Courier's owner now has the whole chain: choose the depot and the loads (Part 3), solve the models exactly (Part 4), route one van (Part 5) and plan the whole fleet (this part), with heuristics for a quick plan and a lower bound to judge it. The course project repeats this chain on benchmark instances.

    1. Savings merges routes in decreasing order of $s_{ij}=c_{0i}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}$ while capacity allows; sweep clusters by angle and then solves a TSP per cluster; local search improves a plan by small moves but can stop at a local optimum.
    2. A heuristic plan (upper bound) and a formulation's LP bound (lower bound) bracket the optimum; on the example the gap is at most 2.87%.
    3. The project compares a two-index model with lazily separated rounded capacity cuts against a compact multi-commodity-flow model, measuring LP bound, nodes, time and gap.

    Which pair of customers has the largest saving?

    Two customers right next to the depot.
    Their $c_{0i}$ and $c_{0j}$ are small, so $s_{ij}$ is small.
    Two customers far from the depot but close to each other.
    $c_{0i}+c_{0j}$ is large and $c_{ij}$ small.
    Two customers on opposite sides, far from each other.
    A large $c_{ij}$ subtracts from the saving.

    On the running example, the savings algorithm with $C=10$ gives five routes while the optimum has four. What does this show?

    The algorithm is wrong.
    It follows its rules; it is a heuristic, not an exact method.
    A greedy merge order can leave loads packed worse than the best plan, but here the cost is only $0.33\%$ above the optimum.
    Greedy choices are made one pair at a time, with no look-ahead at packing.
    Four routes are infeasible.
    The widget's optimal plan uses four routes with loads 9, 10, 9, 7.

    In the lazy-cut loop, when is a candidate solution accepted?

    When every connected group of customers $S$ satisfies $x(\delta(S))\ge 2r(S)$.
    Then no cut is violated and the plan is feasible.
    When the solver reports that its LP bound equals the best known solution.
    That concerns the gap, not feasibility.
    When at least one cut has been added.
    Adding a cut means the solution was rejected.

    A local search finds no improving relocation or swap. What can you conclude?

    The plan is optimal.
    The example showed a plan that is stuck at $99.04$ while $98.71$ exists.
    The plan is infeasible.
    Local search keeps feasibility.
    It is a local optimum for these moves only; a better plan may exist.
    Only an exact method or a bound can certify optimality.

    Seven customers each demand $5$ and $C=12$. What is $r(S)$ for all seven, and what does the capacity cut need?

    $r(S)=3$ from $\lceil 35/12\rceil$; the cut needs $x(\delta(S))\ge6$.
    Check whether three demands of $5$ fit in one van of capacity $12$.
    $r(S)=4$ since only two $5$s fit per van; the cut needs $x(\delta(S))\ge 8$.
    Seven items at two per van need four vans, and each van's round trip crosses the boundary twice.
    $r(S)=7$; the cut needs $x(\delta(S))\ge14$.
    Two customers do fit together, so one van per customer is wasteful.

    Which relaxation of the CVRP is typically the strongest?

    The two-index model with degree constraints only.
    Loops and overloaded routes are allowed, which gave 84% of the optimum.
    The MTZ-type load-variable model.
    Its fractional loads gave 89% on the example.
    The set-partitioning LP, solved by column generation.
    It optimises over fractions of whole feasible routes.

    For arc $(i,j)$: $b_i=30$, $s_i=5$, $t_{ij}=10$, $a_j=25$. The tight big-M is:

    $M_{ij}=30+5+10+25=70$
    $a_j$ is subtracted, not added.
    $M_{ij}=30+5+10-25=20$
    The worst-case lateness when the arc is not used.
    $M_{ij}=30-25=5$
    Do not forget service and travel times.

    The savings plan costs $104$ and the best known lower bound is $100$. What is the largest possible relative improvement over the plan (the gap of Part 4)?

    0%
    The bound and plan differ, so some improvement may exist.
    $(104-100)/100=4\%$
    That divides by the lower bound. The gap divides by the incumbent, the plan in hand.
    At most $(104-100)/104\approx3.8\%$
    The optimum lies between $100$ and $104$, so at most $4$ of the $104$ can be saved.

    The bin-packing model "assign items to bins of capacity $C$ with $y_i=1$ if bin $i$ is used" has which objective?

    Maximise $\sum_iy_i$.
    That would use as many bins as possible; the Lecture 3 and 6 slides print this by mistake.
    Minimise $\sum_iy_i$.
    We want the fewest bins, i.e. the fewest vans.
    Minimise $\sum_i\sum_jx_{ij}$.
    That sum is always $n$ because every item is placed once.

    With $K=1$ van and capacity large enough for everyone, the two-index model with cuts becomes:

    The TSP with degree 2 and subtour cuts $x(\delta(S))\ge2$.
    Here $r(S)=1$ for every $S$, so the cuts are the TSP's connectivity cuts.
    A bin-packing problem.
    One bin only, nothing to choose.
    The assignment problem.
    Assignment has no subtour condition, and the cuts here exclude subtours.

    In branch and bound for a minimisation, a node whose LP bound is $97$ with an incumbent of $96.5$ is:

    Branched on, since its bound is below the incumbent.
    Compare the signs: the bound is above the incumbent.
    Pruned, since no plan in that subtree can cost less than $97$.
    A stronger LP relaxation raises such bounds, so more nodes are pruned.
    Accepted as the new incumbent.
    An LP bound is not a feasible plan unless integral.

    This part is for the last weeks before the paper. It shows how to read an exam question, drills thirty true/false statements of the kind that catch careful students, and ends with a timed mock paper of ten new problems and a cumulative quiz over Parts −1 to 6. Every problem here is new: none is taken from the slides, past papers or the problem set.

    You need: the main course, Parts 1 to 6, as the material to be examined (Part −1 for big-M and Part −3 for LP drawing). Come back to this part after each lecture and again in the week before the exam.

    How to attack an exam question: six types and a first move for each

    Almost every question in this course is one of six types. Naming the type in the first ten seconds tells you which tool to pick up and where the marks are.

    Marks reward visible method: defined variables, a stated objective sense, a labelled bound, a clear reason. A wrong final number with all of these still earns most of the marks; a bare correct number can earn very few.

    It is like a pilot's checklist: the checklist does not fly the plane, but it stops you from forgetting the one step that causes the accident.

    A five-step habit that works for every type

    1. Read the command word and the marks. "Formulate", "branch", "dual", "show that", "state with reason", "interpret the log". Marks tell you how much working is expected: 2 marks means one or two lines, 12 marks means a full method.
    2. Name the type using the table below.
    3. Write the set-up before any arithmetic. Variables with meaning, the objective with its sense (min or max), or the dual with its sign rules, or the node set $S$. The set-up is where most marks are, and it protects you if the arithmetic goes wrong.
    4. Calculate with a check built in. Primal and dual values equal; degrees add to $2$; bound below the incumbent for a minimisation.
    5. Finish with a sentence that answers the question in words, with units: "the cheapest plan costs 98 and opens sites 3 and 4".
    TypeSignal wordsFirst moveWhere the marks areTypical slip
    Formulate an IPformulate, model, write the constraintsSay what each variable means and its domain; fix min or maxvariables, objective, one constraint per sentence of the story, integralitywrong sense (bin packing and lot sizing are minimisations); a forcing row $x\le My$ missing
    Solve or prune a branch and bound treebranch, incumbent, bound, prune, nodeSolve the root LP; draw the tree; label each node with its LP valueLP value at each node, a reason on every closed node, the final proofbranching to $x\ge\lfloor v\rfloor$ instead of $\lceil v\rceil$; pruning on the wrong side of the incumbent
    LP duality and sensitivitydual, shadow price, reduced cost, rangeWrite the dual with the sign rules, or take $B^{-1}$ from the optimal basiscorrect dual, equal objective values, the range of validityequality row given a non-negative dual variable; a price used outside its range
    TSP or VRP model, cut or heuristicsubtour, MTZ, cut, capacity, savingsName the node set $S$ and compute $x(\delta(S))$ or $x(E(S))$ against the right-hand sidethe right $S$, the direction of the inequality, $r(S)$ for capacitymixing $x(\delta(S))\ge2$ with $x(E(S))\le|S|-1$; $\lceil d(S)/C\rceil$ instead of $r(S)$
    True / false and short reasoningtrue or false, justify, explain whyHunt for the smallest counterexamplea one-line reason; the verdict alone earns littlea reason that is true but does not decide the statement
    Read a solver loglog, incumbent, BestBd, gapRead the three numbers: Incumbent, BestBd, Gapthe gap formula; rounding the bound when costs are integersdividing by the bound instead of the incumbent; swapping the two for a minimisation
    Try it

    Read each stem and press the type you think it is. A first-try score is kept at the bottom. Notice that the command word (write, branch, show, state, read) decides the type much more often than the topic does: two stems about the same big-M can be a formulation and a true/false.

    Running example for the formulation type

    The dispatcher at Kaveri Courier plans tomorrow's deliveries to six zones A to F. Binary $y_Z=1$ means "zone $Z$ is served". The statement of a formulation question is usually a list of such sentences, and every sentence becomes one constraint. The skill is translating sentence by sentence.

    Write each rule about the six zones as a linear constraint on $y_A,\dots,y_F\in\{0,1\}$. (1) At most 3 zones are served. (2) If C is served then B is served. (3) Exactly one of D and E is served. (4) A and F are never served together. (5) The amount $x_C$ sent to C is at most 50 units, and only if C is served.

    1. (1) $y_A+y_B+y_C+y_D+y_E+y_F\le 3$.

      Each served zone contributes $1$ to the sum, so "at most 3" is a bound on the sum.

    2. (2) $y_C\le y_B$.

      If $y_C=1$ the row forces $y_B=1$; if $y_C=0$ the row says nothing. That is exactly "if C then B".

    3. (3) $y_D+y_E=1$.

      One of them is $1$ and the other $0$; "exactly one" is an equality.

    4. (4) $y_A+y_F\le 1$.

      The pair $(1,1)$ would give $2$, which the row forbids; the other three pairs are allowed.

    5. (5) $x_C\le 50\,y_C$ with $x_C\ge0$.

      If $y_C=0$ it forces $x_C=0$; if $y_C=1$ it allows up to $50$. The number $50$ is the smallest valid big-$M$, because $x_C$ can never exceed $50$ (Part −1).

    Careful: read the sense of the objective before anything else. Bin packing minimises the number of bins used, and lot sizing minimises total cost, even though some slides write a maximisation. A formulation with the wrong sense scores no objective marks, whatever else is right.

    Six jobs are assigned to three machines. Variables: $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ ($1$ if job $i$ runs on machine $j$) and $y_j\in\{0,1\}$ ($1$ if machine $j$ is used). The constraints are $\sum_j x_{ij}=1$ for each job and $\sum_i d_ix_{ij}\le q_jy_j$ for each machine. How many binary variables and how many constraints (not counting the $0$–$1$ bounds) does the model have?

    Count the pairs $(i,j)$, add the machines, then count one row per job and one per machine.

    Variables: $6\cdot3=18$ for $x$ plus $3$ for $y$, so $21$. Constraints: $6$ assignment rows plus $3$ capacity rows, so $9$. Note that the capacity row with $q_jy_j$ also links $x$ to $y$ (it forces $x_{ij}=0$ when $y_j=0$), so no separate linking rows are needed.

    A minimisation problem has integer variables and integer cost coefficients. A node of the branch and bound tree has LP value $17.4$. What is the smallest value the best integer solution inside that node can have?

    With integer variables and integer costs, every integer solution has an integer cost. The LP value is a lower bound.

    Every integer solution in the node costs at least $17.4$ and is an integer, so at least $18$. The node can therefore be closed as soon as the incumbent is $18$ or lower.

    A primal LP $\min c^\top x$ with $Ax\ge b$, $x\ge0$ has $4$ constraints and $6$ variables. How many variables and how many constraints does its dual have?

    Each primal constraint gets a dual variable; each primal variable gets a dual constraint.

    The dual $\max b^\top y$, $A^\top y\le c$, $y\ge0$ has one variable per primal row, so $4$, and one constraint per primal column, so $6$.

    A minimisation log shows Incumbent $250$ and BestBd $240$. What gap, in percent, does the solver print?

    The gap is the difference divided by the incumbent.

    $(250-240)/250=0.04$, that is $4\%$. Dividing by the bound would give $4.17\%$, which is not what the solver prints.

    • Underline the command word and the marks before you start.
    • Define every variable and state min or max first.
    • Put a one-sentence answer, with units, at the end.
    • Starting arithmetic before the set-up is written.
    • Giving a true/false verdict without a reason.
    • Leaving a question blank: a correct set-up earns marks on its own.
    1. Almost every question is one of six types: formulate, branch and bound, duality or sensitivity, TSP or VRP model or cut, true/false reasoning, and reading a log; name the type first.
    2. Marks sit in the set-up: variables with meaning, the objective sense, the dual's signs, the node set $S$, the stated reason on a closed node.
    3. Build a check into every calculation: equal primal and dual values, degrees adding up, a bound on the correct side of the incumbent.

    A 12-mark question says "Formulate". Which of these earns marks even if every constraint turns out wrong?

    The final numerical optimum.
    A formulation question has no numerical answer to give; the marks are for the model.
    Defining the variables and stating the objective with the right sense.
    These are the first marks on the scheme, and a reader can only follow the constraints if the variables are defined.
    Copying the constraints from the slides.
    Marks go to constraints that fit this story, not to remembered ones.

    A log for a minimisation shows Incumbent $1342$ and BestBd $1301.6$. Which statement about the printed gap is right?

    It is $(1342-1301.6)/1301.6$.
    That divides by the bound. Check which of the two numbers the formula in Part 4 uses.
    It is $1301.6/1342$.
    That is a ratio of the two numbers, not a gap.
    It is $(1342-1301.6)/1342\approx3.01\%$.
    The gap divides by the incumbent.

    The statement says "If C is served then B must be served". Which constraint is correct?

    $y_C\le y_B$
    If $y_C=1$ it forces $y_B=1$; if $y_C=0$ it is silent.
    $y_B\le y_C$
    This says "if B then C", the reverse implication.
    $y_B+y_C=1$
    This says exactly one of them is served.

    True/false drill: thirty statements with traps

    A true/false question with a reason tests one precise fact. The traps are always the same few: min against max, which way an inequality points, "always" and "never", and weak against strong formulations.

    The score on a drill like this tells you exactly which facts are still shaky. Each statement below has a hint and a reason; the reason is the part that earns marks in the exam.

    It is like a spot-the-difference puzzle: the two versions look alike, and one changed word flips the answer.

    Method: counterexample first

    To show a statement false you need only one example where it fails. To show it true you need a rule. So test the statement on the smallest case you can imagine (one variable, two cities, one constraint) before reaching for theory. Pay special attention to words such as always, never, any, only, exactly.

    TrapThe fact to remember
    Direction of boundsMinimisation: LP relaxation value is a lower bound, an incumbent is an upper bound. Maximisation: the reverse.
    Dual signsMinimisation, $\ge$ row: dual variable $\ge0$. An equality row: dual variable free. A free primal variable: an equality dual row.
    Weak against strongA formulation is stronger when its LP region lies inside the other's and has the same integer points. Larger big-$M$ means a weaker bound.
    Children in branch and boundEach child adds a constraint, so its LP value is never better than the parent's.
    MTZ against DFJDFJ LP is at least as strong as MTZ LP; MTZ is compact, DFJ needs cuts.
    Sense of the objectiveBin packing minimises bins used; lot sizing minimises cost.
    Try it

    A single fixed-charge row $x\le My$ with demand $x=40$. Slide the big-$M$ and read the LP bound against the integer optimum. Notice that the bound is best when $M$ equals the demand and falls steadily as $M$ grows: this is the fact behind several statements below.

    Decide: "The dual variable of an equality constraint in a minimisation LP must be non-negative." Use the counterexample method on $\min\ 3x_1+4x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2=-2$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$.

    1. Solve the primal. The equality gives $x_1=x_2-2$, and $x_1\ge0$ forces $x_2\ge2$. The cost is $3(x_2-2)+4x_2=7x_2-6$, smallest at $x_2=2$, $x_1=0$, cost $8$.

      A counterexample needs an actual optimum to compare against.

    2. Write the dual with one variable $y$ for the equality: maximise $-2y$ subject to $y\le3$ (from $x_1$) and $-y\le4$ (from $x_2$).

      Each primal column gives one dual inequality; the right-hand side $-2$ of the equality is the dual objective coefficient.

    3. The dual constraints say $-4\le y\le3$, and $-2y$ is largest at $y=-4$, with value $8$.

      Strong duality: the dual optimum $8$ equals the primal optimum $8$.

    4. The optimal dual variable is negative, so it cannot be restricted to $y\ge0$. The statement is false: the dual variable of an equality is free.

      If we had forced $y\ge0$ the best dual value would be $0$, which is below the true optimum $8$.

    Group A: LP and duality

    1. In the dual of a minimisation LP, the variable of an equality constraint of the primal must be non-negative.

    What does a dual variable multiply, and may an equality be multiplied by a negative number?

    False. An equality can be multiplied by any real number, so its dual variable is free. Only the variable of a $\ge$ row (in a minimisation) is restricted to $y\ge0$.

    2. If a constraint is not tight at an optimal solution of an LP, its shadow price is zero.

    Complementary slackness: price times slack.

    True. At an optimal pair, $y_i\cdot(\text{slack}_i)=0$. A positive slack forces $y_i=0$: extra room in a constraint that is not binding has no value.

    3. If the primal LP is unbounded, the dual LP is also unbounded.

    Weak duality: a dual feasible point bounds the primal objective.

    False. If the dual had a feasible point it would bound the primal value, so an unbounded primal forces the dual to be infeasible.

    4. Adding a new constraint to a minimisation LP can lower the optimal value.

    What happens to the feasible region?

    False. The feasible region can only shrink, so the minimum stays the same or rises. (If the new constraint is violated at the old optimum, the dual simplex repairs it, and the value rises or stays equal.)

    5. In a minimisation LP, a basic feasible solution with all non-basic reduced costs $\ge0$ is optimal.

    Every neighbouring corner changes the objective by (step) times (reduced cost).

    True. Each move from the corner has a non-negative reduced cost times a non-negative step, so no neighbour improves, and for a convex problem a local optimum is global.

    6. A shadow price stays valid for every change of the right-hand side.

    Think of the basic solution $B^{-1}b$ as $b$ changes.

    False. The price holds only while the basis stays feasible, that is while $B^{-1}b+t\,B^{-1}e_i\ge0$. Beyond the range some basic variable would become negative and the basis changes. For the LP $\max 6x_1+4x_2$ with $2x_1+x_2\le b_1$ in the mock paper below, the price $2$ holds only for $19\le b_1\le28$.

    Group B: modelling and formulation strength

    7. For a minimisation IP, the optimal value of the LP relaxation is an upper bound on the IP optimum.

    The relaxation has more feasible points than the IP.

    False. A larger feasible set can only give a smaller (or equal) minimum, so the relaxation value is a lower bound.

    8. Rounding the LP optimum of a pure integer programme to the nearest integers always gives a feasible solution.

    Try two binaries with $2x_1+2x_2\le3$.

    False. For $2x_1+2x_2\le3$ the point $(0.75,0.75)$ is LP-feasible, but rounding gives $(1,1)$ with left side $4>3$.

    9. If polyhedron $P_1\subseteq P_2$ and both have the same integer points, the LP over $P_1$ gives a bound at least as good as the LP over $P_2$.

    Compare the two feasible sets.

    True. For a minimisation the smaller region has the larger (or equal) minimum, so a higher lower bound: $P_1$ is the stronger formulation.

    10. Replacing $M=60$ by $M=1000$ in $x\le My$ (where $x\le60$ always) improves the LP bound.

    The LP sets $y=x/M$ and pays the fixed cost on that fraction.

    False. With $M=1000$ the LP pays only $1/1000$ of the fixed cost per unit, so the bound is weaker. The smallest valid $M$ is the best choice.

    11. In facility location, the $mn$ rows $x_{ij}\le y_j$ give an LP bound at least as strong as the $n$ rows $\sum_i x_{ij}\le m\,y_j$ ($m$ customers).

    Add the individual rows over $i$.

    True. Summing $x_{ij}\le y_j$ over $i$ gives $\sum_i x_{ij}\le m\,y_j$, so the individual rows imply the aggregated ones and cut away at least as much.

    12. Bin packing is a maximisation problem: the aim is to use as many bins as possible.

    What would a warehouse manager want?

    False. The aim is to pack all items using the fewest bins: the objective is $\min\sum_j y_j$. (Some slides write $\max$; that is a slip.)

    13. Adding a valid inequality to an IP never removes a feasible integer point.

    What does "valid" mean?

    True. A valid inequality holds for every feasible integer point by definition; it only cuts off fractional points of the relaxation.

    14. For binary $x,y$, the constraint $x\le y$ forbids the pair $x=y=1$.

    Check the four pairs one by one.

    False. The pairs $(0,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$ are allowed; only $x=1,y=0$ is forbidden. The row means "if $x$ then $y$".

    15. Items of weights $5,6,7$ do not fit together in a knapsack of capacity $15$. Then $x_1+x_2+x_3\le2$ is a valid inequality.

    Total weight is $18$.

    True. The three items weigh $18>15$, so they form a cover; no feasible 0–1 point takes all three, hence $x_1+x_2+x_3\le|C|-1=2$. For example the LP point $(1,1,4/7)$ satisfies $5+6+4=15$ but has left side $2.57$, so the cut removes it.

    Group C: branch and bound

    16. In a minimisation, a node whose LP value is at least the incumbent value can be discarded.

    Can a child be better than its parent?

    True. Every solution inside the node costs at least the LP value, so none beats the incumbent.

    17. In a minimisation, a child node's LP value can be lower than its parent's.

    What does branching add to the parent's LP?

    False. A child has one more constraint, so its feasible set is smaller and its minimum cannot be lower.

    18. Depth-first and best-first search can end with different optimal values.

    What does the search order change, and what does it not change?

    False. The order changes the number of nodes, not the answer: both end with an incumbent proved optimal.

    19. A minimisation has integer variables and integer costs. A node has LP value $41.3$ and the incumbent is $42$. The node can be pruned.

    Round the node's bound up.

    True. Any integer solution in the node costs at least $\lceil41.3\rceil=42$, which does not beat $42$.

    20. Branching on $x_3=3.4$ creates the two children $x_3\le3$ and $x_3\ge3$.

    Does the second child cut off $3.4$?

    False. The children are $x_3\le3$ and $x_3\ge4$. With $x_3\ge3$ the point $3.4$ would stay feasible in the second child.

    21. When the printed gap is $0\%$, the incumbent is proved optimal.

    What do the incumbent and the BestBd sandwich?

    True. The incumbent is an upper bound and BestBd a lower bound for the optimum; a zero gap makes them equal.

    Group D: TSP and VRP

    22. The LP relaxation of the MTZ formulation is at least as strong as the LP relaxation of the DFJ formulation.

    MTZ allows $(1-\tfrac1{n-1})|C|$ on a cycle $C$; DFJ allows $|C|-1$.

    False. MTZ allows more on short cycles, so its LP region is larger and its bound weaker. It is compact, DFJ is strong.

    23. A violated subtour constraint of the symmetric TSP can be found in polynomial time.

    Treat $x^*_e$ as capacities.

    True. A violated cut $x^*(\delta(S))\lt2$ is a minimum cut of the support graph with capacities $x^*_e$, found by max-flow computations.

    24. For the ATSP, the assignment problem (degree constraints only) always returns a single tour.

    Two disjoint cycles also give every city one arc in and one out.

    False. Its solutions are cycle covers: a set of cycles that together visit every city. Only the subtour constraints force a single cycle.

    25. For a symmetric TSP with non-negative costs, the minimum spanning tree cost is a lower bound on the optimal tour cost.

    Delete one edge of an optimal tour.

    True. A tour minus one edge is a spanning tree, so the cheapest tree is no more expensive than the tour minus an edge, and that is no more than the tour.

    26. The 2-opt heuristic always ends at a globally optimal tour.

    What does "local optimum" mean?

    False. It stops when no single swap of two edges improves the tour, a local optimum that can be far from the global one.

    27. A symmetric TSP on $7$ cities has $360$ distinct tours.

    Fix the first city, then divide by two for direction.

    True. $(7-1)!/2=720/2=360$.

    28. Three customers with demands $4,4,4$ and van capacity $6$ can be served by $\lceil12/6\rceil=2$ vans.

    Can two demands of $4$ share a van?

    False. Two demands weigh $8>6$, so each customer needs its own van: $r(S)=3$, while $\lceil12/6\rceil=2$ is only a lower bound.

    29. The savings value $s_{ij}=c_{0i}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}$ is the cost saved by visiting $i$ and $j$ on one route instead of two separate out-and-back trips.

    Compare the two trips with the merged one: $0\to i\to j\to0$.

    True. Two separate trips cost $2c_{0i}+2c_{0j}$ (symmetric costs); the merged route $0\to i\to j\to0$ costs $c_{0i}+c_{ij}+c_{0j}$. The difference is $c_{0i}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}$.

    30. The set-partitioning formulation of the CVRP has a polynomial number of columns.

    How many different routes can be made from $n$ customers?

    False. Every feasible route is a column, and their number grows exponentially with $n$. That is why column generation prices routes with the dual values instead of listing them.

    • Test the smallest case first; one counterexample settles a "false".
    • Write the reason as a rule: "the feasible set shrinks, so the minimum cannot fall".
    • Check min or max, and the direction of the inequality, before the verdict.
    • Answering from the topic ("this is about MTZ") instead of the exact words.
    • Giving a verdict with no reason.
    • Trusting a slide's objective sense without checking it.
    1. Use the counterexample method: one tiny case disproves a statement, and a rule proves it.
    2. The same traps recur: direction of bounds, sign of dual variables, weak against strong big-$M$ and MTZ against DFJ, and children never being better.
    3. A good reason is one line that names the rule: complementary slackness, weak duality, "the feasible set shrinks", "valid means no integer point is lost".

    "A larger big-$M$ never changes the LP bound of a fixed-charge model." What is the best verdict with reason?

    True: big-$M$ is only a technical constant.
    Try the widget: moving $M$ moves the bound.
    False: the LP sets $y=x/M$, so a larger $M$ lowers the fixed cost paid and weakens the bound.
    The integer optimum is unchanged, but the relaxation gets weaker.
    False: a larger $M$ makes the problem infeasible.
    A larger valid $M$ keeps every integer point feasible.

    For $\min x_1+x_2$ with $x_1+x_2\ge4$ and $x_1-x_2=0$, the dual variable $y_2$ of the equality can be:

    Only non-negative.
    An equality row gives a free dual variable.
    Only non-positive.
    The sign is not fixed in either direction.
    Any real number; here the dual optimum has $y_2=0$ but its sign is not restricted.
    Dual: $\max4y_1$ with $y_1+y_2\le1$ and $y_1-y_2\le1$, $y_1\ge0$; the optimum is $y=(1,0)$ with value $4$.

    Which of these is a valid reason for "a child node's LP value is never lower than its parent's" (minimisation)?

    Child nodes use better solvers.
    The reason is about the feasible set, not the solver.
    The incumbent only improves.
    The incumbent concerns integer solutions, not the LP of the child.
    The child has one more constraint, so its feasible set is a subset of the parent's.
    A minimum over a subset cannot be smaller.

    Timed mock paper: ten new problems, 100 marks

    A mock paper trains something the chapters cannot: choosing what to do next with the clock running. Every problem below is new and has the same style and level as the exam.

    Do it with pencil and paper first. Type your final numbers into the boxes only when you have them; the page checks the answer, gives a hint after one wrong try and the full solution after two. Marks are printed so that you can mark yourself honestly.

    It is like a driving test: knowing the rules helps, but you only find out whether you can drive by driving with someone watching the clock.

    Rules of the mock

    • Choose the paper length (the real exam length is on your timetable; 120 min is a good default) and press Start. Do not use the notes tabs or the earlier parts.
    • The timer never submits, locks or marks anything. It only shows time and the pace.
    • Read all ten problems first. Do the ones you can finish quickly before the long ones.
    • If a problem has taken one and a half times its share of minutes, leave it and move on; come back with the time left over.
    Try it

    Pick the paper length, press Start and begin Problem 1 below. Use Pause only for a real interruption. Notice how the pace line tells you how many of the 100 marks should be written up by now; if you are behind it, skip to a shorter problem.

    Plan a 120-minute paper of 100 marks. The marks per problem are 14, 12, 10, 12, 10, 8, 8, 8, 10, 8. How do you split the time, and which problems do you start with?

    1. Reserve $10$ minutes at the start to read and $10$ at the end to check. That leaves $120-20=100$ minutes of working time.

      Reading first lets you choose an order; checking last catches sign slips that cost marks.

    2. Working time per mark: $100/100=1$ minute. A 14-mark problem gets about $14$ minutes, an 8-mark one gets about $8$.

      Marks are the price list; time should follow price.

    3. Start with the three 8-mark problems that need one idea each (problems 6, 7 and 10): about $24$ minutes for $24$ marks.

      Short, self-contained problems bank marks early and make the long ones less frightening.

    4. Set a stop-loss of one and a half times the share: $21$ minutes for problem 1, $18$ minutes for problem 2. At that point move on.

      A single stuck problem is the most common way to lose a paper.

    The paper

    Problem 1 [14 marks] Siting depots. The owner of Kaveri Courier chooses among five candidate depot sites to open (opening costs $f_j$ below). Each of four customers is served from exactly one open site at cost $c_{ij}$. Rules: at most $3$ sites are open; site 2 may open only if site 1 is open; sites 4 and 5 are never both open.

    Customer \ site12345
    Opening cost $f_j$3012261824
    Customer 11227213624
    Customer 2339241827
    Customer 3213062715
    Customer 4361827930

    (a) Write the model with $y_j$ (site $j$ open) and $x_{ij}$ (customer $i$ served from $j$); how many binary variables does it have? (b) Find the minimum total cost (opening plus service).

    For (b) choose which sites are open; then every customer simply takes the cheapest open site. List the allowed site sets and compare.

    (a) $\min\sum_jf_jy_j+\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ subject to $\sum_jx_{ij}=1$ for each customer, $x_{ij}\le y_j$, $\sum_jy_j\le3$, $y_2\le y_1$, $y_4+y_5\le1$, all binary. Variables: $4\cdot5+5=25$.

    (b) For a fixed set of open sites each customer takes its cheapest open site. Without the rule on site 2 the best set is $\{2,3\}$ with cost $12+26+(21+9+6+18)=92$, but it opens 2 without 1 and is forbidden. Among allowed sets: $\{3,4\}$ costs $26+18+(21+18+6+9)=98$; $\{1,2\}$ costs $30+12+(12+9+21+18)=102$; $\{3\}$ alone costs $26+(21+24+6+27)=104$. The minimum is 98, opening sites 3 and 4.

    Problem 2 [12 marks] LP and sensitivity. $\max\ 6x_1+4x_2$ subject to $2x_1+x_2\le b_1$ (with $b_1=20$), $x_1+x_2\le14$, $x_1+3x_2\le32$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$. Give (a) the optimal value, (b) the shadow price of the first constraint, (c) the smallest $b_1$ for which that shadow price stays valid.

    At the optimum the first two constraints are tight. The shadow prices solve $2y_1+y_2=6$, $y_1+y_2=4$. For (c) express $x$ in terms of $b_1$ and keep the third constraint satisfied.

    (a) The first two constraints give $x_1=6$, $x_2=8$; the third reads $6+24=30\le32$, so it is slack. Value $36+32=68$.

    (b) $y_1+y_2=4$ and $2y_1+y_2=6$ give $y_1=2$, $y_2=2$, $y_3=0$ (slack). Check: $20\cdot2+14\cdot2=68$.

    (c) With $b_1$ free: $x_1=b_1-14$, $x_2=28-b_1$. Need $x_1\ge0$: $b_1\ge14$; $x_2\ge0$: $b_1\le28$; third constraint $x_1+3x_2=70-2b_1\le32$: $b_1\ge19$. The binding lower limit is 19 (range $19\le b_1\le28$).

    Problem 3 [10 marks] Dual with an equality and a free variable. $\min\ 3x_1+2x_2+2x_3$ subject to $x_1+x_2+x_3=10$, $2x_1+x_3\ge8$, with $x_1,x_2\ge0$ and $x_3$ free. Write the dual and give its optimal value and the optimal $y_1$ of the equality row.

    A free primal variable gives an equality in the dual: for $x_3$ the dual row reads $y_1+y_2=2$. The equality row gives $y_1$ free; the $\ge$ row gives $y_2\ge0$.

    Dual: $\max\ 10y_1+8y_2$ subject to $y_1+2y_2\le3$ (for $x_1$), $y_1\le2$ (for $x_2$), $y_1+y_2=2$ (for $x_3$, free), $y_1$ free, $y_2\ge0$.

    Substitute $y_2=2-y_1\ge0$, so $y_1\le2$. The first row gives $y_1+4-2y_1\le3$, so $y_1\ge1$. The objective is $10y_1+16-8y_1=16+2y_1$, largest at $y_1=2$, $y_2=0$: value 20, $y_1=$ 2.

    Check with the primal: $x=(0,2,8)$ is feasible ($0+2+8=10$, $2\cdot0+8=8$) with cost $4+16=20$. Equal values prove both optimal.

    Problem 4 [12 marks] Branch and bound. $\max\ 29x_1+20x_2+13x_3+8x_4+18x_5$ subject to $4x_1+3x_2+4x_3+10x_4+7x_5\le24$, $x\in\{0,1\}^5$. Solve by branch and bound with the LP bound from the best value-to-weight order. Explore depth first, always the branch $x_j=1$ before $x_j=0$. Close a node if its LP is infeasible, its LP solution is integer, or its LP value is not above the incumbent. Give the root LP value, the number of nodes created (including the root), and the optimal value.

    Ratios value/weight: $7.25,\ 6.67,\ 3.25,\ 0.8,\ 2.57$ for items 1 to 5. Fill items in decreasing ratio order; the last item may be fractional. The only fractional variable at the root is $x_4$.

    Order of ratios: items 1, 2, 3, 5, 4. Root: items 1, 2, 3, 5 weigh $18$, leaving $6$ for item 4: $x_4=0.6$, value $29+20+13+18+4.8=\mathbf{84.8}$. Branch on $x_4$.

    $x_4=1$: uses $10$, leaving $14$. Take items 1, 2, 3 (weight $11$), leaving $3$ for item 5: $x_5=3/7$; value $8+29+20+13+\tfrac{54}{7}=77.71$. Branch on $x_5$.

    $x_4=1,x_5=1$: uses $17$, leaving $7$: items 1 and 2 fit exactly: integer, value $8+18+29+20=75$. Incumbent $75$.

    $x_4=1,x_5=0$: items 1, 2, 3 fit: integer, value $8+29+20+13=70\le75$: closed.

    $x_4=0$: items 1, 2, 3, 5 fit (weight $18$): integer, value $80>75$: new incumbent. Five nodes in all, optimum 80 (items 1, 2, 3, 5).

    Had we explored $x_4=0$ first the incumbent $80$ would appear at once, and the node $x_4=1$ (value $77.71\le80$) would be closed unexplored: only $3$ nodes. The order does not change the answer, only the work.

    Problem 5 [10 marks] Weak and strong big-M. Three periods with demands $20,30,10$. Production in period $t$ costs $2$ per unit, holding costs $1$ per unit per period, and each period with production has a set-up cost of $60$ ($y_t=1$). Production $x_t\le M_ty_t$. No stock at start or end. (a) The LP bound with $M_t=60$ in all periods; (b) the LP bound with the tight values $M_t=$ demand still to come $=(60,40,10)$; (c) the integer optimum.

    In the LP, $y_t=x_t/M_t$, so a unit produced in period $t$ pays $60/M_t$ of set-up. Compare for each unit the cost of producing it in its own period against producing it earlier.

    (a) With $M=60$ every unit pays set-up $60/60=1$ wherever it is produced, and holding only adds cost, so produce just in time: $2\cdot60+60\cdot\tfrac{60}{60}=120+60=\mathbf{180}$.

    (b) Set-up per unit is $1$, $1.5$, $6$ in periods 1, 2, 3. Demand 1 (20 units) is made in period 1: $20(2+1)=60$. Demand 2 (30 units): own period costs $2+1.5=3.5$ per unit, period 1 costs $2+1+1=4$; choose own, $105$. Demand 3 (10 units): own period $2+6=8$, period 2 costs $2+1.5+1=4.5$; choose period 2, $45$. Total $60+105+45=\mathbf{210}$ (period 2 produces $40$, with $y_2=1$).

    (c) In the IP set-ups are whole. Plans: $y=(1,0,0)$: set-up $60$, production $120$, holding $30\cdot1+10\cdot2=50$: 230. $y=(1,1,0)$: $120+120+10=250$. $y=(1,0,1)$: $120+120+30=270$. $y=(1,1,1)$: $180+120=300$. The minimum is $230$. The gaps are $21.7\%$ for $M=60$ and $8.7\%$ for the tight $M$.

    Problem 6 [8 marks] Finding a violated subtour cut. A fractional point of a six-city symmetric TSP has $x^*_{12}=x^*_{23}=x^*_{45}=x^*_{56}=1$ and $x^*_{13}=x^*_{46}=x^*_{14}=x^*_{36}=\tfrac12$; all other edges are $0$. Every city has degree $2$. For $S=\{1,2,3\}$ compute $x^*(\delta(S))$ and $x^*(E(S))$, and say which subtour constraint is violated.

    $\delta(S)$ are edges with exactly one end in $S$; $E(S)$ are edges with both ends in $S$.

    $\delta(S)=\{14,36\}$ with values $\tfrac12+\tfrac12=\mathbf{1}$. $E(S)=\{12,23,13\}$ with values $1+1+\tfrac12=\mathbf{2.5}$.

    The cut form needs $x(\delta(S))\ge2$ but it is $1$: violated. The edge form needs $x(E(S))\le|S|-1=2$ but it is $2.5$: violated. These agree through $\sum_{u\in S}x(\delta(u))=2x(E(S))+x(\delta(S))$: $6=2\cdot2.5+1$. Adding either constraint cuts off this point.

    Problem 7 [8 marks] MTZ against DFJ. A directed TSP has $n=8$ cities including the depot. A cycle $C$ of $5$ customers avoids the depot. How large can $x(C)$ (the sum of $x$ over the arcs of $C$) be in the MTZ LP, and how large in the DFJ LP?

    Write the MTZ row as $u_i-u_j+(n-1)x_{ij}\le n-2$ and add it around the cycle; the labels cancel.

    Adding the rows over the $|C|=5$ arcs: $(n-1)x(C)\le(n-2)|C|$, so $x(C)\le\tfrac{6}{7}\cdot5=\tfrac{30}{7}\approx\mathbf{4.2857}$. DFJ gives $x(C)\le|C|-1=\mathbf{4}$. MTZ allows a fractional $0.2857$ more on this cycle, so its LP bound is weaker.

    Problem 8 [8 marks] Capacity cut. Four customers have demands $7,6,6,5$ and each van carries $C=10$. For $S$ the set of all four, give (a) $\lceil d(S)/C\rceil$, (b) $r(S)$, the minimum number of vans, and (c) the right-hand side of the two-index capacity cut $x(\delta(S))\ge2r(S)$.

    $r(S)$ is a bin-packing number. Which pairs of demands fit in one van?

    (a) $d(S)=24$ and $\lceil24/10\rceil=\mathbf{3}$.

    (b) Pairs: $7+6=13$, $7+5=12$, $6+6=12$, $6+5=11$ all exceed $10$, so every customer needs a van of its own: $r(S)=\mathbf{4}$, one more than the cheap bound.

    (c) The cut reads $x(\delta(S))\ge2\cdot4=\mathbf{8}$: four vans, each entering and leaving the depot side once. Using the weaker $\lceil24/10\rceil$ would give only $6$.

    Problem 9 [10 marks] Savings. Kaveri Courier has its depot 0 and five customers with demands $d=(4,5,3,6,3)$ for customers $1,\dots,5$ and van capacity $C=12$. Travel costs (symmetric) are below. Run the parallel Clarke–Wright savings algorithm and give the number of routes and the total cost of the result.

    Cost12345
    from depot 07791113
    customer 1–4646
    customer 2–1066
    customer 3–48
    customer 4–4

    Compute $s_{ij}=c_{0i}+c_{0j}-c_{ij}$ for the ten pairs and go through them from the largest. Merge only if both customers are route ends of two different routes and the combined load is at most $12$.

    Savings in decreasing order: $s_{45}=11+13-4=20$, $s_{34}=9+11-4=16$, then $14$ for the pairs $(3,5),(2,5),(1,5),(1,4)$, $s_{24}=12$, $s_{13}=s_{12}=10$, $s_{23}=6$.

    Go through the list. $(4,5)$: loads $6+3=9\le12$, merge into $[4,5]$. $(3,4)$: customer 4 is an end of $[4,5]$, loads $3+9=12\le12$, merge into $[3,4,5]$. $(3,5)$: same route, skip. $(2,5)$: loads $5+12=17>12$, skip. $(1,5)$: $4+12=16>12$, skip. $(1,4)$: customer 4 is now inside the route, not an end, skip. $(2,4)$: same reason, skip. $(1,3)$: $4+12=16>12$, skip. $(1,2)$: both single-customer routes, $4+5=9\le12$, merge into $[1,2]$. $(2,3)$: loads $9+12=21>12$, skip.

    Result: $2$ routes. $[3,4,5]$ costs $9+4+4+13=30$; $[1,2]$ costs $7+4+7=18$. Total 48, a saving of $94-48=46=20+16+10$ over serving each customer separately (cost $94$).

    Problem 10 [8 marks] Reading a log. A minimisation with integer costs prints:

       Node   Incumbent      BestBd     Gap
H     0   1410.0000   1271.0000   9.86%
*    40   1368.0000   1288.5000   5.81%
     95   1342.0000   1301.6000      ?

    (a) What gap is printed on the last row, in percent? (b) What is the smallest value the optimum can still take?

    Use the formula that reproduces the first row: $(1410-1271)/1410=9.86\%$. For (b) use that costs are integers.

    (a) $(1342-1301.6)/1342=40.4/1342=0.0301$, so 3.01%.

    (b) The optimum is at least BestBd $=1301.6$ and, with integer costs, an integer, so at least 1302. It is also at most the incumbent $1342$. The true gap to the optimum is therefore at most $40$ units. The row markers: H means a heuristic found the incumbent, * means branching found it.

    • Write the set-up (variables, sense, the dual's signs, the set $S$) before the numbers.
    • Keep to the minutes-per-mark; at one and a half times the share, move on.
    • Spend the last minutes checking signs and the direction of each inequality.
    • Spending half the paper on a single problem.
    • Erasing working instead of crossing it out: partial marks need to be seen.
    • Stopping at a number without a sentence that answers the question.
    1. Plan the paper: read first, bank short problems early, give each problem time in proportion to its marks and move on at one and a half times its share.
    2. Every problem type has a check: equal primal and dual values, degrees summing to the cut identity, a bound on the correct side of the incumbent, the LP gap shrinking with a tighter $M$.
    3. Practise under the clock: the pace line shows whether you are fast enough, which no amount of untimed reading can.

    A 90-minute paper of 100 marks. You reserve 10 minutes for reading and 10 for checking. How many minutes of working time do you have per mark?

    0.9
    That uses all 90 minutes for working; subtract the reading and checking time first.
    0.7
    $(90-20)/100=0.7$, so a 10-mark problem gets about 7 minutes.
    1.1
    That is more than the total time per mark.

    Halfway through a problem the arithmetic goes wrong and you cannot find the slip. What protects most of the marks?

    Rubbing it all out and starting again silently.
    Work that is erased cannot earn marks.
    Writing a final number that looks plausible.
    An unsupported number earns nothing and may lose method marks.
    Leaving the correct set-up and method visible, stating the result you reached, and moving on.
    Method marks are awarded for the set-up and each correct step.

    In the mock, the LP bound with $M=60$ was $180$ and with tight $M$ it was $210$ against an optimum of $230$. What does this show?

    The bound depends on the solver used.
    An LP optimum is the same for every correct solver; the models differ.
    A tighter big-$M$ gives a stronger formulation: a higher lower bound with the same integer optimum.
    Same integer points, smaller LP region, better bound.
    Tight big-$M$ changes the optimal plan.
    Both formulations share the integer solutions, so the optimum is $230$ in each.

    $\min\ 4x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge6$, $x_1\ge2$, $x\ge0$. What is the optimal value (use the dual)?

    18
    That is the dual value at $y=(3,0)$, which is feasible but not optimal; it uses only one of the two rows.
    20
    Dual: $\max6y_1+2y_2$ with $y_1+y_2\le4$, $y_1\le3$: $y=(3,1)$ gives $20$; primal $x=(2,4)$ costs $8+12=20$.
    24
    That is $6\cdot4$, which breaks the dual row $y_1\le3$.

    $x$ is a quantity with $0\le x\le35$, and $y$ is a binary switch. Which is the best linking row?

    $x\le1000\,y$
    Valid, but the LP bound is far weaker than necessary.
    $x\le35\,y$
    The smallest valid $M$ is the upper bound of $x$, and it gives the strongest relaxation.
    $x\le y$
    This cuts off every feasible value of $x$ above $1$.

    In a maximisation, a node has LP value $12.5$ and the incumbent is $13$. What do you do?

    Branch further, since $12.5$ is fractional.
    A fractional LP does not matter if the node cannot beat the incumbent.
    Close the node: nothing inside it can exceed $12.5$, which is below $13$.
    For a maximisation the LP value is an upper bound on the node.
    Replace the incumbent by $12.5$.
    The incumbent must be a feasible integer plan, and it never gets worse.

    A fractional TSP point has degree $2$ at every city and $x(\delta(S))=1.5$ for a set $S$. Which is right?

    The point is feasible for DFJ.
    DFJ needs $x(\delta(S))\ge2$ for every $S$.
    The cut $x(\delta(S))\ge2$ is violated, and so is $x(E(S))\le|S|-1$.
    The two forms are equal under the degree constraints: $x(E(S))=(2|S|-1.5)/2=|S|-0.75\gt|S|-1$.
    The point violates the degree constraints.
    The statement says every degree is $2$.

    As $n$ grows with the cycle length $|C|=3$ fixed, how do the MTZ and DFJ allowances $x(C)$ behave?

    Both stay at $2$.
    Only DFJ is independent of $n$.
    DFJ stays at $2$, while MTZ rises towards $3$.
    MTZ allows $(1-\tfrac1{n-1})\cdot3$, which tends to $3=|C|$.
    MTZ falls below DFJ.
    The MTZ value $(1-\tfrac1{n-1})|C|$ is never below $|C|-1$.

    Three customers with demands $4,4,4$ and van capacity $6$. How many vans do they need, and what is the rounded capacity cut for their set?

    2 vans, $x(\delta(S))\ge4$
    $\lceil12/6\rceil=2$ is only a lower bound; two demands of $4$ do not fit in a van of capacity $6$.
    3 vans, $x(\delta(S))\ge6$
    Each customer needs its own van, so $r(S)=3$ and the right-hand side is $2r(S)=6$.
    3 vans, $x(\delta(S))\ge3$
    The cut is $2r(S)$, because each van enters and leaves $S$ once.
